The section beginning with "At that time" constitutes the fourth part: Śikhin himself cites what he has seen to resolve the doubts of Śāriputra.

As for why the Brahmā King cites his own vision: followers of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) may doubt the Buddha, wondering who it was that actually saw the Pure Land when he spoke of it. Therefore, the Brahmā King, intuitively knowing the Buddha’s intention, cites what he has seen to testify that the Buddha’s words are not false, thereby universally generating the goodness of faith and belief among the assembled multitude.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the preliminary refutation of Śāriputra’s doubts; second, the formal presentation of what was seen to resolve those doubts.
The first section is easily understood.
From "For what reason? onwards, the second section correctly presents what was seen to resolve doubts.
This text is divided into three parts:
first, the Brahma King sees purity; second, Śāriputra sees impurity; third, the explanation of the reasons for seeing both purity and impurity.

First, regarding the Brahma King’s own account of what he saw, identifying the Heaven of Sovereignty (*Īśvara*) as the category [of gods], there are two heavens both named Īśvara: either the summit of the six desire realms or the summit of the form realm.
This present realm is the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*); its various inhabitants dwell together in a pure land of exquisite and wondrous adornment.

The Western Pure Land is likewise a pure land of cohabitation (*sahābhāva-viśuddhi*). That sūtra also cites the sixth heaven as a point of comparison, hence it says: "Its jewels are like the jewels of the sixth heaven."
However, the primary retribution of the six heavens compared to the bodies in the Western [Pure Land] is like that of a beggar standing beside Śakra;
this is merely citing what is near to illustrate what is far.
"From Śāriputra’s arrival until the fullness" refers, secondly, to Śāriputra describing the filth he beheld.
As the text states:
"From the Śikhin to the Pure"—this third section describes the reasons for not seeing and for seeing.
Because "the minds of you virtuous ones have heights and depths and do not rely on the Buddha's wisdom," they do not see purity.
The Bodhisattva’s mind is without high or low; by being able to rely upon the Buddha-wisdom, one is then able to see purity.
Buddha-wisdom is precisely the cause for seeing purity.
Taking birth-and-death as low and nirvāṇa as high, or alternatively saying that purity is high and defilement is low—because of such views, one sees impurity.
The Buddha’s wisdom is the opposite of this and is thus called "equanimity.

He speaks of defilement where there is no defilement, and speaks of purity where there is no purity; because the characteristics of defilement and purity are not mutually obstructive, the foul land perceived by Śikhin was immediately pure.
Śāriputra perceived a separation between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, and between defilement and purity; because he did not rely on the Buddha’s wisdom, he saw only defilement.
From the words "At this" onwards, the fifth section explains the doubt by means of the Buddha manifesting the pure land.
The text consists of four sections:
first, the manifestation of purity upon the ground; second, the questioning of Śāriputra; third, the response; and fourth, the formal resolution of doubts.
Regarding the first section, its intent is likewise as previously explained through the analogy of the sun and moon.
The "earth" is a metaphor for true cultivation (*bhūtayoga*), while the "finger" represents expedient cultivation (*prāyogikayoga*).
When the true and the expedient unite, the land of response manifests; just as when the finger and the earth meet, the adorned land appears.
Question:
Among the four lands, which land is this? Answer:
There are two interpretations.
First, it is said that this manifests as a pure land of cohabitation; second, it is said that it manifests according to the capacities of sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "the entire great assembly marveled at what they had never before experienced": this was not merely something unseen during the preaching of the *Śrāvaka* sūtras; previously, while the various directions and other matters were extensively revealed as the primary retribution (*pratyaya-phala*), the revelation of the pure land as the secondary environment (*niśraya-phala*) had not been as it is now.
The phrase "and all see themselves sitting upon precious lotus flowers" signifies that this great assembly all possesses the principle of being born in the Pure Land, or will indeed be born there.
"The Buddha spoke of the ultimate purity and adornment": second, the Buddha questions Śāriputra.
As stated in the text:
"From Śāriputra to the manifestation of all. Third, Śāriputra’s response.
This refers to that which was previously said to be unseen and unheard by the followers of the Hīnayāna and the various Vaipulya [Mahāyāna] scriptures.
Below the phrase "The Buddha’s words," section four provides the Buddha’s formal resolution of doubts.
This passage is divided into three parts:
first, the Dharma; second, the parable; and third, the benefits gained by the assembly at that time.
The first part, the explanation by means of the Dharma, is as in the text.
The second part, from "For example" onwards, is the explanation by means of an analogy.
This section consists of two parts:
This consists of the opening analogy and the concluding analogy.
First, regarding the opening analogy: the precious vessel represents the *nirvāṇa-dhātu* (the tranquil light), while the different kinds of rice represent the three lands.
The retributions of the three lands do not transcend the tranquil light; it is by depending upon the tranquil light that their differences are perceived.
"Thus, up to 'adorned'" refers next to the application of the analogy.
Now, ten aspects are used to correspond to the different colors of the rice:

first, regarding those who dwell together, heavy turbidity constitutes defilement (*mala*) while light turbidity constitutes purity; these defilement and purity are separated from one another, such that the defiled do not see the pure.
Second, regarding the "purity with remainder" within the realm of shared cohabitation (*sahā-loka*):

although this realm lacks the heavy turbidity [of the three poisons], it is nonetheless defiled because one is led to rebirth by the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Because these defilements have been severed for a long time within the lands of "remainder," they are termed "pure."
When defilement and purity have not yet merged, defilement does not perceive purity.
Third, regarding the state of having remainder:
when those of the Two Vehicles are born there, that land is inferior, and is therefore termed "defiled."
When Bodhisattvas are born there, because they experience retribution that is both pure and defiled due to their possession of meritorious karma, they do not perceive it as pure.
Fourth, regarding the state of having residual retribution:
in lands where residual [afflictions] remain, ignorance has not yet been destroyed, and thus those lands are entirely defiled.

Regarding those born into the true reward [realm]: having already shattered ignorance, their vision is both pure and defiled; therefore, they do not see purity. Fifth, regarding the fruit-retribution itself:

when comparing the higher and lower levels, the retribution has degrees of excellence and inferiority, which naturally constitute defilement and purity; because it is also defiled, one does not see purity.

Sixth, comparing the retribution lands to the lower *sāmbhogika-kāya* land; seventh, comparing the lower-grade *sāmbhogika-kāya* land to the middle-grade *sāmbhogika-kāya* land; eighth, comparing the middle-grade *sāmbhogika-kāya* land to the upper-grade *sāmbhogika-kāya* land; ninth, correlating all lands collectively with the *dharmakāya* land; tenth, all lands are neither defiled nor pure in the *dharmakāya* land—ultimately there is no teaching of being neither defiled nor pure, yet one speaks of the various lands as defiled and the *dharmakāya* land as pure.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "Although one knows that all Buddha-lands are eternally quiescent like empty space, one manifests various kinds of pure Buddha-lands.
Now, these ten instances of defilement and purity are correlated with the colors of the rice.
Below the section "When the Buddha," part three concerns the benefits gained by the assembly at that time.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the benefit of manifesting purity; second, the benefit of restoring the land.
The manifestation of purity is twofold:

first, five hundred who attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) upon hearing the teaching—this corresponds generally to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), specifically to the first stage (*bhūmi*), and perfectly to the first dwelling (*vihāra*).
Next, eighty-four thousand gave rise to the bodhicitta; the stages of bodhicitta are to be distinguished as previously explained.

"‘The Buddha gathers his supreme intention and understanding’": this next section clarifies that after the foulness has been restored, one awakens to impermanence and attains the path of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
At first, one sees the foul as pure; thus, foulness is impermanent.
When the pure is restored to being foul, it is said that purity is impermanent.

Because impermanence is swift, one attains the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharmanetra-viśuddhi*), clearly perceiving the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths as arising and ceasing; this Dharma-eye of the Hīnayāna pertains to the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) and is not that of the Mahāyāna.
"Eight thousand do not receive [rebirth]" means that having realized the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga), they do not receive the false phenomena of birth and death within the triple world.
Thus, one should know that this sutra still retains the discourse of the "unskillful vehicle" (prādeśikayāna); this is its intended meaning.
A Brief Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Two;
A Brief Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Three. Part One, Minor Scroll Nine.
Compiled by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Zhànrán.
2. Chapter on Expedient Means (3). The Beginning of the Chapter on Expedient Means. *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-lüeshu*, Scroll Nine.

This chapter follows the "Buddha-land" chapter; it is intended to shatter the perception of conditioned co-arising and to reveal the inconceivable Dharma-body, thereby supporting and completing the teaching of the Tathāgata’s Pure Land.
The Great Sage’s intention is manifold; for now, it shall be summarized into three parts:

first, clarifying that this chapter follows immediately after the "Buddha-land" chapter; second, a brief explanation of the meaning of *upāya* (expedient means); and third, an exegesis of the text itself.

Regarding the initial intention: previously, at the *Samantavyūha*, the essence of true-nature liberation was already explained; subsequently, in this sutra, the principle of the causes and effects of the Buddha-land is elucidated. For those who have not yet understood, it is necessary that a superior person such as a Bodhisattva provide instruction and encouragement.

Now, Vimalakīrti dwells in the skillful means of the inconceivable liberation; thus, he is able to assist the Buddha in subduing and gathering those disciples who possess the necessary capacity, causing them to leave behind all conditioned causes and conditions and achieve inconceivable liberation. If their practice in the Pure Land has matured, they will be reborn there according to their karma, each hearing the Dharma in their respective lands to be tamed and disciplined, entering into wisdom and giving rise to the spiritual faculties.
Question:
Since the universal collection of true nature (dharmatā) is derived from the essence of the sutra, how can it be used as the essence of this specific sutra? Answer:
The liberation of true nature (*tathatā-vimukti*) universally constitutes the essence of all sutras; how could it not, by extension, constitute the essence of this sutra?

However, because the text of the "Chapter on the Buddha-land" (*Buddhakṣetra-parivarta*) has not yet explicitly revealed it, it will be clearly explained in various places below; as this does not contradict what was previously stated, it may rightly be taken as the essence of this sutra.
Second, the explanation of the meaning of *upāya* (skillful means) consists of five points:

first, a brief explanation of the name; second, the similarities and differences regarding the teachings; third, the methods employed by skillful means; fourth, the application according to the three karmas; and fifth, the application according to the contemplation of the mind.

First, regarding the brief explanation of the name: "Fang" (方) refers to the specific phenomena that wisdom reaches; "bian" (便) refers to the skillful capacity of expedient means (*upāya-kauśalya*). Because it employs all phenomena to benefit sentient beings according to their individual capacities, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Therefore, the text says: "The Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of the Bodhisattvas; skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) is the father.
There are three types of skillful means, which correspond to the three kinds of twofold wisdom:

first, that for transforming others; second, that for both self-cultivation and transforming others; and third, that for self-cultivation alone. These are fully detailed in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).
Second, regarding similarities and differences, this refers to the four teachings:

First, concerning the three types of two wisdoms of the Buddha according to the Tripiṭaka (Śrāvaka) teaching: for example, in the Abhidharma of the Satyasiddhi school, the illumination of phenomena such as impermanence and suffering is called provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*);
the illumination of the principle (*tattva*) of impermanence and suffering is called true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

The *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) establishes the gate of emptiness by asserting that the phenomena and principles of the Abhidharma are both provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), whereas the illumination of the principle of the truths and emptiness alone constitutes true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*).
Thus, these four gates explain various forms of the two wisdoms according to the needs of sentient beings through the four *saṃgraha-vastu*; all of these are for the purpose of transforming others.

Second, clarifying the two types of wisdom regarding the provisional and the real for oneself and others: the Buddha employs the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold purposes) to expound the aforementioned four gates; these various provisional and real teachings spoken according to the intentions of others are all provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
At the time of sitting upon the site of enlightenment, he realizes the principle of the two truths which is ineffable; this is the real wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) of his own practice.

Third, regarding the two types of wisdom—expedient and ultimate—attained through one's own practice: when sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), the wisdom that realizes conventional truth is fully perfected and distinct, and all obstacles to phenomena (dharmāvaraṇa) are exhausted; this is called the wisdom of expedient practice.

When the principle of ultimate truth is realized with full perfection and clarity, and both active afflictions and residual habits (vāsanā) are simultaneously exhausted, this is called ultimate wisdom.

Second, explaining the three types of two-knowledge (dvividya-jñāna) common to the Buddhas: first, if one explains the three types of two-knowledge according to the *siddhānta* of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*), both the provisional teachings of the specific school and the illumination of illusory phenomena through the gate of existence are termed "expedient wisdom" (*upāya-jñāna*);
the illumination of the principle of illusory transformation is termed "real wisdom" (*bhūta-jñāna*).

If the meaning is elucidated through the gate of emptiness, illuminating the phenomena of illusory transformations is termed provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), while illuminating the principle that the nature of those illusory transformations is empty is termed real wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*); thus, the various provisional and real aspects across all four gates are all the two wisdoms—provisional and real—that transform others.

2. Clarifying the Two Wisdoms of Self and Others: In summary, the three preceding collections (piṭakas) as well as the various provisional and ultimate teachings elucidated within this current teaching are all "speech according to the intentions of others" and thus belong to the provisional wisdom for transforming others. That which is realized within the inner mind of the Buddha and those at the eighth stage is termed "ultimate wisdom."

Third, regarding the two types of wisdom practiced by oneself: for the Buddha and those of the eighth stage, the illumination of the principles of both the ultimate and the conventional constitutes the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real.

Third, regarding the three types of two wisdoms in the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao): first, the three types of two wisdoms from the preceding Treasury (Zang) and Penetrating (Tong) Teachings, as well as the analysis of phenomenal characteristics through the Gate of Existence (You-men) within this teaching, are all considered provisional wisdom; if one illuminates the principle of the Tathāgatagarbha, it is termed real wisdom.

Regarding the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*), the illumination of the phenomena and principles of the gate of existence is termed provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*); the ultimate emptiness and quiescence of the provisional and real within the gate of existence is termed real wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*).

Second, regarding the two types of wisdom—provisional and real—as applied to self and others: the two aforementioned teachings as well as the four gates of the current teaching are all termed provisional wisdom insofar as they accord with others; the principle internally realized by the Buddha and those on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is termed real wisdom.

Third, regarding the provisional and ultimate aspects of one’s own practice: the two wisdoms of the Buddha and those within the ten stages who internally realize the principle of the ineffable true and conventional are called the two wisdoms of the provisional and ultimate.

Fourth, to clarify the three types of provisional and ultimate two wisdoms in the Perfect Teaching: the collective teachings of the previous three vehicles, as well as the "Gate of Existence" (*yu-men*) within this teaching—which involve not severing afflictions while illuminating the various dharma-gates of the Dharma-realm both within and beyond the realms—are called provisional wisdom; that which does not sever afflictions while illuminating the intrinsically pure mind is ultimate wisdom.

Regarding the Gate of Perfect Emptiness (Enkūmon): not severing the afflictions while illuminating the principles of phenomena within and beyond the realms is termed provisional wisdom (gonchi); illuminating that both phenomena and principles are empty is termed ultimate wisdom (jitsuchi).
These four gates, explained through the four *siddhāntas*, show that all various types of dual wisdom are termed "dual wisdom for transforming others.

Second, regarding the clarification of the dual wisdom of self and others: the dual wisdom of the three teachings and the various dual wisdoms within their respective teachings are all "expedient wisdom" (*upāya-jñāna*) in accordance with others; whereas the Buddha and those at the forty-one stages who realize the principle of the inconceivable two truths are all termed "real wisdom" (*tattva-jñāna*).

Third, regarding the clarification of the two types of wisdom in one's own practice: the Buddha and those within the forty-one stages of mind internally realize the principle of the two truths, which are inconceivable; this is termed the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate.
Therefore, when Mañjuśrī requested Vimalakīrti to preach on entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality, the latter remained silent; Mañjuśrī’s praise was intended to convey this very point.

Third, regarding the methods employed by skillful means (*upāya*): when it is argued that all dharmas are neither provisional nor real, yet one speaks of the provisional and the real, these are all instances of the four *siddhāntas* used with skillful artistry to benefit sentient beings. This is the single-voice preaching of the Vaipulya Mahāyāna, which manifests in four different ways according to the various capacities and responses of those who encounter it.

Furthermore, this chapter precisely elucidates the skillful means (*upāya*) that assist the Buddha in propagating the Dharma; by responding to the capacities of sentient beings to benefit them and lead them to give rise to wisdom and develop the faculties, it is called "expedient means" (*upāyakauśalya*).
According to the *Śrīgarbha-sūtra*, there are three types:
first, the refutation of dharmas; second, the establishment of dharmas; and third, the teaching and transformation of sentient beings.
Now, based on this sutra, we shall discuss at length that subduing [the opponent] outside the room is the expedient means for destroying another's adherence to dharmas;
while receiving [them] inside the room is the expedient means for leading others to establish the Dharma.
By means of subduing and receiving, the Dharma is made to endure for a long time; these former two are likewise expedient means for transforming sentient beings.

If we discuss this sutra in its immediate context, the censure of various people in this chapter constitutes the refutation of dharmas through subjugation, while the exhortation to seek the Buddha-body constitutes the establishment of dharmas through gathering; because of this subjugation and gathering, the Dharma is made to endure for a long time.
That the Dharma may endure for a long time means causing sentient beings to enter the true nature, liberation, and the pure Buddha-land.

Therefore, while each chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* clarifies that refutation is the very refutation of dharmas, the subsequent "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths" clarifies the establishment of the Three Jewels, the Four Noble Truths, and the four fruits of the śramaṇa.

Furthermore, the verse concludes by stating: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions—I declare them to be empty. This serves to dismantle and subdue [false attachments to] phenomena; it is also called the provisional establishment of names for the purpose of gathering and sustaining [beings].

"This is also the meaning of the Middle Way. To teach and transform sentient beings so that the Dharma may endure for a long time, and for those who cause the Dharma to endure so that they may see the Buddha-nature and abide in Great Nirvana, the preceding chapter stated: "According to their skillful means, they are able to bring sentient beings to fulfillment; according to the fulfillment of sentient beings, the Buddha-land is purified."
It should be understood that praising the skillful means of Vimalakīrti is, in fact, praising his assistance in propagating the Buddha’s teaching on the inconceivable liberation and the buddha-field.
Fourth, the methods employed are clarified by way of the three karmas.

The reason for this is that the nature of the pure three karmas of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is like empty space; it is neither one nor different and cannot be discriminated. Yet, through the compassionate vows and the responsive manifestations of their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to transform sentient beings, they manifest unspeakably many kinds of physical actions (*kāyakarman*) throughout the ten directions to benefit all within the ten dharma realms. This is the manifestation of the expedient means of the secret of the body (*kāyaguhyaka*).

Furthermore, through compassionate vows and supernatural transformations, they manifest voices identical to all those existing within the ten realms; in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, they demonstrate unspeakably many kinds of teachings. This is the benefit of the expedient means of the secret of speech.

Furthermore, through the compassionate vow and supernatural powers, one manifests a mind that accords with the ten realms; in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, one manifests unspeakably many forms of mental consciousness and various discriminations—this is the benefit of the expedient means of the secret of mind.

In the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings, only the three karmas of supernatural power (*abhijñā*) are clarified; in the *Bie* (Distinct) and *Yuan* (Perfect) teachings, the three karmas manifested by the Dharma-body are also called the "three karmas of supernatural power and transformation. Therefore, the skillful means (*upāya*) are elucidated in terms of these three karmas.

This chapter clarifies that the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) for gathering sentient beings constitute the expedient means of mind-secrecy (*citta-guhyaka*); manifesting various bodies for laypeople and others constitutes the expedient means of body-secrecy (*kāya-guhyaka*); and being seen and honored by all while entrusting illness to propagate the teaching and expound various dharmas constitutes the expedient means of speech-secrecy (*vāk-guhyaka*). These three types of karmic expedient means benefit beings without fixed direction, and their source is unfathomable; they are thus the Three Mysteries (*triguhyaka*), also known as the inconceivable transformation of the three wheels (*tricakra-acintya-vikurvaṇa*), the three things that require no protection (*trirakṣaṇīya*), the three things that need not be guarded (*trirakṣya*), and the three activities that proceed in accordance with wisdom (*trikarma-jñānānuvartin*).

It is because the three karmas of the Dharma-body transform sentient beings without fail; being without deliberation or thought, it is quiescent yet constantly active. It manifests in response within the four lands, displaying body, speech, and mind to subdue, gather, and benefit sentient beings. Thus, while dwelling in the quarters of the principal hall, he manifested illness without actual ailment, thereby awakening others and causing them to transcend the accumulation of conditions to dwell together in the empty chamber.
It is from this designation of the title that it is called the "Expedient Means" (Upāya) Chapter.

Fifth, regarding the contemplation of the mind: if one speaks of the three contemplations according to their distinct characteristics, the first two serve as the expedient means, while entering the Middle Way constitutes true wisdom.

First, entering emptiness from the conventional is the meaning of refuting phenomena and subduing them; next, entering the conventional from emptiness is the establishment of phenomena for the purpose of gathering and sustaining beings; and the correct contemplation of the Middle Way is precisely the teaching and transformation of sentient beings so that they enter true wisdom.
Entering into reality is called the long endurance of the Dharma; when the Dharma endures, the Dharmakāya exists eternally.

If one practices the three contemplations with a single mind, where skillful means and true wisdom are neither identical nor different, one may understand through the mind that the skillful application of these means is clarified by applying the three contemplations across the three karmas.
Question:
By whom was this chapter definitely spoken? Answer:
There are three interpretations of this. One says:
This is the compiler of the sutra praising the virtues of Vimalakīrti and expounding such a Dharma for those who came to inquire after his illness.

Some say: The preceding praise of virtues refers to the compilers of the sutra; the subsequent discourse on the Dharma is the Jewel Accumulation (Ratnakūṭa) spoken by the Buddha, recounting how Vimalakīrti was ill and unable to come, and explaining such a Dharma for those who came to inquire after his illness.
Some say: "The Buddha likewise praised Vimalakīrti for possessing such skillful means of teaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings;
it is likely that this was spoken by the Buddha."
The *Samantaprabhā-sūtra* and the "Buddhakṣetra-parivarta" were intended by [the Buddha] to be elucidated and propagated through the assistance of Vimalakīrti.

Because he was aware from afar of these praises, Vimalakīrti employed the skillful means of feigning illness and came to visit and inquire after him, thereby enabling the teaching to arise. Ānanda, regarding those sūtras not previously heard according to his original vow, requested that the Buddha preach them; when the time for the compilation arrived, they were recited and established following the "Buddhakṣetra-parivarta."

Regarding the six chapters on "Entering the Room" and the passage stating that Ānanda was in the Āmra Garden and everything was entrusted to him, this is also a reiteration for the sake of explanation.
From the words "At that time" onwards is the third section: the word-by-word commentary.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* aids in transformation through nine sections, which are broadly divided into two parts:
first, the half-section praising his virtues, which precisely constitutes the skillful means of benefit through physical manifestation;
second, from the passage "manifesting illness" onwards, which precisely clarifies the skillful means of benefit through vocal instruction.
Form and sound mutually benefit one another; they are merely distinguished as two categories based on their lateral and primary aspects.
First, regarding the benefit provided by form: it serves as the resonance and continuation for the benefit provided by sound. Why is this so?
In this land, the Buddha’s work is performed through sound; therefore, the benefit of sound is preeminent.
This section is divided into two parts:
first, praising his virtues; second, clearly explaining the benefit of his physical form.
The praise of his virtues is divided into two parts:
first, the indication of the location and the person; second, the actual praise of his virtues.
Regarding the first passage, the city is explained as previously described.
"Householder" (*gṛhapati*) refers to one who possesses the virtue of being a leader.
However, the reason only his status as a person is indicated here is that there is a specific purpose intended.
Vimalakīrti and Ratnakūṭa both resided in this city and were originally spiritual friends; yet, while Ratnakūṭa came alone, Vimalakīrti did not come because he was ill.
Because he was ill, I went to inquire after him.
Because I inquired about his preaching of the Dharma, I took advantage of the opportunity to receive his teaching.
Since people have already made inquiries, how could the Buddha, who conforms to worldly etiquette, not send someone to inquire after him?

However, among those who received this command, there were those who were capable and those who were not; those who were not capable numbered five hundred and eight thousand. Furthermore, each recounted their past encounters with the Vimalakīrti to manifest his virtues, and likewise described how he had previously brought great benefit to the needs of the times.
This contains a hidden intention; it is not that they are entirely incapable.
Being capable refers to Mañjuśrī, who, having received the command, entered the chamber to expound liberation, while those who went with him were all fully provided with the benefit of the Dharma.
This is how Vimalakīrti responds to conditions to manifest the Great Dharma, thereby perfecting the merit of the causes and effects of the Buddha-land.
"Vimalakīrti" is explained as before.
As for the "Elder," I shall now provide a brief explanation.
However, as for his original ground, formerly called "Golden Grain Tathāgata," he is none other than the Dharmakāya Elder.
As the *Lotus Sūtra* states, "The great wealthy elder is the Tathāgata," which refers to his manifested traces (*traces*).
Occupying the stage of Dharma-Cloud (dharmameghā) or Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), when viewed from the perspective of a Buddha, one is a bodhisattva—like the son of an elder;
yet when viewed from the perspective of the lower stages, one is an "Equal Enlightenment Buddha"—that is, the elder himself.
Now, briefly stated, there are four types:
first, those who possess ten external virtues are called worldly elders;
second, those who internally accord with the ten virtues of the Dharmakāya are supramundane elders.
Third, regarding the contemplation of the mind, it possesses ten virtues;
fourth, the word-by-word commentary on the scriptural text.

First, as for the external endowments: first, noble nature; second, high status; third, great wealth; fourth, majestic power; fifth, profound wisdom; sixth, advanced age; seventh, freedom from faults; eighth, complete etiquette; ninth, praised by superiors; tenth, venerated by inferiors.
One who possesses these ten virtues is called a great elder (mahā-śreṣṭhin) in the world. Why is this?
Among the eminent persons within a kingdom, those designated as elders are necessarily of noble lineage;
Though one may be of noble lineage, if their rank is lowly, it does not accord with their ancestral prestige;
though one may hold a high position, if they are poor and lack the gift of wealth, they will not be esteemed by the world;
though one’s wealth may be abundant, if they lack favor and authority, others will not stand in awe or reverence of them.
Though one possesses great power, if their spiritual capacity is dark and limited, they will be held in contempt by the wise;
though one possesses divine insight and clear discernment, if they are young in years, the sentiments of the world will not accord with them;
though one is advanced in age and white-haired, if their inner conduct is evil, they will be despised and regarded as strange by others.
Though one’s conduct may be flawless, if one lacks external propriety and etiquette, there will be nothing for others to admire;
though one’s movements may be graceful and composed, if one does not treat superiors with harmony, one’s reputation will not spread afar;
though one may be praised by the wealthy and noble, if one shows no kindness to subordinates, one will not be revered by the world.
If these ten virtues are complete, one is called a great elder (*mahā-śreṣṭhin*).

Second, regarding the internal correspondence of the ten meanings with the ten virtues of the Dharmakāya: the traces of Vimalakīrti reside within the human world, and he possesses the ten worldly virtues; therefore, as recommended by Vaiśālī, he is titled a "Great Elder."

However, its fundamental nature possesses a multitude of virtues that are wondrous and beyond description; to speak briefly, it internally possesses ten virtues, which is precisely the supramundane Dharmakāya Elder.

First, from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, one constantly encounters Buddhas and receives their teachings; through right contemplation of the Middle Way, one gives rise to the wisdom of the principle, which is precisely being born within the lineage of the Dharma King.
Second, by accumulating merit and virtue, one realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Third, one becomes fully endowed with the wealth of the myriad wholesome dharmas.
Fourth, through the ten powers and fearlessnesses, one subdues Māra and overcomes external adversaries.
Fifth, they possess unimpeded mastery over both provisional and ultimate wisdom.
Sixth, having encountered many Buddhas over a long period, their contemplative practice is fully matured.
Seventh, their three karmas follow wisdom, such that they attain the three absences of error.
8. He possesses the majestic deportment of a Buddha, such that his every movement and stillness brings benefit.
9. All Buddhas bestow upon him predictions and praise him with truthful words.
10. He is revered by Śakra and Brahmā, and is honored as the object of their devoted hearts.
The fulfillment of these ten perfections constitutes the perfection of the virtues of the Dharmakāya; therefore, he is named the "Elder of the Dharmakāya.
For this reason, he was able to assist the World-Honored One Śākyamuni in expounding the inconceivable Dharma-gate and manifesting the teachings on the causes and effects of the Pure Land.

Third, regarding the clarification of the ten virtues by way of contemplating the mind: first is the nobility of lineage. This refers to the arising of wisdom through right contemplation that accords with the teachings and accords with reality; this is called the arousal of the mind, being born into the family of the Buddhas, and possessing a truly authentic spiritual lineage (*gotra*).

Second, regarding the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*): when one contemplates the principle of the three truths and the three delusions do not arise, this is precisely the cultivation of the patience of non-arising.

Although it is not yet the contemplative mind of the higher stages, it is nevertheless termed "non-arising. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "If one preaches this sūtra, one should don the robe of the Tathāgata; the robe of the Tathāgata is the mind of gentleness and patience."
This patience is precisely the patience of quiescence; how could it not be termed "non-arising"?
This stage is thus of high rank.

Third, as for being "greatly wealthy": the mind of correct contemplation purifies the three karmas and encompasses the three truths within a single mind and myriad practices, thereby possessing the wealth of the Dharma.
Fourth, as for "power," it means subduing the demons of craving and views through correct contemplation.

Fifth, as for "depth of wisdom," it means that within contemplation, [the ultimate] is taken as the real and the simultaneous illumination [of both truths] as the provisional; thus, the two wisdoms are fully possessed.
Sixth, as for those who are aged, they must have long cultivated roots of goodness before practicing this contemplation.
Seventh, as for those without faults, they correctly contemplate the nature of the mind, so that the three karmas are free from blemish.
8. Regarding the perfection of ritual: from the lifting of the foot to its setting down, there is nothing that is not a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);

even when putting on the *saṃghāṭī*, one does so with single-minded concentration. 9. Regarding the praise of superior persons: those who practice such contemplation are constantly extolled by the Buddhas of the ten directions; thus the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Those who can uphold this sutra bring joy to all Buddhas, who manifest immeasurable spiritual powers and praise the upholders of the sutra."

10. "Respected by Inferior Persons": The *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies that those who practice and uphold this sūtra are honored, respected, and provided with offerings by devas, nāgas, and the fourfold assembly.

One should know that a practitioner of contemplative cultivation, possessing the virtues of pure renown, is equal to a Mahāsattva and is a true son of the Buddha; thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "When a son of the Buddha dwells on this stage, it is the very enjoyment of the Buddha."
"Always remaining therein, whether walking, sitting, or lying down.
Since he enjoys the same as the elder, how could he not be called the elder’s son?
"Having already made offerings" and below, secondly, is the formal praise of his virtues.
This constitutes ten sections explaining the ten virtues, neither more nor less.
Regarding the phrase "making offerings to all Buddhas," these two lines praise the first kind of nature as being truly authentic, just as a worldly elder is noble by birthright.
Now, since Vimalakīrti has encountered many Buddhas and heard the Dharma extensively, he must surely practice according to what he has heard and deeply contemplate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

If he gives rise to the wisdom that realizes the principle, he is "born from the mouth of the Buddha" and "transformatively born from the Dharma. Having obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma, and with the three types of wisdom manifesting the principle such that his nature is in accord with the Dharma-nature, he is called a true son of the Buddha; thus, being born into the family of the Buddha, his spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is truly authentic.
"Deeply planting the roots of goodness" explains the accomplishment of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
"Planting" means sowing; one contemplates ultimate emptiness and sows the seed of great wisdom.
Wisdom is the root of practice; from understanding, practice arises, such that no virtue remains unperfected.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Although all phenomena are empty, a single mind is fully endowed with the myriad practices.
This means that at the initial birth of the Dharmakāya, it is already complete with all virtues.
Regarding the phrase "attaining the patience of non-arising" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti): secondly, it praises the high status of the Dharmakāya, just as a worldly elder holds a high position.

The reason for this is that, according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the first stage (Prathamabhūmi) is fully endowed with the merits of all stages; this principle remains consistent throughout.

Now, regarding Vimalakīrti—also called Golden Grain Tathāgata—it is said that he has already attained the supreme *śānta-nirvāṇa-kṣānti*; alternatively, it is said that his rank is equal to that of a Buddha and he has attained the intermediate *śānta-nirvāṇa-kṣānti*; or it is said that his rank is that of the Dharma-cloud stage and he has attained the inferior *śānta-nirvāṇa-kṣānti*.

If one abides in the middle or lower stages and ignorance has already been severed, such that only subtle habitual tendencies remain and can no longer induce rebirth, this is called "patience regarding non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which signifies a high stage.

The reason it is not designated by the name "patience regarding cessation" (*śānti-kṣānti*) is precisely to reserve that title for the Buddha, while this remains merely "patience regarding non-arising."
"These three phrases, 'Eloquence reaching to the dhāraṇīs,' constitute the third [section], praising the merits of the three karmas.
The virtue of the Dharma-body and the four types of eloquence as the wealth of the Dharma are likewise immeasurable, like the great riches of a worldly elder."
"Differentiating eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) refers to unimpeded eloquence of speech, which can encompass all merits of vocal karma;
"sporting in supernatural powers" (*abhijñā-vikrīḍita*) refers to bodily action, which encompasses all merits of bodily karma;
and "attaining all dhāraṇīs" refers to the various *dhāraṇīs*, which sustain all merits of mental karma as well as all other meritorious treasures of the Dharma.

The two phrases, "attaining fearlessness and subduing the toil of Māra’s enmity," constitute the fourth [point]: praising his external lack of timidity, which is like that of a worldly elder possessing majestic power.

What are they? They are the ten powers (*daśabala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), which subdue Māra and restrain externalists. "Māra" refers to the four Māras, the eight Māras, and the ten Māras, as explained above.

Regarding "the enemy of toil": Māra possesses the power of defilement (*kleśa*), which can harm the Mother of the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Father of Skillful Means (*upāyakauśalya*), and all kinsmen of wholesome dharmas; therefore, he is called the enemy of toil.
"Entering the profound, reaching the sharp and the dull"—these eight lines constitute the fifth section, praising the two kinds of wisdom, just as a worldly elder possesses profound wisdom.
The first four lines are the direct praise, while the latter four lines explain that praise.
"Entering the profound Dharma-gate" praises true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
The principle of the non-dual Dharma-gate is exceedingly profound; it is only the Buddha who has fully exhausted its depths, and therefore it is called the "profound Dharma."
"Skilled in the Perfection of Wisdom" refers to reaching the further shore and bottom of [wisdom], praising true wisdom (*jñāna*).
"Thoroughly penetrating skillful means and accomplishing great vows" consists of two phrases praising expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
"Skillful means of power and wisdom can fulfill great vows; the fulfillment of great vows accomplishes the application of skillful means.
These two phrases, "clearly understanding the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings," explain the praise of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; all who have a mind shall attain bodhi, like a stream flowing toward the sea.
Furthermore, the two phrases "and being able to discern the sharpness or dullness of the various faculties" explain and praise his provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

The faculties of sentient beings differ in being either sharp or dull; that one can skillfully adapt to these capacities to enable them to attain awakening and understanding is precisely what constitutes *upāya* (skillful means).

Regarding the three phrases "having long since [entered] the Supreme Mahāyāna," the sixth point praises the long duration of his practice and his clear realization of the principle, just as a worldly elder is distinguished by his advanced age and long experience.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clearly states that Mañjuśrī has already encountered various Buddhas over long kalpas, cultivating and training for many eons.
This case is likewise; thus, it is said that he is "fully matured.
As for "resolutely [established] in the Mahāyāna," it means that his vision of the principle is clear and distinct, enabling him to roar like a lion.
The "Lion’s Roar" refers to the teaching that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Regarding Buddha-nature, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states that it is none other than the Mahāyāna.

The two phrases, "Whatever they do, they are able to contemplate skillfully," constitute the seventh [point]: praising the three karmas for proceeding in accordance with wisdom and thus attaining the three kinds of non-failure, just as a worldly elder has no faults in his inner conduct.
Why is this? All that is done consists of the three karmas; one must be able to deliberate skillfully upon them.
If one acts first and gains wisdom only afterward, the error cannot be pursued or rectified.

Now, because prior wisdom and subsequent action are without discrepancy and free from error regarding the capacities of beings, the three karmas follow the movement of wisdom and thus attain the three absences of failure.
These two phrases, "Abiding in the Buddha’s majestic deportment with a mind like the great ocean," constitute the eighth section: the praise of both form and mind.

In physical form, his movements and halts accord with ritual propriety; in mind, he is vast and inclusive, free from obstruction—like a worldly elder fully endowed with etiquette yet possessing the magnanimity of a great man.

Furthermore, regarding one who abides in the majestic deportment of a Buddha: like a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage who trains in the Buddha’s lion-like gaze and other such gestures, every movement, whether lifting or setting down the foot, is nothing other than a Buddha-activity.
Some say it refers to being endowed with the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha;
here, however, it means that one can, like the Buddha, remain in the samādhi of neither-arising-nor-ceasing while manifesting various dignified demeanors to universally benefit all beings.
Regarding the phrase "the mind is as vast as the ocean," the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* explains that the ocean possesses eight inconceivable qualities, and the Buddha-dharma is likewise so.
The full passage from that sutra is cited here:

"Now, it is said that the Bodhisattva’s great compassion without object (anālambana-mahāmaitrī) encompasses all beings while the mind remains free from grasping at signs; therefore, it does not increase.
Although one contemplates that all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent, one does not abandon sentient beings; therefore, it is called 'non-decreasing'."

It is like the great ocean: though all rivers constantly flow into it, it does not increase; though parched lands constantly evaporate its water, it does not decrease. Therefore, it is said that the mind is as vast as the sea.
The phrase "the Buddhas praise" constitutes the ninth point, clarifying the eulogies of the Buddhas.
Just as a worldly elder is praised by celestial kings and superior men,
so too is the Great Being, who possesses all virtues and accords with the conditions of sentient beings, extolled by all Buddhas.

The two phrases, "A disciple revered by Śakra, Brahmā, and the lords of the world," constitute the tenth [point]: praising the Great Being for whose internal virtues are fully perfected and who externally serves as a model for teachers; because his grace is necessarily profound, he is held in reverence and admiration, just as a worldly elder is venerated by those beneath him.
"Disciples" refers to the various śrāvakas; "Śakra, Brahmā, and the World Rulers" refers to the lords of the desire and form realms.
Once the lords have turned their hearts [toward the Dharma], there are none among the subjects and people who do not pay them full respect.
Below "desiring to deliver," second, the clarification of the skillful means of benefiting others through physical form.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, indicating the locus of benefiting beings; second, properly clarifying the act of benefiting beings; and third, the conclusion.

Regarding the first point, the elucidation of the location: the Great Being, desiring to assist the Buddha in proclaiming the Great Way and employing skillful means to deliver sentient beings, resided in the country of Vaiśālī; this is the underlying purpose for the introduction of this chapter.
As stated in the text.
Following "wealth and resources," the second section correctly explains the matter of benefiting sentient beings.
This section consists of three parts:
The first six phrases clarify the secret of mind;
second, the nine phrases from "Although he... onwards clarify the secret of body;
third, the twenty phrases from "All... onwards clarify the secret of speech.
The first six phrases concern the gathering of sentient beings through the six pāramitās; these represent the manifestation of traces from the fundamental source.
The subsequent twenty-nine phrases all depict the traces as identical to those of ordinary people, thereby revealing the fundamental source through those traces.
Question:
Why is the secrecy of mind the manifestation of traces, while body and speech are the revelation of the fundamental? Answer:

The principles of the Six Perfections regarding body and mind are profound and obscure; they involve expedient means for transformation and manifest according to circumstances. Thus, in outward appearance, body and speech may seem identical to those of the mundane world.
Yet, if one seeks their ultimate realization, only then will one know that they reveal the fundamental source.
Now, from the initial descent of the trace from the source, the benefiting of beings and the manifestation of the source are both based upon the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

These six perfections constitute the body of the fulfillment of the *pāramitās*, wherein the three bodies and three virtues are neither vertical nor horizontal, like the worldly character "I" (*ī*); thus they are called the "I-character" (*i-akṣara*).

Regarding the phrase "With immeasurable wealth, he gathers in all the poor," the traditional commentaries mostly explain that "wealth" refers merely to worldly riches and silk, and "the poor" refers merely to worldly indigent people.
If this is so, how does this differ from the ordinary practice of giving?
Is it not sufficient cause for admiration that Vimalakīrti manifested his traces with such skillful means to gather sentient beings and lead them to birth in the four lands?

Now, it is said that wealth possesses both the phenomenal and the noumenal; while the phenomenal is easily understood, the noumenal refers to the true principle, which is the wealth of wholesome dharmas. Thus the text says: "The Dharma-King’s Dharma-power transcends all living beings; he constantly bestows the wealth of Dharma upon all."
By bestowing the wealth of the fourfold Dharma-teachings upon all beings, one fulfills the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) within the dharma-realm; therefore, it is called "immeasurable.
Regarding the gathering of the poor, this refers not only to the poor of the mundane world who are gathered through material wealth and then instructed with the Way and its teachings;
here, the term "poor" also refers to those who lack the seven kinds of skillful means.
One should know that all these are the Tathāgata’s skillful means and esoteric teachings.
If they are base, ordinary people or impoverished folk, he gathers them in through worldly wealth and resources, or through precepts and goodness.

If there are those of the Two Vehicles who, like impoverished sons, abandoned their father in their youth to seek food and clothing, he gathers them in by means of the wealth of the dharma of arising and ceasing—the price of a single day’s worth of salt, vinegar, rice, and flour from the Tripiṭaka.

The Two Vehicles may be considered wealthy, yet compared to a Bodhisattva, they are still poor in terms of the wealth of Dharma; thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Reflecting on my own poverty, I thought, 'I do not possess this thing.'"

Although the merits of a Bodhisattva over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are immeasurable, when compared to a Śrāvaka, they are considered wealthy; yet when compared to one who has attained the Bodhisattva path, they are still but poor folk.

One who has mastered the principle of the Truth of Non-arising and possesses the wealth of the various *pāramitās* considers themselves rich, yet compared to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), they are still but poor folk.

The Separate Teaching involves the sequential cultivation of immeasurable truths and principles; though its practitioners consider themselves wealthy due to their immeasurable Dharma-treasures of the various *pāramitās*, compared to the Perfect Teaching, they remain but poor commoners.

In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the principle of the three truths as the unconditioned truth (wu zuo di) brings all the Dharma-treasures of the *pāramitās* to full completion. Possessing this adamantine treasure-store without any deficiency is what is meant by being "wealthy. Therefore, Cunda lamented his own poverty regarding the treasures of the unsurpassed Dharma; only upon attaining the unconditioned (*wu zuo*) does one truly possess the treasures of the unsurpassed Dharma.

The Dharma-body of the Great Being abides in the perfection of *dāna* that is neither stingy nor giving; it can raise the wealth of the four kinds of Dharma-teachings to gather in the seven types of poor people.
Even those whose roots of goodness in the Perfect Teaching have not yet sprouted are considered poor people, such as Cunda.
By means of the four kinds of Dharma-wealth, one gathers in sentient beings and causes them to be born in the four lands; this is the manifestation of traces to lead beings back to the source.

Furthermore, by means of the fourfold Dharma-giving—sudden, gradual, indefinite, and secret—one gathers in sentient beings, perfects their bodhisattva practices, and causes them to be born in the pure lands.

When Vimalakīrti attains Buddhahood, those sentient beings whom he has gathered through the practice of giving will be reborn in his land; thus we know that these words support and complete the preceding chapter, wherein the Buddha taught that giving is a bodhisattva’s pure land, and that all sentient beings capable of renunciation will be reborn in that land.
How could one not take the Buddha-land as the fundamental principle?

If we speak in terms of contemplating the mind, among the fourfold assembly today, are there any who can abide in the three contemplations within a single mind, such that they do not perceive [the distinction between] stinginess and giving, but instead practice compassion to benefit others, rescue the poor and destitute, and joyfully participate in and encourage the performance of meritorious offerings?

If this elder practices giving throughout a village and preaches the Dharma as a result of that giving, those who receive his gifts will feel gratitude and admire his virtue; they will turn their hearts toward transformation and, as their stinginess gradually diminishes, they too will learn from the donor to relinquish wealth and cultivate merit.

If a magistrate or district official abides in right contemplation and practices the giving of material wealth and the giving of the Dharma, then all the impoverished people under their jurisdiction will turn their hearts toward them and receive their transformation; their stinginess will naturally cease, and they will also be able to relinquish their wealth.

Even down to the celestial kings and worldly monarchs who abide in the mind of right contemplation, they no longer perceive stinginess or giving; with loving-kindness for the poor, they bestow gifts through the wisdom of compassion. Because they skillfully expound the fourfold Dharma gates, the fourfold assembly receives their grace, turns their hearts toward the Way, and likewise becomes capable of giving.

It is like a single lamp that kindles hundreds of thousands of lamps; those in darkness all become bright, and the light never ceases. This is how the fourfold assembly, kings, and elders dwell in the Dharma-gate of the inexhaustible lamp of giving (*dāna*) to gather in sentient beings.

All those who have been gathered under their care will, in future ages, once again become their kinsmen; they shall be born together in the Pure Land, encounter Buddhas, hear the sutras, and have their correct wisdom awakened. These donors shall attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment in lands where they have karmic connections. All those previously gathered through their acts of giving shall come to that land to cultivate the paths of the Three Vehicles; if they hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they shall all enter the Buddha Vehicle together.
This is the Great Being Vimalakīrti; where else would he go to Vaiśālī?

"Upholding the precepts with purity to encompass all who violate them": the Dharma-body of Vimalakīrti dwells in neither observance nor transgression, being a body perfected in the three virtues of śīla (ethical discipline). Through skillful means, he is able to encompass all who violate the precepts by means of the ten treasuries of the precepts.

First, one gathers those in the realms of humans and devas through the ten wholesome paths of action and the five precepts. Next, one gathers those who have violated or not violated the precepts through the restraint of the *prātimokṣa*. Next, one gathers those who have violated or who follow the path without attachment through right speech, right action, and right livelihood. Next, one gathers those who have violated or who are praised by the noble ones and possess mastery through the three kinds of right [action] and right [livelihood] that are immeasurable. Finally, one gathers those who have violated or who are fully endowed with concentration through the three kinds of right [action] and right [livelihood] that are unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*).

Since others who have not yet attained [the state where there is] neither upholding nor violating are all termed "corrupted," the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Only the Buddha alone possesses pure precepts; all others are termed those whose precepts are defiled."
"Since these sentient beings have been embraced by the precepts, they fulfill the bodhisattva practice through not violating the prohibitions and accordingly cultivate the goodness of the precepts.

When the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) attains Buddhahood, those sentient beings embraced by the goodness of the precepts will come to be born in his land. As stated in the previous passage: "The upholding of the precepts is a bodhisattva’s pure land; when the bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, those who uphold the precepts will come to be born in his land."

Regarding the contemplation of the mind: now, the fourfold assembly of the Buddha’s disciples—whether noble or humble—can cultivate the three contemplations within a single mind. Abiding in this contemplation of the mind, they do not perceive transgression or observance; through compassion, they benefit all beings and purely uphold the prohibitions. Possessing the virtue of upholding the precepts, they become a refuge for all beings, demonstrating the Dharma-gates to them.

If this elder can cause the sovereign of the Great Continent to observe the fasts and precepts, then the ministers, subjects, and the fourfold assembly of that district, county, continent, and nation will naturally cease their evil and cultivate virtuous discipline; this is transformation through non-speaking.

By cultivating the fourfold path of the teachings through the causes of the four kinds of pure lands, one abides in the *śīla* (precepts) and the Dharma-gate of the Inexhaustible Lamp to gather all sentient beings. Those who are thus gathered will, in future lives, become one's own kin; the rest is as explained in the section on giving.
The four subsequent contemplations of the mind may be understood by analogy with this.

"To subdue conduct through patience and gather in all anger" means that Vimalakīrti dwells in a body perfected by the three virtues of *kṣānti* (patience) that is neither in a state of anger nor in a state of patient endurance; he is able to manifest dwelling in the submission to and accord with non-arising and quiescent extinction, employing skillful means to discipline sentient beings who harbor the four types of anger, so that each may abandon their resentment and accomplish the practice of a bodhisattva.

When Vimalakīrti attains Buddhahood, those sentient beings who were gathered through patience will come to be born in his land to assist in the establishment of that Buddha-land; other points should be understood according to the preceding examples.

Regarding "gathering the indolent through great diligence," Vimalakīrti’s Dharma-body dwells in a body that is neither diligent nor indolent, yet complete. Through the eight types of diligence within each of the four factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), he gathers those who are indolent to be born in his land; the remaining meanings follow the previous analogy.

"Single-mindedly practicing meditative stillness to gather in all distracted thoughts": Vimalakīrti’s Dharma-body dwells in a body of the three virtues that is neither fixed nor distracted; he is able to skillfully employ the four *bodhipākṣika-dharmas*, each with eight kinds of concentration, to gather the four kinds of distracted thoughts, causing them to each attain eight kinds of dhyāna and various samādhis, thereby accomplishing the bodhisattva practices and being born in the Pure Land, as clearly explained in the "Buddhakṣetra-parivarta."

“Gathering all those without wisdom through decisive wisdom”: the Dharma-body of Vimalakīrti abides in the ultimate body of the three virtues of *prajñā* (wisdom), which is neither ignorance nor [ordinary] wisdom; it is well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena while remaining unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Through the eightfold decisive wisdom of each of the four factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*), it gathers the four kinds of sentient beings who lack wisdom, as clearly explained in the "Buddhakṣetra" chapter.

Therefore, Bodhisattvas arise from the six pāramitās of the true original ground of the Dharma-body to manifest the traces of expedient means; they demonstrate the practice of the six perfections to gather in sentient beings, thereby accomplishing the maturation of beings and the purification of Buddha-lands, leading them back to their original ground, and assisting in the establishment of the Buddha’s teaching on inconceivable liberation and the pure land.

The nine matters listed below constitute transformation through wordlessness; this is the secret of the body (*kāyaguhyaka*), wherein one practices on what are not paths, yet through skillful means (*upāya*) attains penetration into the Buddha-way to benefit sentient beings.
The initial statement, "although he appears as a layperson," refers to the manifestation of traces; "yet he practices as a śramaṇa" leads back to the fundamental source.

A śramaṇa is named for being "unattached" and is also called "diligent practice. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "The Tathāgata is the Great Śramaṇa," which refers to the śramaṇas revealed through the four teachings.

The "Vinaya" (Lü) is that which weighs the gravity of offenses; it weighs the lightness or heaviness of the transgressions within the four teachings, all for the purpose of leading sentient beings back to the fundamental realm of tranquil light.
This "teaching through silence" is a subtle censure of those who have left the household life and a subtle exhortation to those who remain at home.

Regarding "secretly censuring," the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Though one may wear dyed robes, the mind is still not yet dyed. This means that because one has not yet been dyed by the Mahāyāna teachings of the four methods (*catur-yāna*), although such a person is outwardly a śramaṇa, they are in truth called a "white-robed one" (*avadāta-vastra*).
As for my secret exhortation: why must one dye one's robes? It is sufficient simply to dye the mind and establish the conduct of a śramaṇa; this is itself the cause for the inconceivable Pure Land.
Is this not the teaching of transforming and perfecting the Pure Land through wordless action?

When Vimalakīrti later attains Buddhahood, the sentient beings he has gathered to be born in his land will all have been brought to maturity through skillful means; thus, the principle of establishing a Buddha-land remains perfectly intact.

However, the "Chapter on the Buddha-land" clarifies that skillful means (*upāya*) constitute the pure land of a bodhisattva; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who are fully endowed with skillful means come to be born in his land—this is merely the formal designation of the title.

Now, Vimalakīrti has manifested illness to give rise to the teaching; those who extol his virtues have set forth twenty-nine matters, opening the beginning of the praise for Vimalakīrti’s skillful means (upāya). Thus, we know that his skillful means are immeasurable.
The meaning of "expedient means" (*upāya*) as presented in the "Chapter on the Buddha-land" becomes manifest precisely in this chapter.

From the perspective of contemplating the mind, even a lay believer (*śrāvaka*) of the present day—whether a householder, a merchant, a regional lord, or a sovereign—if they can sever evil and cultivate good, practicing the threefold contemplation with single-mindedness so that their meditative cultivation remains unstained by various desires and becomes clear and pure, is one who, though a layperson, maintains the conduct of a *śramaṇa*.
The following eight phrases all consist of the first half describing the manifestation of traces and the second half returning to the source.
"Though dwelling in a household, he is not attached to the three realms": since he still shuns even celestial pleasures, how much more so would he avoid residing among humans?
In order to attract the four types of sentient beings, so that they may leave the three realms and be born in the four lands,
there are two ways of classifying the three realms— both broad and detailed— which can be understood by carefully examining them in relation to the four lands.
In all such cases and phrases, one must observe the mind; there is no desire for prolixity, as these can be understood by analogy with what precedes.
"Appearing to have a wife and children while constantly practicing the Brahma-faring" means internally cultivating the four kinds of Brahma-faring and remaining free from the four attachments.

He also subtly censures those who have left the household life and secretly encourages those who remain at home, leading people to accomplish the causes for the four lands through inconceivable practice.

By stating that "one currently possessing a retinue should always delight in seclusion," he practices the four kinds of seclusion, causing all sentient beings to distance themselves from the four bonds and enter the cause of the inconceivable to be reborn in the four lands.

"Though he wears precious ornaments, his body is adorned with the primary and secondary marks. This means that he constantly cultivates the various marks and signs through the four types of patience (*kṣānti*) to adorn the Dharma-body, thereby leading the four classes of sentient beings into the four pure lands.

"Though they partake of food and drink, they take the joy of dhyāna as their flavor. By means of the fourfold path-factors (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), each with eight types of dhyāna-joy, they bring about a wondrous cause that leads them into the four lands.
"If one reaches a place of gambling or games, one immediately uses [the opportunity] to deliver others. "Gambling" refers to betting with dice; "games" refers to chess and similar pastimes.

"Immediately using [the opportunity] to deliver others" means transforming them so that they do not become attached to indeterminate states, agitation, or idleness, thereby wasting the merit of transcending the world. One should cause each person, according to their own faculties and nature, to seek the four kinds of true benefits that transcend the world; this is called "delivering others."
This means causing them to enter the inconceivable liberation and placing them within the four lands.
As for the term "immediate" (chê), it refers to transformation occurring as soon as the capacity [of the recipient] arises, without waiting for an inquiry or request.
Regarding the phrase "accepting various heterodox paths without destroying right faith": although one studies heterodox paths in order to subdue sentient beings, one does not destroy right faith.
If one's internal faith remains undiminished, one should immediately deliver them by means of the True Dharma.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* clarifies that although Pūrṇa was reviled and rebuked when he attempted to convert non-Buddhists, Mañjuśrī manifested in their likeness to go and transform them.

In the past, these various non-Buddhists also encountered Buddhas and heard the Dharma; possessing internal roots of goodness, they were guided according to their capacities into inconceivable practices, thereby establishing the causes for the four lands.

"Though he is well-versed in worldly classics, he always delights in the Buddha-dharma. Here, "worldly classics" refers to the Five Classics and so forth in this land, and to the four Vedas, the eighteen great scriptures, and the medical prescriptions and incantations of the seers in the Western Regions.
One should always delight in the Buddha-dharma, specifically the Buddha-dharma elucidated by the Four Teachings, which guides beings into the inconceivable liberation of the four Buddha-lands.

It is through the secret power of the three virtues in the original ground of the Dharma-body that karma is perfumed; like placing poison in milk as a skillful means to lead sentient beings back to the four lands, they enter the inconceivable Dharma-gate.
Below "All," the third section contains twenty phrases; these constitute the skillful means (*upāya*) of the secret of speech (*vāg-guhya*).
Through the benefit of vocal teaching, this also represents the manifestation of traces to lead sentient beings back to the source.
Regarding the phrase "respected by all who see him," there are two meanings:
first, it means that Vimalakīrti perceives all sentient beings as being identical to the mark of Bodhi and identical to Great Nirvāṇa; for this reason, all revere him.

Second, it means that as the master of transformation, the Great Being bestows grace upon all things; thus, among all classes of beings, there are none who do not receive his bounty, admire his virtue, and recognize his kindness, and so all pay him respect, honor, and make offerings.

Furthermore, he is among the foremost of fields of merit; for even an Arhat of no-more-learning is worthy of offerings, how much more so Vimalakīrti, who uses skillful means to preach the Dharma and transform beings so they return to the fundamental source.
This single phrase runs through the subsequent nineteen phrases.

The reason for this is that if, when the teachings are established through skillful means, sentient beings do not show reverence, how could the guidance and transformation [of others] be far-reaching?

"Upholding the True Dharma and gathering together the elderly and the young": in foreign lands, those of virtuous character are established as "Three Elders" (Sān-lǎo) to maintain the laws of the state; this is the manifestation of his traces.
Regarding the terms "senior" and "junior": not only do humans have seniors and juniors, but all roots of goodness also have degrees of magnitude, which constitutes being senior or junior.

Although these distinctions of seniority and juniority differ, when one discusses their roots of goodness, they do not exceed the four teachings; they respond to the capacities of the four types of faculties and are subsumed within the four lands.

"Whether engaged in all manner of livelihoods or in harmonious partnerships, though one may obtain worldly profit, one does not rejoice. "Harmony" (*xie*) refers to having one's intentions fulfilled; "partnership" (*ou*) refers to obtaining gain.
Although his outward traces are the same as those of ordinary people seeking worldly success, he does not rejoice because he leads beings back to the fundamental source and thus feels no delight.
Ordinary beings harbor affectionate love and delight, and their fetters and delusions shroud the four roots of goodness;

the Great Being leads sentient beings with a mind free from attachment, whereby the objects of attachment are dissolved and the four roots of goodness are awakened, causing them to be gathered and returned to the four lands.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva realizes four merits, three of these are conventional (*saṃvṛti*); practicing these three dharmas to give rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) is called "attaining conventional benefit.

Explaining this to others is called "providing for livelihood" (*jīvikā*). Those who hear it and thereby gain benefit are said to have "harmonious association. The bodhisattva’s constant practice of the cultivation of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is called "non-delight" (*anabhirati*).

"Roaming through the four crossroads to benefit sentient beings" means that he manifests traces identical to those of ordinary people; "roaming the four thoroughfares" signifies roaming through the Four Noble Truths, using the fourfold application of the Four Noble Truths to benefit the four types of sentient beings and lead them into the four lands.

"Entering governance to rectify the True Dharma and rescue and protect all beings": in outward appearance, he conforms to worldly customs by employing both ritual propriety and penal law; yet ordinary people who cling to fixed laws often cause injustice and stagnation.

The Bodhisattva governs and rectifies as a skillful means to protect sentient beings, bestowing or withholding according to need, and thereby employs the four teachings to rescue and uplift them, leading them into the four kinds of Pure Lands. This is not a case of abandoning the Way and mistakenly taking up secular office.

"Entering the lecture halls and debating arenas to guide them with the Mahayana" means that, while manifesting entry into the realms appropriate for ordinary beings and followers of the Hinayana, he employs skillful means to preach the four teachings of the Mahayana and leads them into the four lands.
"Entering various schools to entice and enlighten the ignorant": in his manifested traces, he entered schools to entice and enlighten the ignorant.
"Tóng" refers to the young; "mǒng" refers to those whose emotions and intellect are obscure.
The four kinds of wholesome roots are minute and are obstructed by the delusions of ignorance; because supramundane understanding has not yet opened, they are called "blind.

The Four Teachings guide and lead them to shatter these delusional obstructions, opening the four wholesome roots so that they increase and reach fulfillment, leading them to be born in the four lands.

"Entering brothels to demonstrate the faults of desire": in his manifested traces, he enters brothels to preach that the nine orifices constantly flow with foul and impure secretions, thereby causing them to know the faults of desire.
If the mind of desire ceases, the four roots of goodness will arise.

If one becomes greedily stained by the four dharmas, this is also called lust; yet, by knowing the faults of craving and remaining unstained and unattached through a pure mind, one attains entry into the four inconceivable lands.
Therefore, the text says: "First, one uses the hook of desire to draw them in; later, one causes them to enter the Buddha's wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "entering all wine shops while being able to establish his resolve," this refers to his manifest entry into wine shops.
Alcohol has thirty-six faults; if ordinary people drink it, their spirits become clouded, they lose their way, and all their noble aspirations collapse.
A Mahāsattva is able to establish his own resolve and cause others to establish their practice so that they do not regress, leading them into the four lands.

Furthermore, wine represents afflictions (*kleśa*), while the tavern represents the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Ordinary persons drink the wine of afflictions, whereas those of the Two Vehicles drink the wine of emptiness and signlessness. Because they have not yet disgorged this wine, they conceive the notion of impermanence regarding the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "One holds the vessel of the samādhi of emptiness and is intoxicated by the signlessness of prajñā.
In the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), this is identical to the Two Vehicles;
in the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), one perceives the Middle but has not yet fully realized it, remaining intoxicated by the wine of ignorance.
