Although the Great Being enters into various afflictions, he employs them as a Buddha-work; even if he drinks a thousand vessels of wine, he does not become confused or disordered. Therefore, it is said that he is able to establish his resolve.

"If he is among householders, he is honored as the most eminent among them, and for their sake he expounds the supreme Dharma. From here below, the text praises his sublime and victorious virtues, employing the skillful means of the secret of speech (*vāg-guhyaka-upāya*) to benefit sentient beings.
The Great Being manifests in all forms without distinction between high and low; however, we now specifically cite those who are most exalted in order to fulfill the purpose of extolling his virtues.
Virtue serves as a model for all beings and stands at the pinnacle of the multitude of sages.

Regarding the phrase "the most venerable among householders": because worldly householders are esteemed by their fellow villagers and thus consider themselves noble, the Great Being (Mahāsattva), whose conduct is similar yet whose virtue surpasses theirs, is therefore held in the highest honor.

First, he proclaims the superior dharmas of the conventional world to cause all to submit; next, he accords with the four capacities of beings to preach the four superior dharmas. Since they regard him as their honored one, there are none who do not comply, and thus he leads them to the four inconceivable lands.

"If he is among householders, he is the most honored among householders, severing their greedy attachments. In foreign lands, one who possesses one hundred million in wealth is called a "lower householder," while one with even a billion is called an "upper householder";
in this land, those whose domestic virtue is eminent are likewise called householders.
Now, those who dwell at home and possess great wealth and vast riches are called *gṛhapati* (lay masters), and they constantly harbor thoughts of profit and gain.
Vimalakīrti manifested his superior virtues by showing that although he accumulated immeasurable wealth, his giving was inexhaustible; therefore, he was honored by them.
According to their respective capacities, he taught the four methods of giving (*dāna*) to cause them to abandon greedy attachment and lead them into the Pure Land.
"If among the *kṣatriyas*, he is the most honored among the *kṣatriyas*, teaching them through patience"—*kṣatriya* here means "royal lineage," that is, the great lords of the fields.
Vimalakīrti manifested the supreme virtues of compassion and forbearance, and thus he was held in the highest esteem.
As for teaching through patience: since those of the kṣatriya caste possess sovereign power and often indulge in displays of majesty and severity, he taught them patience.
According to the four types of spiritual faculties, the four teachings reach them, and he preaches various forms of loving-kindness and patience.

"If among Brahmins, he is the most honored among Brahmins, removing their arrogance. Regarding "Brahmin," this is translated as "one of external intent"; it refers to those who have inherited excellent external studies from generation to generation, and is also called "pure conduct."
When Vimalakīrti manifested his traces in the world, those of external paths excelled so remarkably that none could equal him; thus he was held in the highest esteem.

The various Brahmins, relying on their own pure conduct, looked down upon others with pride; yet when they beheld Vimalakīrti’s profound learning and superior Dharma, their arrogance was naturally shattered.
"Based on the four types of faculties, he teaches the four methods of instruction as appropriate, so that each may abandon the notion of a self.

'If among ministers, he is the most honored among ministers; he instructs them with the True Dharma. Among the great ministers of a kingdom, each has their own domain of responsibility, and some may lack clarity."
Vimalakīrti’s traces were identical [to the Buddha's], yet he manifested through his clarity and penetration; thus, he was held in the highest esteem.
The path of governance and the True Dharma rely upon the four types of spiritual capacity, leading even those to be introduced into the four lands.

"If he is among princes, he is the most honored among them, demonstrating loyalty and filial piety. Vimalakīrti manifested himself as one who clearly understands and practices reverence and filiality; therefore, he was held in the highest esteem.

As for the prince, he serves as both a son and a minister; as a son, he must be filial, and as a minister, he must be loyal. Relying upon the four root dispositions and employing the four teachings, one expounds for him the fourfold path of sincere filiality; thus, he becomes a son of the Dharma King in four ways.

To practice in accordance with the four teachings is called filial piety; to propagate the four teachings without sparing one's own body or life is called loyalty; and to lead all sentient beings to enter the four lands is [the ultimate goal].

"If he is among the inner officials, he is the most honored among them, transforming and governing the palace women. According to the laws of foreign nations, those who have been free from sexual misconduct for seven generations and possess virtue are appointed as inner officials; they are entrusted with entry into the palace to manage internal affairs and serve as confidential advisors.
Vimalakīrti manifested his traces as the most supreme and unsurpassed, serving as an object of veneration.

Since the palace ladies were externally constrained, they internally gave rise to perverse thoughts that obscured their latent roots of goodness; the Mahāsattva, responding to their capacities, preached the thirty-two aspects of the Path, enabling them to attain right view and leading them into the four lands.

"If he is among the common people, he is the most honored among them, causing the power of merit to arise. The common people possess little merit; as retribution for this, they dwell in poverty and lowliness, constantly feeling base and inferior, and are cut off from aspiring toward higher stations.
Although this Great Being outwardly manifested a position of high status, he universally loved his subordinates; thus, the common people were moved by gratitude and redoubled their respect for him.

According to their respective capacities and natures, he preached the Four Teachings to them, teaching that through the power of giving and meritorious deeds, they shall be reborn in the Pure Land and attain supreme karmic rewards.

"If he were in the Brahma Heaven, as the most honored among the Brahmas, he would instruct them with supreme wisdom. This is because the eighteen classes of Brahma heavens mostly indulge in attachment to the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables; thus, their entry into these states is not profound.
The traces of Vimalakīrti demonstrate that through contemplation, refinement, and cultivation, he has entered deeply into the boundless; thus, he is honored by all the Brahmās.
For them, he expounds the pure and stainless dhyāna, the skillful wisdom of entering, emerging, and abiding, and according to their respective capacities, he leads them into the four lands.

"If he were among the Śakras, he would be the most honored among the Śakras, yet he manifests impermanence. Because the Deva Śakra is attached to pleasure and knows himself to be sinking into it, while Vimalakīrti is free from desire and pure and lofty, he is thus revered by him.

The Lord of Devas maintained the notion of permanence, so the Great Being expounded for him the fifteen contemplative gates on impermanence, as clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
According to his faculties and nature, he employed the four teachings to respond to conditions; thus, the characteristics of impermanence he taught were likewise not the same.

In the Tripiṭaka teaching, the clarification of impermanence as arising and ceasing possesses a determinate characteristic; in the Shared Teaching, all impermanence is like an illusion or a transformation; in the Distinct Teaching, everything from the stage of the Diamond-like Samādhi downward is impermanent; and in the Perfect Teaching, all dharmas tend toward impermanence, and there is no going beyond this tendency—these four types of doctrinal gates lead into the four lands.

"If they are among the World Protectors (Lokapālas), they are the most honored among the World Protectors, protecting all sentient beings. The Four Heavenly Kings of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings dwell upon the four terraces at the midpoint of Mount Sumeru; each presides over two classes of spirits and deities, ensuring that they do not cause harm to the inhabitants of the four continents.
The Great Being’s traces are identical [to theirs], yet his compassion in protecting sentient beings exceeds theirs; therefore, he is the one honored.

According to their faculties and natures, he preaches the Dharma as appropriate, causing them to give rise to the four kinds of vows, to protect the four roots of goodness, and to cultivate the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths—these are the Four Kings.

Within each of the four truths, there are two classes of spirits—those of view and those of thought—which are summoned and restrained so that they do not disturb the various wholesome mental factors; this is precisely to protect all sentient beings.
By teaching the four doctrines according to the conditions of the occasion, one causes them to protect the true Dharma arising from the four kinds of four truths.
Each of the preceding points is a melodic prelude for drawing beings to be born in the four inconceivable lands; this is deeply understood by those who explain them.
From "The Elder" to "Sentient Beings," the third section concludes the formation of the skillful means.

While residing in Vaiśālī, Vimalakīrti alone, through the skillful means of his three karmas, assisted in manifesting the Buddha-land throughout the ten directions and the ten dharma-realms; how could it have been limited merely to the thirty-five matters mentioned above?
Question:

Regarding what is now called "being honored by the world," does this honor consist in entering many bodies with a single body, or does it consist in being entrusted with birth in various successive existences?

Answer: All these meanings apply; it is analogous to the Universal Gate (Samantamukha) manifesting various bodies. Here, we specifically take up the manifestation of illness to give rise to the teaching.

Because the Elder’s single physical trace can be skillfully employed, everyone shows him respect wherever he appears; by responding to their capacities and transforming them, all receive benefit. One should know that the Elder’s Dharma-body is free from all karmic conditions, yet he manifests in this way for the sake of sentient beings.

The Elder, who was about to realize that his body was fundamentally free from illness, manifested illness as a skillful means for the sake of sentient beings to give rise to the teaching; therefore, it is necessary first to describe the preceding expedients as a prelude.

Summarizing these points, the preceding section establishes the "trace-manifestations descending from the source" as the skillful means (*upāya*) for manifesting the source through forms and sounds to benefit beings.

*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-brief-commentary*, Scroll Ten, Section Two on Skillful Means (Upāya): From the passage beginning with "By means of skillful means" down to the conclusion of the entry into the room, there are eight and a half chapters of text. This constitutes the second major section: Vimalakīrti’s skillful means in manifesting the teaching by feigning illness. It assists the Buddha in propagating the transformation [of sentient beings], leading them into inconceivable liberation (*acintyavimokṣa*), removing the defilements of their transgressions, and introducing them to the four lands (*catur-kṣetra*), thereby perfecting the practice of purifying the Buddha-land.
There are four intentions for feigning illness:

first, to transform kings, ministers, and the common people; second, to initiate the "Chapter on the Disciples"; third, to initiate the "Chapter on the Bodhisattvas"; and fourth, to initiate the "Chapter on Inquiring about the Illness."

As for the initial intention: because he feigned illness, kings and elders all came to offer their condolences; thus, by using his physical ailment as a pretext, he could express his criticisms of them and provide admonitions and exhortations with ease.

If a mind of weary detachment from pleasure arises, one can sever the conditions of accumulation and cultivate the myriad practices; this constitutes the seed for entering the inconceivable liberation and becomes the cause for birth in the Pure Land of Shared Existence with Remainder.
Second, regarding the purpose for initiating the "Chapter on the Disciples": if he did not manifest illness, there would have been no occasion for him to summon his disciples for inquiry.

Had he not issued this summons, how could they have dared to recount what he had previously rebuked, so as to allow those of the Two Vehicles to universally hear of their past attachment to the Lesser Vehicle and their subsequent being rebuked?
There are those who delight in the small and cling to the limited; upon hearing this, their hearts are broken with longing as they aspire to the Mahāyāna.

In the near term, it serves as the scriptural basis for entering the inner chamber and hearing how the inconceivable is produced from the clarified butter (*sarpis*); in the distant term, it serves as the precursor to the matured *sarpis* and *ghṛta* (clarified butter) found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. It is likewise a virtuous condition for producing the fruit of rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Third, regarding the initiation of the "Bodhisattva Chapter": if [the Buddha] did not feign illness, how could the bodhisattvas have been commanded to each recount their past experiences of being rebuked? By doing so, he causes the bodhisattvas of the three teachings to universally abandon the stagnation of their provisional methods, collectively turning toward the perfect and sudden path, thereby establishing the supreme cause for entering the inconceivable liberation and purifying the Buddha-land.

Fourth, regarding the purpose for initiating the "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter: if one did not feign illness, by what means could Mañjuśrī have been summoned into the chamber to discourse on the Way and awaken the minds of sentient beings? It was through this that the disciples' voices came to resound throughout the great trichiliocosm, advancing the bodhisattvas in the practice of the three contemplations, leading them into the path of inconceivable liberation, and establishing the causes for the purification of Buddha-lands.
These four intentions all arise from feigning illness; since the illness is not real, they are called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
The power of expedient means is entrusted to the teaching of the Dharma, which properly belongs to the benefit of sound.
Now, to clarify the intent behind the manifestation of illness by the Vimalakīrti to arouse the teaching, there are four sūtra texts which, when broadly divided, consist of two sections:

first, from here below through the "Bodhisattva Chapter," there are two and a half chapters; these constitute the teaching given outside the room, clarifying the censure, rebuke, and subduing [of the disciples].

Second, from the "Inquiry into the Sick" chapter onward there are six chapters; these constitute the teaching given within the inner chamber, clarifying how to guide, lead, and receive others. Through these causes and conditions, the True Dharma is made to endure for a long time, which is precisely to abide in inconceivable liberation.
The summary [of the text] fully encompasses [the meaning], and the same applies to the contents of that summary; however, there is a distinction between the secondary and primary meanings.
Now, regarding the subjugation (*prahāṇa*) outside the chamber, the text is divided into three parts:

first, this half-chapter clarifies the subjugation of the conditioned collection of conditions within the realm; second, the "Chapter on Disciples" (*Śrāvaka-varga*) constitutes the subjugation of the unconditioned collection of conditions; third, the "Chapter on Bodhisattvas" (*Bodhisattva-varga*) constitutes the subjugation of the collection of conditions of the dharma-realm itself (*dharmadhātu*).
Question:
Is the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) identical to or different from its own essence (svabhāva)? Answer:
Various explanations differ; here, it is said that while their names are distinct, their essence is the same.

The followers of the Two Vehicles are deluded regarding their own essence and give rise to attachment to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); because they are attached to the unconditioned, they receive the name "unconditioned."

The Bodhisattva likewise gives rise to an unconditioned accumulation (asaṃskṛta-samudaya) based on delusion regarding their own essence; yet, while the Bodhisattva contemplates and breaks through this unconditioned state, because this affliction remains attached to the essence as long as the unconditioned is not yet exhausted, it is specifically designated by the name "essence" (svabhāva).

Just as ordinary beings, deluded regarding the truth, give rise to the conditioned and the collection of conditions, so too do those in training—though they have severed views and afflictions of thought—still possess the designation of "stained" by form and formlessness within the true principle.
Question:

A practitioner on the path of training has not yet exhausted conditioned phenomena; although they have attained the vision of reality, they still possess delusions, and thus it is not designated as "self-nature" based on that reality.
Since a Bodhisattva has likewise not yet exhausted unconditioned phenomena yet also attains the vision of reality, why is it specifically designated by the name "self-nature"?

Answer: The Two Vehicles perceive the True [Nature], which is merely the principle of emptiness; because this emptiness is not the Dharma-body, it cannot be designated by the name of a "self-substance.
Bodhisattvas perceive the True [Nature] as the Dharma-body; because the Dharma-body is eternally present, it can be separately designated by the name of a "self-substance."
Because the Bodhisattva’s afflictions have not yet been exhausted, he must undergo subjugation.
This half-chapter is divided into four parts:
first, manifesting illness through skillful means; second, people coming to inquire after him; third, preaching the Dharma on their account; and fourth, the assembly attaining benefit at that time.

Regarding the first passage: by manifesting illness where there is no illness, this signifies that the Dharmakāya is free from the afflictions of cause and effect arising from dualistic conditions; yet, as a skillful means to attract sentient beings, he manifests the two kinds of accumulation of conditions belonging to ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles, as well as the afflictions of cause and effect pertaining to the Bodhisattva’s own being.
Question:
How is this known to be so? Answer:

The subsequent text states: "The illness of the Bodhisattva arises from great compassion; because sentient beings are ill, I am also ill. If sentient beings attain freedom from illness, then I shall be free from illness."

Question: Vimalakīrti’s traces reside in the human realm; thus, he may share the physical ailments of ordinary beings. Internally, he is identical to a bodhisattva and possesses the illness of his own essential nature. Since he is certainly not of the two vehicles, how can he be said to share their illness of non-conditioned existence?

Answer: The Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) dwells in the inconceivable; for those who are to be delivered by means of the bodies of the Two Vehicles, he manifests in their forms and shares in their illnesses.

Furthermore, he manifests the illness of a Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching, sharing in the manifestation of illness with the Two Vehicles, and so forth—this shall be fully distinguished in the "Inquiry into Illness" chapter.
"Because he came specifically to inquire after his illness," secondly, clarifies the inquiry after the illness.
Mañjuśrī is revered by all beings, as previously extolled.
This great assembly has all received his grace; now that he is ill, how could we not inquire after him?
Therefore, all the kings, ministers, and subjects came to inquire after his illness.

Yet, those who came were all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) manifested by Vimalakīrti in this world; they had previously established karmic conditions for the four teachings. As their spiritual capacities were activated and they were moved to respond, they relied upon the occasion of inquiring after the illness as a condition for their arrival. Thus, they came to inquire after his illness.
"Regarding 'those who came before' and below: thirdly, it is for the purpose of preaching the Dharma.
If he did not manifest illness, there would be no means by which to rebuke the various noble clans; even if they were to come, there would be no occasion to censure them."
However, to speak of the faults based on the bodies of others would be difficult; since I myself am afflicted by illness, how could they possibly be free from it?
Therefore, I have used my own illness as a cause to explain this extensively, so that [beings] may develop weary detachment and be exhorted to seek the Buddha-body.
The text consists of three parts:
first, a general introduction to the teaching of the Dharma; second, the actual exposition of the contemplative gate; and third, an exhortation to seek the Buddha-body.
The first part may be understood as it stands.

Next, as for the two kinds of preaching the Dharma, these constitute the general purport of the Buddha-dharma: namely, admonishing one to sever evil and exhorting one to give rise to goodness; by means of this, one accomplishes the karma for the Pure Land.

Furthermore, if one merely exhorts others to cultivate revulsion and abandon evil without exhorting them to seek the Buddha-body, they will fear the mundane world and fall into the two stages [of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha].
If they fall into these two stages, both this sutra and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin) would become treatises for those whose faculties are ruined.
If one relies on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, one will deviate from the Buddha-way.
This present gate of contemplation mostly belongs to the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* [teachings]. Why is this so?

The analogies of the plantain tree and so forth pertain to the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), while the analogies of illusions, dreams, and so forth pertain to the pervasive [consciousness].
From the words "O virtuous ones" onwards, there are two parts: first, the formal exposition of the gates of contemplation.
Regarding this, some masters provide an interpretation in terms of five gates, while others explain it by means of the five aspects of impermanence.
Now, using two gates to clarify the meaning, five types [of cessation] are briefly set forth:
first, according to the two paths of insight (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). How is this known?

The first four lines clarifying suffering pertain to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); the subsequent clarification of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) pertains to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*) as follows: "The first three belong to the path of seeing, the middle four to the path of cultivation, and the final three to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*)."
Now, in encouraging the pursuit of the fruit of Buddhahood, the latter three [foundations of mindfulness] are not required.
Second, regarding the two kinds of foundations of mindfulness:

the four modes of contemplation within the foundation of suffering are the *dharmasmṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness of phenomena in their intrinsic nature), while the teaching on the contemplation of impurity is the *sāmānyasmṛtyupasthāna* (common foundation of mindfulness).
3. In terms of the two practices:
the four practices following "suffering" constitute the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*), whereas that which is called "impurity" constitutes the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanā-caryā*).
4. In terms of the two contemplations.
The four aspects under "suffering" constitute the actual contemplation (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*); if one speaks of impurity, this constitutes the liberating contemplation (*vimokṣabhāvanā*).
Fifth, regarding the primary and auxiliary paths:
the four aspects under "suffering" are the primary path (*mārga*), while the discourse on impurity and so forth constitutes the auxiliary path (*sahakārimārga*).
Through various such pairs of approaches, he extensively instructs, benefits, and gladdens all people.
Now, regarding the intention behind teaching the Dharma by means of these pairs of approaches, it has many paths; briefly stated, there are five modes of cultivation.

First, for the sake of causing those who hear the Dharma to cultivate contemplation with weary detachment and seek the unsurpassed path, if their conditioning factors have not yet been severed, they will be born in a defiled pure land.
Second, if [the conditioning factors] within the realm are severed, they will immediately be born in the land of residual existence (*sopadhiśeṣa*).

Third, if one relies on the Buddha’s wisdom, it is as seen by Śaṅkhakuñjara; thus, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* clarifies that through the power of repentance, karmic obstructions are gradually eliminated, and one perceives the pure and wondrous land within this very body.
4. If one realizes the true non-arising, that itself is the arising of karmic fruition.
5. If one abides in inconceivable liberation, one is then able to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-lands.
When the conditions of sentient beings have matured and he sits at the site of enlightenment, he takes up a Buddha-land according to those he transforms.
Under the pretext of illness, he expounds these two types of contemplative gates and other practices to benefit sentient beings; this is a brief understanding of the general meaning.
Now, regarding the four aspects of the suffering of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), first, the teaching on impermanence involves three matters.

As for "this body is impermanent": the body is acquired by gathering these three matters; the body is merely a provisional designation (*prajñapti*). Because these three matters are impermanent, it is said that this body is impermanent; there is no separate body apart from them.

As the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* states: "At the stage of the *kalala*, there are three things: first, life; second, warmth; and third, consciousness. The inhalation and exhalation of breath is called 'life-span';

that which is neither putrid nor decomposed is designated as 'warmth'; and that which is the mental faculty within this [body] is termed 'consciousness. The integration of these three things is named the *kalala*."

The continuous succession of the arising and ceasing of the three things, continuing even until old age, is all sustained by karma. Ordinary beings do not understand this; they give rise to various afflictions and create manifold karmas. Unaware that [the breath] has ceased and the three things have separated, they pass an entire lifetime in vain, such that regret comes too late.
Now, Vimalakīrti declares this to be impermanent in order to shatter that inversion of regarding things as permanent. Why?
Because the body, composed of the three elements, breathes out and does not return; the body is like rubble—how can life be relied upon?

As for the claim that the body is maintained by warmth and thus exists eternally: fire arises from conditions and ceases when conditions disperse; once the body becomes putrid and decays, how could it possibly exist eternally?
It is only the deluded consciousness, bound by karma, that claims "I" exist eternally; yet when the rope of karma suddenly snaps, the mind immediately transfers to another birth.
One should know that these three matters are all impermanent.
If one can thus awaken to coarse impermanence, one will then be able to abandon coarse objects of perception and contemplate subtle impermanence.
If the mind abides in meditative concentration and perceives the principle of impermanence, one enters the Path of Seeing and is named a Srotāpanna.
If it is according to the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā), the gate of existence, seeing the subtle principle of impermanence is itself the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).
If it is according to the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), the gate of emptiness, one enters emptiness by means of the subtle impermanence; only then is it the Path of Seeing.

Now, according to the perspective of existence (*sat*), one who skillfully cultivates impermanence can destroy the view of a self and extreme views (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and immediately enter the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*). That is to say, by realizing that the sixty-two views—including views of existence and non-existence—as well as all views and cognitions, are all impermanent, one is able to perceive the principle and sever the delusions of vision (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

Thoroughly contemplating impermanence not only severs the view of nihilism, but can also sever latent tendencies; therefore, the Buddha said, "By skillfully cultivating the perception of impermanence, one can sever the defilements of the realms of form and formlessness."
"Absence of strength" means that, in order to establish impermanence, the body—which is merely a conventional designation—depends upon three factors.
If these three factors were strong, nothing could alter its arising and ceasing.
If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) arise, perish, and undergo transformation, one should know that the substance of these three factors is weak and lacks strength.
"Lack of power" also serves to establish impermanence (*anityatā*).

If the body, as a conventional designation (*prajñapti*), possessed power in these three factors, it would be able to resist; however, because conditioned phenomena arise, perish, and transform without autonomy, one should know they lack power.
"Without solidity" means that the essence of these three dharmas lacks any fixed nature.
If they possessed such a nature, they would be like a vajra; how then could they be destroyed by arising and ceasing?
Because these three dharmas, which are merely provisional designations, lack self-mastery, they are destroyed by arising and ceasing; one should know that they possess no solidity.
As the Arhats said in a verse before they wished to compile the Dharma-piṭaka: "The diamond of impermanence arrives and shatters the mountain-king of the Holy Lord."

Regarding the "dharma of rapid decay": it is a provisional designation for the three dharmas whose substance is transformed and weakened, and whose arising and ceasing are swift and urgent; one should know that this body is the dharma of rapid decay.
"It is not to be trusted": this concluding phrase refutes attachment.
If these three aspects of this body were permanent, strong, powerful, firm, and indestructible, then one might calculate them to be permanent.

If one's karma is exhausted without prior appointment with others, then one cannot guarantee that the next breath will follow the outgoing breath, nor can one guarantee that the subsequent thought will follow the preceding thought.
We see before our eyes that worldly people pass away in an instant without self-awareness; how, then, can one reckon them as permanent?
Believing in these deluded sentiments, one excuses oneself for committing evil and fails to cultivate the Path.
"Because suffering arrives and there is no reliance" refers to the teaching according to the gate of suffering.
"Because of suffering" means that because it is impermanent, it is suffering.
Why is this? The body is composed of the three elements and is cut by impermanence.
Furthermore, it is afflicted by the three sufferings, the four sufferings, and the eight sufferings; its suffering is extreme.

Regarding "affliction" (*nāha*): this provisional body, composed of the three aggregates, is constantly oppressed by the nine afflictions and various painful objects; thus, internal suffering is termed "suffering" (*duḥkha*), while external suffering is termed "affliction."
Furthermore, the initial suffering is "suffering" (*duḥkha*), while the intense oppression is "affliction" (*upāyāsa*).

Regarding the phrase "the gathering place of all diseases": the three factors—the provisional body, respiration, and warmth—constitute form (*rūpa*). Within this body, the four great elements of form give rise to the four hundred and four types of physical ailments; within the mind, the four divisions of afflictions give rise to eighty-four thousand mental diseases. Since these physical and mental diseases gather in this provisional body, it is said that "all diseases gather therein."
Furthermore, "being suffering" refers to the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
Because the nature of impermanence is suffering—lacking both protraction and brevity, and lacking lightness or heaviness—it is said to be suffering.
"Being affliction" refers to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
Because adverse conditions destroy happiness, it is called "affliction.
As for "various illnesses," this refers to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Since the body is already subject to four types of suffering, the addition of various illnesses constitutes what is termed the "suffering of suffering."
Question:
There are four types of suffering in general, and there are also four types of specific suffering.

Since specific suffering is identical to general suffering, all four types would then be "suffering-as-suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). Why, then, is illness specifically designated as "suffering-as-suffering"?
Answer:

Because the suffering of birth has already passed, the suffering of death has not yet arrived, and the suffering of old age is slight, it is therefore explained as the "suffering of suffering" (duḥkha-duḥkhatā) with reference to the suffering of illness.
Furthermore, another interpretation states:
Vimalakīrti feigned illness; therefore, he spoke only in terms of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
"That which the wise do not rely upon" concludes the meaning of suffering.
To examine with precise discernment and clearly perceive that there is not even a moment of pleasure within suffering—this is what is called a wise person.
If this provisional body, composed of the three elements, is constantly afflicted by the three types of suffering and possesses not a single moment of happiness, how can it be relied upon?
Thus, the *Śrī-sūtra* says: "The sage constantly regards the body as a source of affliction;
yet the fool cherishes it, never reaching satiety even unto death."
"‘This body reaches non-abiding’—these ten serve as analogies for the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatācaryā*).
Now there are two interpretations:
first, an explanation of the general and the specific; second, a comprehensive explanation of the whole."
Regarding the alternative interpretation: the first five [similes] illustrate the five aggregates individually, while the subsequent five illustrate the five aggregates collectively.

How is this known? The explicit texts of the sūtras and śāstras state: "Contemplate form as like a mass of foam; contemplate feeling as like a bubble; contemplate perception as like a mirage; contemplate formations as like a plantain tree; contemplate consciousness as like an illusion."
Since there is no separate textual correspondence for the latter five [aggregates], it should be understood that they are collectively used as a metaphor for the emptiness of the body.
Question:
To which teaching do these specific metaphors for the five aggregates belong?
If it were the Tripiṭaka, the illusions and phantoms would not be appropriate as metaphors.
If it were the Shared Teaching (Pāryāyika), the bubbles, foam, and plantain trees would not be appropriate as metaphors. Answer:
Regarding the four teachings of the Vaipulya, the various parables are not to be doubted.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the sūtras of the Śrāvakas, for the sake of certain individuals, parables such as those of illusions are taught."
Generally speaking, each [text] has its own school of followers.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, there are instances where the two preceding teachings are cited to explain the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); furthermore, the six similes and ten similes collectively illustrate everything from the five aggregates up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Question:

Since the ten similes, both collectively and individually, all illustrate that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are empty, why do the preceding and following sections not establish the conventional designation of the person (*pudgala-prajñapti*) in relation to the five aggregates, but instead treat them all in terms of the three factors?
Answer: Where else could this be?

At times the Buddha taught that two factors constitute the person, namely name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); at other times he taught three factors as currently employed; at other times he taught five factors, which are the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); and at other times he taught six factors, which are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). All of these appear in the sūtras and śāstras.
Joining and separating according to conditions, responding to capacities with appropriateness, there is no loss of principle.
Now, employing these three matters serves as a convenience for the gate of contemplation.
Next, in a general explanation, these ten metaphors all illustrate the emptiness of the body.

Although other sutras employ the first five similes to represent the five aggregates (skandhas), this sutra states that all ten similes refer to "this body" (*kāya*) and does not specifically use five to represent the five aggregates; therefore, it differs from the former.

Now, these ten similes collectively illustrate both the emptiness of the body and the emptiness of dharmas. Regarding these ten similes, five belong to the Tripiṭaka (Zàng) teaching and five belong to the Shared (Tōng) teaching; this chapter is so designated because it concerns the contemplative gates (guānmén) of both the Tripiṭaka and the Shared teachings.
The five [analogies] of the Tripiṭaka are foam, bubbles, plantain trees, clouds, and lightning.
The five [analogies] of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) are mirages, illusions, dreams, shadows, and echoes.
Question:
How is this known to be so? Answer:
There is a passage in the *Mahā-śāstra* that has already been fully explained above.
Question:
What is the distinction between the froth and so forth, and the mirage and so forth?
Answer: Foam and the like possess this material substance, yet they are merely false and deceptive, easily reduced to emptiness through analysis.
Because people do not realize that the physical body is empty, this is used as a metaphor for it.

Flames and the like appear to exist, yet they lack substantial substance; by using this absence of substance as an analogy for coarse and subtle forms that do possess substance, one comes to know that all phenomena are empty.
Question:
If all phenomena are empty, how can one use emptiness as an analogy for emptiness?

Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states, "The easily understood emptiness is used as a metaphor for the difficult to understand emptiness. Therefore, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) is illustrated by means of six and ten metaphors.
Question:
Since the metaphors such as "bubbles" apply universally to all three vehicles, why are they not considered "Great"?
Since metaphors such as "mirages" also apply to the three vehicles, why are they specifically termed the metaphors of the Shared Teaching?
Answer:
The "blazing fire" and so forth are not intended only for the Three Vehicles; they also serve the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles], and are therefore employed in the Mahāyāna sūtras.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Based on the ālayavijñāna, it speaks of the eight similes such as 'like an illusion'"; the "mass of foam" is not like this—how could it possibly serve as a comparable category?
Now, I shall explain these ten similes as illustrations of the dual emptiness of persons and phenomena.
In the Tripitaka Teaching, there are many similes for the emptiness of persons and few for the emptiness of phenomena;
however, the reason why these two teachings are explained in a blended manner without being strictly separated is precisely because they are taught according to the capacities of sentient beings.

Regarding the statement, "This body is like a mass of foam that cannot be grasped or rubbed": when water is struck by a current, it forms a mass of foam; at first glance it seems to exist, yet if one tries to grasp it, it vanishes.

This body is likewise so: through ignorance, formative forces, and consciousness, it flows and takes refuge in the aggregates of another. Those who are deluded claim it exists, but the wise, when observing it, do not perceive any fixed reality; it is like a mass of foam—there is no foam, there is only water.
This analogy clarifies the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), but the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) has not yet been explained.

Regarding "like a bubble": when a drop of water falls upon the surface of the water, the upper water acts as the cause and the lower water acts as the condition for the arising of a bubble; yet it vanishes in an instant, or is extinguished by contact.
At first glance it appears different from water, yet one knows it as it truly is: apart from water, it does not exist.

The body is also like this: with past karma as the cause and parents as the condition, there arises the bubble of a body; it gradually grows until the conditions are exhausted and it ends, or it dies through the harm of others.
Ignorance consists in asserting that which exists;
yet if one examines it closely, the three factors are empty of a body, and there is no separate body.
"Like a mirage" means that when sunlight is stirred by the wind, a mirage arises in the wilderness.
A continuous succession of flames arises, and the deluded perceive them as water;
yet when sought with careful scrutiny, neither the flames nor the water exist.

This body is likewise: the light of mental consciousness and the movement of the winds of karma grasp at the three other elements, forming an uninterrupted succession that is mistakenly conceived as a self through the failure to understand it as defiled craving.
Through wisdom one fully realizes that not only is the body empty, but even the three factors [of agent, action, and object] are unobtainable; therefore, it is said to be "like a mirage.
This can thus serve as an analogy for the two kinds of emptiness—of birth and of phenomena—which differs from the metaphors of "froth" and so forth found in the Tripiṭaka.
Regarding the phrase "as firm as a plantain tree": from its birth, the plantain tree consists of layers of bark and leaves wrapped one within another, yet it possesses no core reality whatsoever.

This body is likewise so: from the *kalala* stage onward, this provisional body composed of the three elements has nine hundred and ninety layers each of skin, flesh, bone, and marrow; if one examines each of these individually, they are found to be empty and false, incapable of being grasped as substantial.
Just as the succession of inhalations and exhalations continues for hundreds of thousands [of moments], within each individual breath, the body cannot be found.
Momentary consciousness arises and ceases in succession; in each and every moment, a body cannot be found.
Apart from these three factors, there is no separate body. Therefore, one knows that the characteristics of the body are empty both internally and externally, just like a plantain tree.
"This body is like an illusion, arising from perversion," just as when an illusionist conjures up rabbits or horses, outsiders who see them all claim they are real.

The illusionist of ignorance and the illusory phenomena of the formative forces (saṃskāra) conjure up the three bases; seeing the body, one grasps its characteristics and claims it to be definitively real.
If one knows that ignorance does not give rise to the various formations (*saṃskāra*), then the illusory phenomena and the three factors are like an illusion and empty.

As for the statement, "This body is like a dream and a false vision": when the nature of sleep covers the mind, the body lies here while it sees itself traveling there; one says that what is there is real, but upon waking, one realizes it was a dream.

With ignorance shrouding the mind as one lies prostrate, one falsely gives rise to the various formations; through these three factors, one takes conception in a womb, proceeding through all stages up to old age and death, like seeing a body in a dream, reaching everywhere.
Through the awakening of contemplating the mind, one realizes that the illusory body and its three components are empty and non-existent; therefore, it is like a dream.

As for the statement, "This body is like a shadow manifested from karmic conditions": when an object obstructs light, a shadow appears; as the object changes, the shadow changes, and as the object moves, the shadow moves.

When the light of wisdom and principle is obscured by the karma of ignorance, the reflections of the three types of retribution appear; as karma differs, so do the retributions, flowing and changing in manifold ways from birth until death.
If one knows that ignorance, karma, and volitional formations are fundamentally non-existent, and that the three factors of the retribution-body are ultimately empty, like a shadow;
and that "this body is like an echo, dependent upon various causes and conditions"—for an echo arises from the striking together of two objects, such as a sound resonating in an empty valley.

The body is also like this: the internal movement of ignorance is like objects striking one another; karmic formations are like sound; and the three factors within the mother’s womb are like an echo in a valley. Through the conjunction of these three factors, a provisional name for a "body" is formed.

Regarding those things that belong to causes and conditions: ignorance and volitional formations act as the cause, and the empty valley of the mother’s womb acts as the condition. That which is produced by such causes and conditions has no self or other; therefore, it is said to be "unborn," and birth is like an echo.

Furthermore, just as sound is produced when the wind of retribution strikes the seven locations—the lips, tongue, teeth, palate, and throat—so too this sound belongs to a multitude of conditions and cannot be apprehended as a self-existent entity.
The body is also like this; therefore, it is like an echo.
Question:
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* clarifies that each of the eight similes has its own specific object of comparison; why, then, do these five similes in the present sutra all compare the body?
Answer: The intent of clarifying the commonalities and differences between the general and specific [teachings] lies precisely here.

Regarding both the general and the Perfect (Circumstantial) teachings, five, six, eight, or ten analogies may all be applied as common illustrations; as clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, everything from form (*rūpa*) up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is like an illusion or a transformation.

This sutra also applies [to the other teachings], yet the specific meaning of the eight parables is that of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*), such as when the four virtues are matched against the four samādhis to refute the four types of people.
When examined from the perspective of the Perfect Meaning (*pariniṣpanna-artha*), none of these can be fully resolved.

Regarding the statement, "This body is like a floating cloud that changes and perishes in an instant": clouds arise from dragons, being transformations of the qi of yin and yang into various colors; they appear to exist when viewed from afar, yet vanish when one approaches them.

The dragon of ignorance and volitional formations, through the union of the vital energies of the parents, gives rise to a body of provisional designation; from birth until old age, various activities are performed. To the foolish who look from afar, the appearance of a body exists; yet to the wise who observe closely, the body cannot be found.
That which "changes and perishes in an instant" refers to the method in the Tripiṭaka of refuting impermanence to enter into emptiness.
Regarding the statement that "this body is like lightning, not abiding for even a single thought-moment," the meaning of "lightning" is not yet fully detailed.
However, as for the three factors of ignorance, volitional formations, and consciousness, the bodily radiance perishes moment by moment, extinguishing as swiftly as lightning;
this analogy makes the meaning of impermanence even clearer.
Regarding the phrase "this body reaches its transformation," eight sections clarify non-self, examining and dismantling the sixteen views of selfhood through six types of phenomena.

The first five instances concern the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); the next instance concerns the element of space (*ākāśa*); and the second instance concerns the element of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Question:
What is the difference between selflessness (*anātman*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*)?
Answer: The four propositions are not fixed.

First: sentient beings are termed "empty" and the aggregates (skandhas) are termed "selfless. This means that internally they are empty because they are devoid of a person (pudgala), and they are selfless because phenomena (dharmas) lack sovereignty.

Second, the aggregates (skandhas) are called "empty" and sentient beings are called "selfless. Because the aggregates are merely phenomena (dharma), they are termed "empty"; because sentient beings are persons (pudgala), they are termed "selfless."
Third, both are termed emptiness (*śūnyatā*), as in the case of the two kinds of emptiness.
Fourth, both are termed non-self (*anātman*), as in the case of the three kinds of non-self.
In this sutra, the preceding section clarifies the gate of emptiness, which for the most part refers to the two kinds of emptiness.
Now, the clarification of non-self refers to the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Question:
Previously, the practice of emptiness was clarified; one enters emptiness by means of the two teachings.
"Now, is the practice of non-self also twofold?
Answer: "Although the text is a single unit, it may be explained in two ways."
What is meant by this?
To say that there is no master is to be like the earth; if one analyzes and deconstructs the earth until one finds it has no master, this is the "no-self" of the Tripiṭaka.

If one realizes that both the nature of phenomena and the nature of self are all like [the earth], such that the self and all phenomena ultimately do not exist, this is the "no-self" of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
The first five sections are divided into two parts:
first, individual examination; second, collective examination.
The individual examination consists of four sections:
"This body has no master and is like the earth. Now, this shall be explained in two ways:
first, refuting the externalist; second, applying it to internal contemplation.
Regarding the refutation of the externalist, the externalist says:
If there is no self (ātman), how can one bear burdens?
The internal [proponent] says:
If the earth can support mountains, could there not be a self?

Next, regarding internal contemplation: the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā) clarifies that sentient beings are provisional designations (*prajñapti*), while the earth element is a substantial dharma (*dravyadharma*).
The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* clarifies that the earth element is a provisional designation, while the four subtle particles (*paramāṇu*) are substantial.
Now, although there is a distinction between the provisional and the real, both are equally subsumed under the contemplation of suffering, impermanence, and non-self.

It is like the four subtle elements of earth: if one element is the master, then the other three are also masters; if one is not the master, then all three are likewise not masters. One should know that there is no master.
Since external objects do not exist, and internal things composed of the four subtle elements are likewise devoid of a master,
if both internal and external lack a master, how can there be a self within this body consisting of these three factors?
Therefore, it is said that this body has no master and is like the earth.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Invoking Avalokiteśvara* states: "The earth has no nature of solidity. If the earth were to exist, would it have a nature of self, another, both, or no cause?"
"Among the four [extremes], whichever one is adhered to is itself the view of existence (*astidṛṣṭi*).
If one claims that 'this alone is the truth and all else is false,' 'truth' (*satya*) carries the sense of solidity; it is the essence and the master."
If, upon investigation, one cannot find [it], one should know that it is non-existent, even to the point of being neither existent nor non-existent.
If one harbors conceptual attachment toward any of these four propositions, that itself constitutes a substantial nature.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If the mind grasps at signs, or grasps at the absence of signs, it clings to 'self' and 'others.
Not grasping at the four propositions is itself contemplation."
Because it is without a master and without a self, it is said that "this body has no master, being like the earth.
Regarding the statement, "This body has no self, being like fire," an outsider says:
"There exists a spiritual self (ātman)."
How is this known?
Because the body is able to run and produce sounds, we know there is a self.
The internal [opponent] says:
By means of the single phenomenon of fire, one refutes both of these positions. Why?
When fire burns wild grass, it can move east and west; when it burns bamboo and wood, it can also produce sound. Does it also possess a self?
Regarding internal contemplation: fire is composed of two atoms and lacks a fixed nature.
Name-and-form (nāmarūpa) that constitutes the body likewise lacks a fixed nature; if there is no fixed nature, this is precisely non-self (anātman).
Furthermore, the warmth within the body is itself fire. If external fire lacks a self, then internal fire likewise lacks one.
The *Sutra of the Invocation of Avalokiteśvara* states: "Fire arises from conditions; since conditions lack intrinsic nature, they are without self."
The fourfold negation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) may be understood by analogy with the [analysis of] the earth element.
Regarding the statement, "This body is without life-force (*jīva*), being like the wind," the outsider says:
"There is a life-force."
How is this known? If there were no life-principle (*jīva*), how could the continuity [of existence] cease?
The internal [proponent] says:
In-and-out breathing is merely the characteristic of wind; external wind has no life-force, nor does internal wind.
Next, regarding internal contemplation: because the characteristic of wind strikes and impacts, it is light, empty, and moves freely without obstruction within; how could there be any life-force?
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "Inhalation and exhalation are called life-span.

Contemplating these inhalations and exhalations, one finds that when entering there is no accumulation, and when exiting there is no dispersal; they come without a path traveled and go without a track followed, like the wind in space, which cannot be found upon seeking.
Since wind is not life, its cessation is likewise not.
The *Sutra on the Invocation of Avalokiteśvara* states: "The nature of wind is unimpeded.
The fourfold contemplation of wind may be understood by analogy with what preceded.
Regarding the statement, "This body is devoid of a person and is like water," the opponent says:
"Because there is a self (*ātman*), there is a person. How do you know this?"
If the body has no soul, how can it moisten what is below and conform to the circumstances of things?
The internal [opponent] says:
Water can moisten what is below, yet it merely follows the squareness or roundness of its vessel; if water has neither person nor soul, you are likewise so.
Next, regarding internal contemplation: the three subtle elements of water do not possess a fixed nature; that which lacks a fixed nature is not water.

Since the body is composed of these three elements, it likewise lacks a fixed nature; that which lacks a fixed nature is not a person. Therefore, it is said that this body is devoid of a person, being like water.
It is like seeing a reflection in water and saying there is a person; yet, though one enters the water to seek that person, they can never be found.

Regarding the three factors of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one considers the body to be a person. However, by deeply contemplating these three factors, when the characteristic of a body is not perceived, then there is no person.
The *Qing Guanyin* says: "The nature of water does not abide; it only appears to abide when obstructed by the squareness or roundness of a pond or pool—it is not that its nature abides.
Humans are likewise: they receive names according to their dharmas, for there is no fixed nature in a person."
The examination of water by means of the four lines may be understood by analogy with earth.

As for the statement, "This body is unreal; the four great elements constitute its abode," this is a general exposition of the practice of non-self (*anātman*) with respect to the four great elements.
The opponent says:
"If there were no self, we would not see the six sense faculties abiding in dependence upon the body; therefore, we know that a self exists.
The proponent replies:
We observe that the six sense organs abide based upon the four great elements; there is no self upon which they could depend.
If one were to contemplate internally, the body would be designated as a single entity, and a single body ought not to abide in four locations.
If one single self were to abide, then the other three would be bodiless.
If each possessed its own [body], there would be four bodies.
Whether they are identical or distinct, when examined through the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), no body can be found; therefore, one knows that it has no reality.
If one does not perceive a body, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is destroyed.
When the view of a self-identity is destroyed, the sixteen types of speculative views, including the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), are all destroyed.
As for the statement, "This body is empty, being devoid of 'I' and 'mine,'" the second point concerns the destruction of the self by means of the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*).
The outsider said:
"If there is no self (ātman), how can lands, people, and things truly exist?
If these are real, one should know that the self is real."
The internal proponent says:
If that is so, since the object is empty, the self must also be empty.
Just as there is emptiness within the body and external emptiness, the external is the object; because the object is empty, the self is empty.
Regarding internal contemplation, it specifically employs the element of space (*ākāśa*) to dismantle [wrong] views.
Because the four great elements and derived matter enclose empty space, they are conventionally designated as a "body"; apart from space, there is no body.

If both the internal and external are empty, and emptiness itself cannot be apprehended, then the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is destroyed; when the view of a self is destroyed, one is liberated from "I" and "mine.
As for the statement, "This body is insentient, like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles," this third point refutes the self with respect to the seeds of consciousness.
The outsider said:
"If there is no self within the body, how can one know the four seasons?
The insider replied:
Just as grass, trees, tiles, and rubble also undergo transformation according to the seasons through the influence of yin and yang, appearing to possess cognition yet lacking divine consciousness;
so too, although this present body possesses cognition, that cognition has no intrinsic nature, being like grass, trees, tiles, and rubble.
Furthermore, it is reckoned that there is a spirit within the body, and this spirit causes cognition to know.
Internally, it is said:
If the spirit causes cognition, who then causes that cognition?
If the spirit ultimately has no causer, why would it need to cause cognition?
If there is no causer by the spirit, then there is no cognizer; if there is no cognizer, one is like grass, trees, tiles, or pebbles.
Regarding internal contemplation, it refers to contemplating the seeds of consciousness.
Why? Because the body is constituted by the three factors—vitality, warmth, and insentience—and "cognition" (jñāna) is nothing other than consciousness (vijñāna).
If one claims that consciousness cognizes, [we reply: past consciousness has already ceased; because it has ceased, it does not cognize.
Present consciousness does not abide; therefore, it also cannot cognize.
Future consciousness does not yet exist; how could it possibly possess cognition?
Seeking consciousness throughout the three periods of time, one finds it cannot be apprehended.
Since there is no separate cognition apart from the three periods of time, it is said that this body is without cognition, like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles.
Regarding the statement, "This body is without agency and is turned by the power of wind," this refers to the movement of wind, which assists in the deconstruction of consciousness.
An opponent says:
"Because there is a self within the body, it grasps at and performs actions that cause movement and turning."
The internal [opponent] says:
This is not produced by a soul (ātman), but is turned by the power of wind.
According to internal contemplation, when the mind of deluded thought moves, the body within is able to perform actions by depending upon wind.

Thus, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says: "There is wind that can move upward and wind that can move downward. If the mind thinks of going up, it is pulled upward by the mind; if the mind thinks of going down, it is pulled downward by the mind. All movements and actions are performed by the wind following the mind to accomplish every task."
If the channels of the vital energies (vāyu) are not unobstructed, the hands and feet will not function; though the mind may have thoughts, there is no means for movement.
It is like a mechanical device that performs various actions: if its cords are severed, it can no longer act.
"You should know that all these are produced in dependence upon wind.
Now, observing that what depends on wind is neither self nor other, its arising is itself emptiness.
Now, observing that the body is formed by the three factors, it ultimately cannot be apprehended; who, then, is the agent?
From the passage "This body is impure" onwards, secondly, it explains the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to destroy the discursive thoughts of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

If one connects this with what was previously explained, it constitutes the practice of the path of liberation through the shared foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), serving as an auxiliary to the practice of the path.
Therefore, this is not fixed; rather, what was explained previously clarifies the preparatory means for the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Since it is now explained after the Path of Seeing, it refers to the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

If a Bodhisattva enters the Path of Seeing and wishes to advance in cultivation by using the meditation on impurity (*aśubha*) to destroy craving and counteract the various dhyānas, they first employ these four [immeasurables] to destroy the fetters of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). If six categories [of afflictions] are severed, one becomes a Sakṛdāgāmin; whether it be wisdom or abandonment, this is the "non-arising" (*anutpāda*) of the Bodhisattva.
If the nine grades [of defilements] are exhausted, one is an Anāgāmin; this wisdom and abandonment constitute the non-arising of the Bodhisattva.
Now, regarding the contemplation of impurity in relation to the four perceptions, the scriptural text generally conveys this meaning.

Regarding the "four perceptions," they are: first, the perception of the impurity of the body; second, the perception of the impurity of food; third, the perception that the world is not to be delighted in; and fourth, the perception of death.
The first, "this body is impure," refers precisely to the perception of the impurity of the body.
Next, "though provisioned with food and clothing" refers to the perception of the impurity of food.
Next, "this body is a calamity" refers to the perception that the world is not worth delighting in.
Next, "this body is without constancy" refers to the perception of death (*maraṇasaṃjñā*).
Next, the analogies such as "a poisonous snake" collectively illustrate the four perceptions (*saṃjñā*).

Next, regarding the application of these to the four sufferings: from the impurity of this body up to its being provisionally sustained by food and clothing constitutes the suffering of birth (*jātiduḥkha*).
Next, it says "one hundred and one ailments and afflictions," which refers to the suffering of illness.
Next, it says "the dilapidated well," which refers to the suffering of old age.
Next, it says "one must inevitably die," which refers to the suffering of death.
Next, the venomous snakes and so forth are also general metaphors for the four types of suffering.

However, there are two ways to understand these four sufferings: if one says they are "birth itself," "old age itself," "sickness itself," and "death itself," this is an explanation according to principle (*nyāya*), which belongs to the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*), as fully explained previously;
whereas the four sufferings according to phenomena (*vastu*) belong to the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanā-caryā*).
Now, this matter consists of four types of suffering.

Regarding the statement, "This body is impure and filled with foulness," there are five kinds of impurity. If one perceives this impurity by means of following the breath, it is *viśeṣa-labdha* (special mastery); if one perceives it by means of contemplating the breath, it is *sāmānya-vidyā* (universal clarity); and if one perceives it by means of mental visualization, it is the nine notions of repulsiveness and the liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Regarding the statement that birth is suffering: with the exception of the ultimate [purity], all five kinds of impurity constitute the suffering of birth. This body persists until its dissolution;

it is the perception of impurity regarding food, for once food enters the belly, it becomes excrement and filth. Furthermore, impurities constantly flow from all the pores; though one bathes, defilement continues to arise. Though well-fed and finely adorned, one becomes foul and putrid in an instant; both the body and clothing must inevitably return to decay and destruction.
The substance of food is impure, like spittle mixed with vomit; even the thirty-six components all arise from food—this contemplation destroys craving for food.
As for what is called "the suffering of birth," it exists as soon as one is born.
"This body reaches the point of being oppressed" refers to the two sufferings of old age and illness.
Since these phenomena of suffering exist within the world of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of sentient beings, they belong to the perception of the world as being "unpleasant."
Because the primary retribution itself is not to be delighted in, the secondary retribution of the land is likewise entirely not to be delighted in.
Various sufferings of illness arise from the body; one should know that the body is a locus of calamity.

Regarding the "one hundred and one afflictions of disease": when the four great elements are out of harmony, one hundred and one diseases arise; when the four great elements are out of harmony, four hundred and four diseases manifest based upon the body.
All these sufferings of illness afflict the body and constitute calamities and misfortunes.
The fourth division of the suffering of phenomena concerns the suffering of illness.

"This body is like a dilapidated well, pressed by old age": these four perceptions still pertain to the five aggregates of sentient beings; because they are pressed by old age, they are not to be enjoyed.
If one relies on the four types of suffering, this refers precisely to the suffering of old age.
Master Kumārajīva said:
"The 'dilapidated well' (qiūjǐng) is a decayed well, no longer fit for use."
"This body is not fixed and must inevitably die" refers to the perception of death (*maraṇasaṃjñā*); the four types of suffering are precisely the suffering of death.

This body is sustained by the power of karma through the accomplishment of three factors; it is a provisional confluence of causes and conditions, and when these conditions disperse, the body perishes—whether through being harmed by others, or by mountain, sea, sky, or marketplace, none can escape it. Therefore, it is said that one "must inevitably die."
As the Buddha asked a bhikṣu,
"How do you cultivate the perception of death? a bhikṣu replied:
"It will not last seven days.
Some say it will last six days, down to one day, or even half a day.
The Buddha said:
"All these are those who practice the contemplation of death with indolence.
Some say: "One cannot guarantee that the next breath will enter once the current breath has gone out."
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent! This is truly the cultivation of the perception of death.
If one can practice in this way, before long one shall attain liberation and nirvana."
"‘This body is composed of the four elements’" next provides a general analogy for the four perceptions (*saṃjñā*).
The body is like a venomous snake, an empty village, or hostile bandits—objects of dread; thus, the four perceptions are further elucidated.
If categorized according to the four types of suffering, this serves as a general analogy.
This body possesses these four sufferings; like a venomous snake or a thief, it is devoid of any notion of pleasure.
While the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* provides a detailed exposition, the present sutra merely sets forth the outline.
Regarding the term "venomous snake," it is like four venomous snakes placed together in a single basket, each of which is antagonistic toward the others;
the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are likewise.
Furthermore, it is like a venomous snake that, even if nurtured by a person, will bite them when provoked by anger, showing no gratitude for its care.

The four great elements of the body are likewise thus; a practitioner who nurtures them ought to repay their kindness. If even one element rebels and harms the person's goodness, it will cause them to fall into the ocean of suffering from which it is difficult to find a time of escape.
"Like a hostile robber" means that just as one seizes another's wealth and property and harms their body and life, so too are the five aggregates:
dwelling within the body, they plunder one's wholesome wealth and sever one's life of wisdom.
"Like an empty village" means that an empty village has no substance and does not give rise to human affection.
Contemplating the emptiness of the six sense faculties, one should realize there is no essence of a self (ātman) to savor, and thus no defilement should arise.
Furthermore, just as an empty village has no inhabitants, yet is merely a gathering place for malevolent spirits,
one should observe that the collection of the six sense faculties is not only devoid of a self, but is likewise a place where the malevolent spirits of the afflictions gather.
The aggregates (skandhas) are the five aggregates; the elements (dhātus) are the eighteen elements; and the bases (āyatanas) are the twelve bases.
Since the essence of these aggregates, elements, and bases is fundamentally without reality, how could there be a self?
Contemplating the principles of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth is itself the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*); by extensively contemplating these matters, various practices are initiated.
From the words "O virtuous ones" onwards is the third section: the exhortation to seek the Buddha-body.
The text consists of three parts: first, the presentation of the heading; second, the formal exhortation; and third, the concluding exhortation.

Regarding the initial presentation of the heading: ordinary beings cherish their bodies and remain submerged in the cycle of birth and death. Having already extensively explained the gates of contemplation and the reprimands [against such attachment], they may instead seek the extinction of the Buddha-seed through the Two Vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha) out of weary detachment. Therefore, it exhorts them, saying: "One should delight in the Buddha-body."
Question:
Regarding this exhortation to seek [enlightenment], what teaching’s Buddha-body is being referred to? Answer:
It is difficult to determine definitively whether this refers to the two teachings as skillful means, or to the eternally abiding body of the Buddha.
How is this known?
The fruit is fundamentally a recompense for the cause; since you have already spoken of skillful means, you should instead encourage the pursuit of abiding in the fruit of Buddhahood with remainder.

Or, if it is to encourage the pursuit of the eternally abiding fruit, since all people loathe this body as an impermanent aggregate of suffering, they should be encouraged to seek the eternal bliss of Nirvana; how could one possibly encourage them to seek the extinction like ashes under the King of Trees?
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The body of the Tathāgata arises from reality.
Question: If one is exhorted to seek the eternal fruit, why is the gate of skillful means (upāya-mukha) explained?
Answer: As the Buddha replied to the Brahmin’s question in the *Mahā-sūtra*:
“In your doctrine, the cause is eternal, while the fruit is impermanent.”
"Why is it that in my Dharma, the cause cannot be impermanent while the fruit is permanent?

For if members of the noble families and the common people are all still bound by fetters, how could they enter into the provisional and exercise supernatural powers without first severing delusions through the gate of expedient contemplation and entering emptiness?
Furthermore, one cannot open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through the single mind of emptiness and the provisional;
thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Since these sentient beings have not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, and death, by what means could they understand the wisdom of the Buddha?"
Question: By what means is meditative concentration (samādhi) determined? Answer:

In the Vaipulya Mahāyāna, what prevents a single voice from being explained as a universal exhortation? Since it accords with the various capacities through which beings are moved, it cannot be definitively determined.

Furthermore, considering that the responses elicited by the various flavors differ, we can infer from the present case of the Vaipulya—that its four causes yield two kinds of fruits. Thus, the exhortation given here may either be a response to the two previous contemplations by citing the fruits of the two Buddhas, or it may represent different understandings of the single voice according to their respective root-natures, wherein they look toward the fruit and cultivate the cause.
Question:
Why are there four kinds of Buddhas, while there are only two kinds of nirvāṇa? Answer:
The Buddha distinguishes them based on the application of wisdom, rather than treating *nirvāṇa* as being solely a matter of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
As it is said:
"Skillfulness and clumsiness are two ways of crossing; the recovery from illness is one."
Furthermore, it opens up *nirvāṇa*, which is not something unattainable;
the teaching lacks explicit textual passages.
Regarding the section beginning with "Why is this so?", there are two parts: first, the explanation, and second, the formal exhortation.
However, there are four types of *dharmakāya*.

According to the Tripiṭaka, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) constitute the *dharmakāya*; at other times, it may also refer to the truth of partial emptiness, as in the *Saṃyukta Āgama* and the *Dhyāna Sūtra*, which states: "If heavy hindrances obstruct dhyāna, one should contemplate the *dharmakāya* of the Buddha; the *dharmakāya* is emptiness."
"When the Buddha descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the fourfold assembly pressed forward in eager anticipation to see him, yet Subhūti sat upright in his stone chamber and beheld emptiness.
The Buddha said to Utpalavarṇā:
'Subhūti sees emptiness; this is seeing my Dharma-body.'"
The Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) correctly takes the union of true wisdom with the principle of *dharmatā* as the *dharmakāya*.

At times, it refers only to the principle of partial emptiness (*śūnyatā*), as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "You should contemplate emptiness; the dharma of emptiness is the Buddha, for emptiness has no coming or going."

In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the Middle Way itself is taken as the Dharma-body of the Buddha; merit and wisdom constitute the Reward-body (bāoshen); and because the Dharma-body and Reward-body are unified, there is the Response-body (yingshen).
In the Perfect Teaching (yuánjiao), the distinction lies solely in the fact that the Dharma-body is manifested through non-interruption.
Regarding the phrase "born from immeasurable merit and wisdom," this is precisely an exhortation to aspire toward the fruit by practicing the cause.
Through the causes of merit and wisdom in the *pitaka* and *āgama* [teachings], one brings forth the fruits of merit and wisdom.
The merit and wisdom within the fruit are themselves the Dharma-body; therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] is born from immeasurable merit and wisdom.

In the Separate and Complete Teachings, merit and wisdom manifest the Buddha-nature, and thus that which is manifested is taken as "birth. However, both merit and wisdom consist of the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*) and the practice of conduct (*caryā-caryā*).
The Bodhisattva resolves to seek the Dharma-body; from these two dharmas, they cultivate two practices, and when these two practices are perfected, the Dharma-body manifests.
