Regarding the statement, "It arises from precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation": the *saṃskṛta* (conditioned) and *asaṃskṛta* (unconditioned) precepts constitute the body of precepts (*śīla-kāya*). The fundamental pure meditations, cultivated through training and refinement, constitute the body of concentration (*samādhi-kāya*). The contemplation of the four truths of arising and ceasing, up to the realization of the four truths at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), is called the body of wisdom (*prajñā-kāya*). The total exhaustion of both active and residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) is called the body of liberation (*vimukti-kāya*). The clear knowledge and vision that the active and residual habit-energies are already exhausted, that precepts, concentration, and wisdom are fulfilled, and that one will not receive further existence, is called the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-kāya*).

The fivefold division of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*) is as follows: regarding precepts, as previously explained, because neither transgression nor non-transgression can be apprehended, it is called the aggregate of precepts (*śīla-skandha*);
regarding concentration (*samādhi*), as previously explained, being neither distracted nor savoring [meditative states] is called the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*);

regarding the contemplation of the four truths of non-arising, from the realization of truth by the *aṣṭamaka* up to the perfect culmination of the realization of truth at the stage of Buddhahood, is called the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*).

From the initial stage of the Ground of Seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*), one is liberated from the delusions of views and enters the higher stages; continuing until the time of sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), when the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the wisdom of single-moment correspondence are entirely exhausted, one abides in *nirvāṇa with remainder*, which is called the "Body of Liberation" (*vimukti-kāya*).

One clearly perceives neither bondage nor liberation, yet through the Buddha-eye of the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one personally sees that one abides in *nirvāṇa with remainder* as being free from the bondage of seeds, and enters *nirvāṇa without remainder* as being free from the bondage of fruits. Furthermore, seeing that sentient beings are fundamentally without bondage or liberation, yet perceiving their liberation, is called the "Body of Knowledge and Vision of Liberation" (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-kāya*).

The Separate Teaching (biejiao) takes the ninefold precepts as the body of morality (śīlakāya), the ninefold meditations as the body of concentration (samādhikāya), and the ninefold wisdoms as the body of insight (prajñākāya); this is set forth in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
The exhaustion of habitual tendencies outside the realms constitutes the body of liberation;

the manifestation of the Dharma-body through the thorough knowledge and vision of the Buddha-eye of all-encompassing wisdom, as well as the unconfused perception of the sequence and stages of the appearance and disappearance of the Dharma-bodies of others, is called the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is, for the time being, no different from the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*).

To distinguish them: to be able to accomplish the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) without severing the ordinary person’s physical body (*skandha-kāya*) is precisely the inconceivable fivefold Dharma-body; it is like a mountain as vast as Mount Sumeru not obstructing a mustard seed.

Regarding those who wish to know the cultivation of the causes: upon hearing the two preceding practices, when one feels weary of and detached from the world such that unwholesome thoughts do not arise and wholesome states spontaneously emerge, this is called the cultivation of the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*);

when one single-mindedly cultivates the practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is called the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*); and when one single-mindedly cultivates the practice of wisdom (*prajñā*) by taking principle as its object, it is called the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*).
When the primary and auxiliary practices are unified, one subdues and severs afflictions according to one's capacity; this is called the body of liberation.
To discern the six stages of identity without overstepping or confusion is called the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
By means of these five bodies, one gives birth to the Buddha-body.

Regarding the phrase "arising from compassion, mercy, joy, and equanimity," this refers to the practice of the four truths—both with and without arising—as applied to the general treasury [of teachings]. By taking the four immeasurable minds as the object of focus, one gives birth to the great compassion of the Dharmakāya, the fruit of Buddhahood.
The Separate Teaching employs the practice of the four immeasurables based on the four truths with measure, taking as its object the four immeasurable minds that have conditions.

The Perfect Teaching employs the four truths of non-fabrication, practicing only the four immeasurable minds that are without conditions; both result in the Buddha-fruit, which is the Dharma-body and the great compassion without conditions.

If one begins their practice with wisdom, that wisdom enters into emptiness; by taking sentient beings as its object, it causes them to attain happiness and be free from suffering. To rejoice in this while forgetting one's own self is precisely the cultivation of the four immeasurable minds, which can give rise to the great compassion of the Dharma-body.

Regarding the phrase “from giving up to the arising of the pāramitās,” the four teachings and six perfections are as previously explained; therefore, it is clearly evident that the four teachings and six perfections give rise to the four Buddha-fruit bodies of fulfillment. The meaning is manifest and self-evident.

Regarding the term "various," it may be expanded from six to seven, ten, or a hundred; or expanded to eighty-four thousand, and even to the unspeakably unspeakable. Therefore, it is said that "the various pāramitās arise."

If one wishes to know how those who first resolve to practice the six perfections do so: the performance of various wholesome deeds constitutes the cultivation of the five perfections, while the practice of wisdom constitutes the cultivation of *prajñā*.
Regarding the statement, "From skillful means up to the arising of the three types of clear knowledge," each of the four teachings possesses three kinds of skillful means, as previously explained.
Because the Dharma-body of the stage of fruition arises from the skillful means of the cause, it is said to "arise from skillful means.

Regarding "arising from the six supernormal powers": the five supernormal powers of the Tripiṭaka masters are attained through the cultivation of refined practice based on the fundamental pure dhyāna-vision; the untainted supernormal powers are attained through the cultivation of wisdom-practice regarding the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing.

The Bodhisattva achieves the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) during the causal stage; by cultivating the untainted powers (*anāsravābhijñā*) through the wisdom of the four noble truths of arising and ceasing, they fulfill the thirty-four moments of mind and thereby possess the six supernormal powers of the Dharma-body at the stage of fruition. Therefore, it is said that [the powers] arise from the six supernormal powers.

Regarding the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*): the five supernormal powers are, for the time being, the same as those in the Tripitaka.

When one cultivates the untainted supernormal powers (*anāsravābhijñā*) based on the four truths of non-arising (*anutpāda-satya*), they are either five or six within the mind of a Bodhisattva; they are six because the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) have been severed, and five because the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been exhausted.
Now, because one employs the six causes to attain the six supernatural powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) of the resultant stage, it is said that they arise from the six.

Regarding the Distinct (Bie) and Perfect (Yuan) [teachings]: the Distinct school refers to cultivating and perfecting the six supernatural powers within the three lands outside the triple world; at the first stage (bhūmi), one partially attains the six supernatural powers of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). The distinction between the Distinct and the Perfect is merely a matter of whether these are severed or not severed.

Regarding the "three types of clear knowledge" (trividyā): in both the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings, the threefold penetration is taken as the basis for clearly perceiving the events of the three periods of time, which constitutes the three types of clear knowledge.

As for the distinction between the *Tongming* (Shared Clear Knowledge) and others: generally speaking, seeing distant matters is termed "penetration" (*tong*), while seeing their fundamental source is termed "clear knowledge" (*ming*).

In the causal stage, a bodhisattva practices both types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*): through the practice of wisdom (*prajñā*), they cultivate untainted clear knowledge (*anāsrava-vidyā*). Upon realizing the fruit, they attain the threefold clear knowledge of the Dharma-body at the stage of Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] is born from the threefold clear knowledge.
Regarding the Separate and Perfect [teachings], both involve penetrating the dharmas of the three periods of time beyond the realms as the "three types of supernormal knowledge" (trividyā).

As the subsequent text states, "The three types of supernormal knowledge are equal to ignorance," this refers precisely to the three types of supernormal knowledge of the inconceivable Perfect Teaching.

"Born from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, born from tranquility and insight. As previously explained, the factors of enlightenment according to the four teachings are cultivated by each of the four teachings respectively;
because they realize the fruit of Bodhi, it is called the Dharma-body.
The categories of the Path (mārga-varga) all pertain to the practice of wisdom within the specific teaching.
As for the arising of śamatha and vipaśyanā, śamatha and vipaśyanā are themselves the causes of meditative concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā).
Taking principle as the object is the practice of wisdom; taking phenomena as the object is the practice of conduct.

The four teachings each cultivate the causes of phenomenal and principle *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, thereby realizing the fruits of the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*—namely, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Therefore, it is said that they "arise from *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
As for the statement that they "arise from the ten powers up to the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*)," these three categories of dharmas are the merits inherent in the fruition.

The illumination of internal wisdom is called "power" (*bala*); the absence of timidity in external application is called "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*); because the eighteen qualities belonging to the stage of Buddhahood do not share in common with the dharmas of lower stages, they are called "unshared" (*āveṇika*).
These three are all based on the merits of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*).

As for the statement that they arise from these three dharmas, it refers to the fact that within the causal stage of the four teachings, one employs these two practices to cultivate these three dharmas; therefore, it is said that they "arise from" them.
For the Separate and Perfect Teachings, this can be understood by reference to the realm beyond the world (*lokottara-dhātu*).

"It arises from severing all unwholesome dharmas and gathering all wholesome dharmas. Regarding this, the bodhisattvas of the four teachings each employ the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*) to sever views and afflictions (*kleśa*), and the practice of conduct (*caryā-caryā*) to sever ignorance; this is termed "severing the unwholesome."

The practice of wisdom gathers the principle of conditioned phenomena as wholesome dharmas, while the practice of conduct gathers the phenomena of conditioned things as wholesome natures; these give rise to the four dharma-bodies, wherein all evils are eternally severed and all virtues are universally assembled.
However, regarding the two teachings of Distinct and Perfect, there are differences in their analysis of what is severed and what is accumulated beyond the triple world.
"Arising from reality" and "arising from non-negligence": in the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings, one contemplates arising as non-arising; entering into the limited truth is termed "reality."
The separate and perfect teachings contemplate the immeasurable and the unconditioned, entering the Buddha-nature of the Middle Way; this is termed "the real.

When the Bodhisattvas of the four teachings reach the ultimate in their contemplation of the true, they realize the fruits of the four Buddhas; therefore, it is said that [the latter] arises from the real.
Regarding the arising of non-diligence: if a bodhisattva at the stage of the four wisdoms (prajñā-caryā) regresses while contemplating true conditions and phenomena, this is called negligence.
If, while practicing with wisdom, one contemplates principles such that the mind-moments continue in succession without abandoning great compassion, this is called "great negligence."
Heedfulness is the characteristic of non-retrogression.
Because the mind and mental factors are quiescent and naturally flow [into liberation], it is said that it "arises from heedfulness.
The statement, "The body of the Tathāgata arises from such immeasurable pure dharmas," is an exhortation by citing a broad category.

However, Vimalakīrti uses this as a point of exhortation: since the gateways of the Dharma are immeasurable, they must all be cultivated and accumulated based on what precedes them; therefore, it is said that these various merits are born from such immeasurable pure dharmas, and they all give rise to the body of the Tathāgata.

When a single sound is preached, each according to their kind understands it; thus, the categories of cause, effect, and practice elucidated by the four teachings employ the four *siddhāntas* to reach sentient beings according to their capacities and benefit them, so that all may universally receive, practice, and obtain their benefit.

As for those who seek to study this, if they can carefully grasp the two types of teachings from the preceding five sections—encouraging the emulation of the fruit by practicing the cause—then this sutra will not have come in vain.
"O virtuous ones, [you should] give rise to the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*. Third, this is the summary exhortation.

Since it is known that the merits of the Buddha-body are such as these, arising from various superior causes, if one desires to seek the fruit by practicing the cause, how could it stop at mere self-benefit? A Great Being, feigning illness, assists the Buddha in promulgating the teaching precisely for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.

Virtuous ones, if you are able to aspire to the fruit and practice the cause, you should likewise follow the example of the Buddha and Vimalakīrti in order to sever the illnesses of all sentient beings.

As previously explained, the "illnesses of sentient beings" refers to the illnesses of the causes and effects—both conditioned and unconditioned—possessed by ordinary persons, the Bodhisattvas of the Six Perfections, and the Bodhisattvas of the Two Vehicles and the Shared Teaching; as well as the illnesses of the causes and effects inherent in the self-nature possessed by the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct and Complete Teachings.

Therefore, now each of the four teachings, according to their respective understandings, should sever [delusions] and seek the unsurpassed path; this constitutes the fulfillment of the intention to transform others.
"Thus, up to the bodhicitta" (the fourth section) clarifies the benefits obtained by the assembly at that time.

Vimalakīrti, according to the capacities of sentient beings, employs the two gates of admonition and exhortation; by means of the four *siddhāntas*, he accords with the conditions of the four types of faculties. Since his teachings are without error, it is said that he preaches the Dharma as is appropriate.
"Causing countless people to all resolve their minds" refers to the arousal of the four kinds of bodhicitta.

According to these four conditions, the path-mind develops in each case; this is what is meant by "universally receiving, practicing, and obtaining its benefit. This is the unique quality of spiritual power (*asādhāraṇa-dharmatā*).
The arousal of the bodhicitta according to the four teachings is fully detailed in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) of the Four Teachings.

*Tiantai Śramaṇa Zhànrán’s Abridged Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, Fascicle 11, Chapter 3: Disciples (4–5), Part 1.

This chapter follows the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāya-paṭala*) because it serves to refute [the notion of] unconditioned causes and conditions for the accumulation [of merit], thereby establishing the teaching for purifying the Buddha-land.
As previously stated, the underlying intent is manifold and cannot be fathomed by ordinary beings.
Now, I shall briefly provide a general explanation of this chapter using three points:

first, clarifying the purpose for which this chapter appears; second, providing a brief explanation of the meaning of "disciple" (*śrāvaka*); and third, entering the text for a detailed interpretation.

The initial intention is that the Great Sage, out of compassion, desires to enable sentient beings to attain the inconceivable dharma-body of liberation as their primary retribution, and the pure Buddha-land as their environmental retribution.

However, the transformation of sentient beings must necessarily depend upon the presence of karmic affinity. Vimalakīrti had long since established the superior karma of Bodhi with beings in this Sahā world; thus, anticipating the Buddha’s intention, he first used his illness as a pretext to preach various teachings, thereby supporting and completing the doctrine of liberation and the Buddha-land.

Now, as I lie ill and reflect in silence, my heart’s intent is that the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, might deign to inquire after me; if he were to entrust his final instructions to his disciples, I would certainly decline to speak of the matters concerning my past censure, so that what the Tathāgata has taught may be clearly established.
Now, to clarify the underlying intent, five layers are briefly set forth: first, to manifest the supreme wisdom of Vimalakīrti;

second, to cause the fourfold assembly to abandon the Lesser Vehicle and aspire to the Great Vehicle; third, to support the accomplishment of the Buddha-land; fourth, to subdue the followers of the Two Vehicles and establish the *amṛta* (deathless) teaching; and fifth, to provide a seal of authentication for the completion of the sutra.

The initial intention is this: if one instructs the disciples, one must recount past events in one's speech. If the great assembly hears this, they will immediately conceive of Vimalakīrti as someone beyond measure, thereby increasing their reverence and compliance;
if deep faith arises within them, they will then be capable of hearing the teaching on the Pure Land spoken in the inner chamber.
Regarding the second intention: Śrāvakas who have realized the fruit have not yet been able to turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], just as lotuses do not grow on high plateaus or dry land;
however, those who have not yet entered the stages, though they may delight in the Hīnayāna, will certainly resolve upon the Great Mind upon hearing of the matter of being rebuked.

As it is said, when the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was being preached, there were those who had not yet entered the stages of realization; they relinquished their robes for upholding and made offerings to the Tathāgata, immediately giving rise to the Great Mind. The Buddha then emitted light and conferred upon them predictions of enlightenment; this also universally opened the Great Way for the fourfold assembly, benefiting immeasurable beings.

Why is this? In the past, when [the Buddha] rebuked others, those who heard it were few; for example, his reprimand of Upāli brought mental purity to only two bhikṣus, and his reprimand of Aniruddha caused these ten thousand Brahmās to resolve upon Bodhicitta. However, if one were to reach this assembly, the entire multitude would hear it, and the benefit would be immeasurable; therefore, each must recount the matter of being rebuked.

Regarding the third intention: it is intended to show that the reprimands administered to the followers of the Two Vehicles in the past are identical in intent to the present doctrine of the Buddha-land. How is this known?

Because sentient beings fail to see the Pure Land due to their own transgressions; it is as Śāriputra himself described regarding Vimalakīrti’s past efforts to shatter his attachment to the Lesser Vehicle, causing each to despise the small and aspire to the Great. Thus, the fault of clinging to the Small was gradually eliminated, and the mind aspiring to the Great was secretly awakened.

Now that I have been granted a seat here and, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, am able to hear this teaching, my heart is as if I were one of the five hundred disciples; thus I have entered the inner chamber to hear the inconceivable, and the lands of King Lamp, Fragrant Accumulation, and Akṣobhya all appear before my eyes.

Regarding the fourth meaning: as in the initial opening of the Sudden Teaching, there were only those with great capacities; those with small faculties and heavy defilements derived no benefit from it, which is likened to milk.

Next, the Tripitaka Teaching arose, opening up the three vehicles through skillful means; followers of small faculties thereby severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), transcending the state of ordinary beings to become sages—this is like transforming milk into curds.

Next, hearing the Great Being’s rebukes from the past, up to the sound of his entering the chamber shaking the trichiliocosm, one then despises the small and yearns for the great; as faith gradually transforms, this process is like the production of ghee from milk.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "After this, their minds will accord with one another in essence, and they will enter and exit [the teaching] without difficulty.

When one reaches the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it transforms into mature ghee (*sarpis*); upon entering the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it becomes clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
This is a reiteration of what was previously refuted, serving as the reason for the production of the *sūtra*.
Question:

If each of the five hundred [disciples] individually recounted the virtues of Vimalakīrti as the reason for entering the room and producing the *sūtra*, then this must belong to the introduction (*nidāna*) and not to the formal exposition (*dharmadeśanā*).
Answer: If it were established that [the *sarpis*] is formed only upon entering the chamber, how could it be exclusively so?

It may have been formed previously when hearing various Vaipulya sūtras, such as those refuted by Aṅgulimāla; or it may have been formed at the time of that former refutation, or when hearing them restated now, or upon reaching the chamber, or later when discussing the various Vaipulya sūtras. Since it is formed during all such times, how can it be definitively asserted that the formation of *sarpis* occurs only upon entering the chamber, thereby making it a subordinate element belonging to the Introduction (*nidāna*) section?

If the reason for using the *yūsō* (ghee) as the introduction is that it serves as the cause for entering the room, then the reason for returning to the Āmrapālī Garden would likewise constitute an introduction.

Regarding the fifth point: Vimalakīrti, in the past, moved according to the capacities of beings and rebuked them wherever he was; yet, had he not been commanded by the Buddha, how could the great assembly have heard this together and received its certification from the Tathāgata, thereby benefiting the fourfold assembly during the periods of the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the Final Dharma?
Question:
Regarding these refutations of the Śrāvakas, how many of each of the three contemplations and four teachings are employed? Answer:
It fully employs the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).

First, the refutation proceeds from the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) into the contemplation of entering the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), employing the three teachings of the Mahāyāna to refute the Tripiṭaka.
Second, there is a brief explanation of the meaning of "disciple" (*śrāvaka*).

This consists of nine points: first, a brief explanation of the meaning of the term "disciple"; second, an explanation of the ten types of disciples; third, a general correlation with the mental factors (*caitta*); fourth, a specific correlation with the ten mental factors; fifth, clarifying the adornment of the twin trees; sixth, clarifying birth in the land of retribution; seventh, clarifying the purification of the Buddha-field; eighth, an analysis according to the contemplation of the mind; and ninth, clarifying the sequence of the questions and answers.

Regarding the initial intention: the teacher possesses the capacity to mold and perfect, while the student possesses the virtue of being a recipient of instruction. As for the recipient, they leave their father to follow the teacher and revere the teacher as a father; the teacher, in turn, practices humility and treats the recipient as a younger brother. Thus, the Master said, "Hui treats me as a father, and I treat Hui as a younger brother."
"Now, those such as Śāriputra have received instruction from the Buddha; thus, they are both teacher and disciple, and are therefore called 'disciples' (śrāvaka).
Question:

The Buddha is the compassionate father of all sentient beings, and all sentient beings are his children. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: 'This triple world is now all mine; the sentient beings within it are all my children.'"
"Is this not established according to what the Master has formulated? Answer:
"The sūtras have two meanings: some establish names based on the underlying principle, while others adopt designations in accordance with worldly convention."
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "When I was a crown prince, Rāhula was my eldest son; now that I have attained the Buddha-way, he receives the Dharma and is my son by Dharma.
This refers to the principle that, both in the mundane and the supramundane, all are father and son.

If one conforms to worldly convention, it is like our Master: while seeking to propagate the gateway of the teaching in accordance with worldly custom without dispute, his mind does not deviate from the true Dharma; therefore, there is no fault in explaining names based on external meanings.
Question:
If that is so, then since this applies to all laypeople as well, why is it mentioned only in relation to śrāvakas? Answer:
In general, this is indeed so; however, in specific cases, it is not.

Although worldly people may occasionally come to receive the Way, since their physical forms remain within the secular framework—serving their parents and their sovereign—how could they possibly attend upon [the teacher] morning and night to constantly receive his instruction?
The Bodhisattva constantly cherishes the benefit of sentient beings; when there is an opportunity, he responds to it without being restricted solely to the Buddha’s side.

The Śrāvaka leaves home to become an internal member of the retinue; understanding arises from hearing, and he provides support in every matter, fulfilling both the ritual decorum and the underlying principles of a disciple.

Furthermore, in the Śrāvaka sūtras, it is explained that the five sons of the Buddha attain five kinds of fruits, yet the Bodhisattvas are not mentioned therein; for this reason, the title "disciple" (śrāvaka) applies exclusively to the Śrāvakas.
In contrast, within the Mahāyāna, the Bodhisattvas are frequently described as the sons of the Buddha.

Now, following the original convention, the term "disciples" (*śrāvaka*) is used as the title for the Śrāvaka sūtras; because this is widely accepted and trusted in the world, it is employed here to designate the chapter.
Second, the explanation of the ten disciples:
while various sūtras clarify the ten great disciples with many different sequences, we shall follow the sequence established by this very sūtra.
At first glance, this is largely consistent with the intent of the "three roots" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, differing only in that Kātyāyana appears after Pūrṇa.

However, as the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, guides the three realms, he must initially have assistants when first opening the Three Piṭakas. These ten śrāvakas, who rule over these [realms], each possess their own strengths and preside over a specific teaching to assist the Buddha in his work of conversion and edification.

Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyāyana in supernormal powers; Mahākāśyapa in the ascetic practices of *dhūta*; Subhūti in the practice of emptiness and non-contention; Pūrṇa in eloquence and preaching the Dharma; Kātyāyana in the dialectical exchange of doctrinal arguments; Aniruddha in the divine eye; Upāli in the upholding of the Vinaya; Rāhula in secret conduct; and Ānanda in extensive learning—all were acclaimed as the foremost in their respective fields.
Question:

If one is designated by the preeminent among ten virtues, then consider the case where Śāriputra held his robe-belt while Maudgalyāyana exhausted all his supernatural powers to move the three thousandfold world-system, yet he could not move Śāriputra’s belt. How is this to be understood?
Maudgalyāyana reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When the Buddha enters meditative absorption, Śāriputra does not know its name;
when Śāriputra enters meditative absorption, Maudgalyāyana does not know its name."
"If Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal powers were not superior to those of Śāriputra, it would follow that the other eight [disciples] do not necessarily each have their own area of excellence.
Answer: "Some are specialized in certain areas, while others are not."

Why is this? When comparing others, it is not necessarily the case that one has a definitive superiority; rather, among their ten virtues, each may have its own particular excellence, and thus is called "foremost.

However, the Buddha is the Dharma-King, and those he appoints as Dharma-Ministers are like the ministers of a worldly state; although each possesses various abilities, the eight high-ranking officials each have their own specific domains of responsibility.

Although each of the ten great disciples possessed multiple qualities, it was impossible for a single person alone to embody two tasks; therefore, the ten virtues were divided and assigned to each individual to assist the Buddha in proclaiming the ten types of teaching gates so that sentient beings might admire and look up to them, and thus each was designated as "foremost."
According to those faculties and conditions, they return to the mind where they reside; though each assists in its own way, they ultimately converge upon the One Path.

Third, regarding the general correspondence with the ten mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*), the *Abhidharma* verse says: "Perception (*saṃjñā*), desire (*chanda*), contact (*sparśa*), wisdom (*prajñā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), volition (*cetanā*), and liberation (*vimukti*); attention (*manasikāra*) toward objects, and concentration (*samādhi*) together with feeling (*vedanā*)."

This [mental factor] pervades the universal ground (mahābhūmika), supporting the mind-king to give rise to all mental enumerations. It is like ten ministers of a state who together assist a single sovereign: if they collectively engage in unrighteousness, the people all commit evil; if they collectively practice righteous governance, the people all possess goodness.

The mind-king of sentient beings and its associated mental factors are likewise so; because these associated mental states penetrate both good and evil, they arise together with the king in immeasurable instances of both good and evil.
Furthermore, the king is the teacher and the subjects are the disciples; their mutual support in both good and evil is likewise so.
Thus the text says: "The multitude of afflictions are the disciples, turning according to the will [of the mind]."

The Buddha is the Dharma King, and his disciples are his ministers; together they transform the mental factors associated with the king. If sentient beings believe, accept, and practice the path of wisdom, they immediately accomplish the various wholesome mental factors of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). By cultivating and practicing the path of conduct, they immediately accomplish the various wholesome mental factors of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Furthermore, the ten numbers are themselves ten Dharma-gates that enable one to enter Nirvana.
Initially, the ten numbers serve as the seeds; by practicing from this point, one eventually achieves the Way, just as a tree with a trunk thick enough to embrace grows from a tiny sprout.

Now the Dharma King wishes to teach and transform all sentient beings through both the partial and the complete [teachings]; first, he accords with their inclinations and desires, as the subsequent text states: "First, one uses the hook of desire to lead them, and later causes them to enter the Buddha-wisdom."

"Now, as each of the ten disciples propagates a single Dharma, people gather according to their kind and things are divided into groups; following their respective inclinations and desires, they are gathered as a retinue within one specific Dharma-gate."
Although each [of these] presides over a single dharma, how could it ever not be endowed with the ten virtues?
It is like the ten mental factors (*caitta*): whenever one arises, the remaining factors arise accordingly; thus, although one factor may bear the specific name, in reality all ten are present.

Fourth, regarding the specific correspondence: [The Buddha] corresponded with Pūrṇa because his mental formations (saṃjñā) were particularly strong; thus, he entered the Path through mental formations, and for this reason, he was foremost among the disciples in preaching the Dharma.
Why is this? The *Abhidharmasamaya-śāstra* states: "Consciousness apprehends real dharmas; perception apprehends provisional names.

Because his application of the mental factor of perception was so distinct, he was able to differentiate names and characteristics with unimpeded eloquence, becoming the foremost among those who preach the Dharma. All who delight in preaching the Dharma took Pūrṇa as their teacher.
Why was this? Because the Buddha’s virtue is so sublime and exalted, none dared to question him abruptly.
Disciples who were newly trained each followed the teacher they preferred and served them; therefore, the two bhikṣus did not dare to question the Buddha.
Therefore, ten individuals each entered the Path by means of one of these [ten] numbers, and among the śrāvakas, each was designated as the foremost.
Corresponding to each of these texts, I shall explain them according to their respective meanings and contexts, as appropriate.

Nowadays, people of the world follow the three trainings, each having their own teachers; thus it is said that the Vinaya and the Vinayasāmagrī, etc., are the teachings initiated by the Tathāgata for entering the Path through both the withered and the flourishing.
He wished to count himself among the ranks of Mahākāśyapa; because his aspiration was particularly strong, he thereby entered the Path.
Why is this? Aspiration is the root of all wholesome dharmas.

Kāśyapa severed his worldly glory and set his mind on delighting in the mountain valleys; thus, by means of a virtuous desire, he abandoned worldly evil desires. Those who delighted in *dhūta* practices he took as teachers, gathering them as his followers, and he manifested the teachings for entering the Way through the austere practices (*dhūta*) that flourish amidst witheredness.

Furthermore, the *gaṇanā* (counting) method was specifically matched for Kātyāyana; because this method was particularly effective for him, it was employed to enable his realization and entry into the Path.
Why is this? Because in the exchange of questions and answers, there was no obstruction or impediment—this was the power of that method.
The rest is as with Kāśyapa.
As for the category of wisdom, it corresponds to Śāriputra; because he entered the Path by means of this category, he is the great general who turns the Wheel of Dharma.
The rest is as with Kāśyapa.
Regarding mindfulness and counting in relation to Upāli: one enters the Path by employing mindfulness and counting to uphold the Vinaya. Why is this?

To create conditions and maintain them through recollection is called mindfulness; to weigh and evaluate objects without forgetfulness is the power of counting, which is supreme for upholding the Vinaya.
The rest is as in the case of Kāśyapa.

As for the contemplation of mental formations (saṃskāra-smṛtyupasthāna) being applied to Rāhula, it was because his faculty of contemplation of mental formations was particularly sharp, allowing him to enter the Path through secret practice. Why is this?

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is volition (*cetanā*). If this faculty of volition is sharp, one cultivates various ascetic practices and conceals one's merits, excelling in secret conduct.
The rest is as [stated] for Kāśyapa.

As for the faculty of liberation (*vimukti*), it corresponds to Śāriputra; because he primarily employs this faculty to enter the Path, his Samādhi of Non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*) is serene and uniquely detached, never contending with other beings.
The rest is as in the case of Kāśyapa.
As for Aniruddha, he was repeatedly instructed in counting because his faculty of memory was particularly sharp.
Since he had lost his eyesight, the Buddha directed him to develop this practice of counting in order to cultivate the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and enter the Path.
Why is this? To cultivate the divine eye, one must fix the mind upon an object and apprehend the light of the sun and moon before the supernormal power of the divine eye can arise.
The rest is as described for Kāśyapa.
The *samādhi-skandha* was addressed to Maudgalyāyana because he was particularly proficient in the number of meditative concentrations; by cultivating these, one enters the Path. Why is this?
All ordinary beings possess these numbers, yet those without concentration fall flat on their faces; because sentient beings are unable to practice them, they do not attain profound concentration.
The rest is as in the case of Kāśyapa.

As for Ānanda, he was frequently admonished because his faculty of receiving instruction was particularly sharp; it was through listening and receiving the teachings that he entered the Path. Why was this so?

Regarding the category of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*): the *Catuḥśataka* refers to it as "sensation" (*duḥkha*), while the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* refers to it as "feeling" (*vedanā*); here, we speak of it generally as "feeling.
Since "feeling" has the meaning of experiencing or receiving, this category clearly receives and maintains the Buddha-dharma, just as a complete vessel holds water.
The rest is as explained regarding Kāśyapa.
Fifth, concerning the clarification of the twin trees (*śāla-druma*): although the preceding section clarified withering and flourishing, the phrasing was brief and the meaning obscure.

These ten disciples together assisted the Tathāgata; they adorned the teachings of the Half- and Full-Wheel Dharma (*ardha-pūrṇa-cakra*) to lead sentient beings to see their own nature and abide in Great Nirvāṇa—this is precisely the meaning of entering Nirvāṇa between the twin trees.

The Tripitaka destroys the four inversions by means of impermanence, adorning the four withered aspects to attract and guide sentient beings; within each numerical category, it gathers beings through the four *siddhāntas*, employing skillful means to assist the Buddha, the Dharma King, and thereby accomplishing the teachings of the "half-letters" to benefit all.

If one person possesses the four *siddhāntas*, ten people will have forty adornments; likewise, up to five hundred people will have two thousand adornments—this refers to the "four kinds of witheredness.
Question:
If ten people correspond to the number ten, how does this apply to five hundred?
Answer: What the Dharma King has spoken must necessarily have its underlying reason.
Since we have not yet seen what the five hundred [disciples] have transmitted, it is improper to speculate rashly.
Now, investigating the underlying principles, I shall briefly provide an explanation.
One unit consists of ten; ten units constitute one hundred. When these are grouped in relation to the five sense organs, they amount to five hundred.

Furthermore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that each of these five hundred [teachings] describes the causes of the body—all of which are "half-words" (*ardhākṣara*)—and through these four types of austerity, one enters the Way.
Next, it clarifies that in order to assist the Buddha in propagating the *pūrṇa* (full) teachings, ten numerical dharma-gates were established;

however, sentient beings were unable to endure them, so through the power of skillful means, the four "withered" teachings were set forth. These ten disciples are all manifestations of the Dharma-body, secretly abiding within while appearing outwardly.
Since the Tathāgata was born into a royal palace, his disciples likewise appeared in accordance with conditions.
When the Tathāgata awakened to the Way beneath the tree, his disciples were all intelligent and possessed sharp wisdom, serving as teachers to the non-Buddhists.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "In the past, I was attached to false views and served as a teacher to various brahmins.
The World-Honored One, knowing my mind, uprooted my heterodoxy and preached nirvāṇa."
The reason he served as their teacher was that it was easy to subdue them.
Once the Tathāgata attained the Way, they all came to take refuge in him and received his teachings on the four types of austerity.

Since the master had been subdued, the disciples followed suit like grass bending in the wind; from that time forward, they accorded with one another in heart and mind, and there were no difficulties in their coming and going.

For this reason, Vimalakīrti rebukes the followers of the two vehicles, causing them to rejoice in the Great [Vehicle] and abandon the Small. Thus, he manifests as one who dwells in a state inferior to theirs and receives the hammering of censure; together with others, he matures the vessels of sentient beings to accomplish the Great Matter. He reveals the Tathāgata’s skillful means to teach sentient beings in secret, so that they all feel shame for the Small and aspire to the Great, opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, attaining the permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and entering the Dharma-gate of the *pūrṇākṣara*. All of these are achieved through the disciples’ assistance in accomplishing the Buddha’s work by means of ten numerical Dharma-gates.
The meaning of the five flavors is detailed in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; it is not the primary intent here, and thus it is not explained in full detail.

Furthermore, when the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies the four glories of adornment, it should have designated all ten persons; however, it mentions only six because it aims to counteract the destruction of the twin trees by the six heretical masters.

What is this? All sentient beings possess the numerical categories of kingship, which refers to the meaning of the three Buddha-natures: "king" is the direct cause (*zhengyin*), "wisdom" is the revealing cause (*liaoyin*), and the remaining numbers are the conditional cause (*yuan-yin*).

The Buddha-nature is perfectly present, yet because it is repeatedly shrouded by afflictions, it cannot manifest. Therefore, the Tathāgata, together with his ten disciples, uses the hammer and anvil to strike and refine it into "matured ghee" (*sarpis*). This causes them to enter the *pūrṇa* (full) letters, open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, reveal the three Buddha-natures, and enter the secret treasury.
Now, by pairing the disciples as subjects and the Tathāgata as their sovereign, the benefit of both the "half" and the "full" teachings is realized; this meaning is perfectly clear.

From antiquity to the present, those who have not understood this principle have surely failed to recognize that the intent behind designating the disciples as subjects was to support and perfect the teaching of inconceivable liberation.

Sixth, regarding the clarification of the birth in the land of retribution: the ten great disciples employ these ten gates to assist in adorning the twin trees. If the sentient beings being transformed achieve the four types of withered states and enter the nirvana without remainder, they are born in the land of remainder; such persons have dull faculties, as they take a circuitous path toward the Buddha-way.

Now, facing Vimalakīrti, one enters the four stages of flourishing; if one reaches the *Lotus Sūtra*, opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), then upon casting off this retribution, one is born in the Pure Land of Fruitional Reward as an attendant of Rocana, hearing only the Perfect Teaching, with every thought extinguished and naturally flowing therein.

7. Regarding the clarification of purifying the Buddha-land: these ten disciples use ten dharma-gates to adorn the twin trees; this is precisely the accomplishment of sentient beings and the purification of the Buddha-land.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he receives the Buddha’s prediction that when he later attains Buddhahood, all those he has transformed will abide [in his land].

By practicing the ten dharma-gates—the causes for withering and flourishing—he purifies the Buddha-land; at the time of his attainment of Buddhahood, such sentient beings will each be born in that land.
If one aligns this teaching with that, it is simply a matter of rebuking the śrāvakas and praising the bodhisattvas who dwell in inconceivable, pure buddha-fields.
Since those of the two vehicles have forever severed [the roots of goodness] and their faculties are ruined and incapable, Kāśyapa’s voice thus resounds throughout the trichiliocosm.

Now, taking the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, I anticipate that the prediction of enlightenment will be bestowed upon Śāriputra and the others, such that "that which you all practice is itself the bodhisattva path";
furthermore, it says, "Those with few desires who weary of birth and death shall in truth purify their own buddha-fields."

Reasoning from this principle, Vimalakīrti’s rebukes and refutations were all directed at those of the Two Vehicles; yet, through successive stages, these very acts became causes for the realization of a Pure Land.

Thus, my disciple’s reiteration serves to support and complete the "Chapter on the Buddha-land" (Buddhakṣetraparivarta), its intent remaining perfectly clear. From antiquity until the present, who has understood this?
8. Regarding the clarification of contemplating the mind (*cittāvalokana*): examining the previous explanation, this too is the contemplation of the mind. Why is this?

Because the practitioner’s *rājñī-saṃkhyā* (royal numbers) constitutes the relationship between teacher and disciple; yet, all the immeasurable dharmas—both false and correct—that sentient beings constantly produce day and night arise from these royal numbers. Therefore, the practitioner must skillfully master this principle.

If one diligently practices contemplation and discernment to give rise to the wisdom of both the Half and the Full [Teachings], thereby transforming oneself and others, one will be like Śāriputra adorning the twin trees; in this way, each and every action is accomplished through mental factors to transform sentient beings.

Conduct is manifested through the mind; if one can contemplate the nature of the mind with true discernment, one immediately perceives the Buddha-nature and abides in Great Nirvana, becoming identical to the Tathāgata’s adornment beneath the twin śāla trees.

If, through the mind of contemplative practice, one clearly perceives the mind itself, then the sovereign is the Dharma King and the enumeration is the disciple; the adornment of the twin trees will appear as if before one's eyes.
As for the secret language of contemplating the mind, how could a commentary ever exhaust its depths?
9. A Critical Examination of the Sequence of Visiting the Sick.
Question:
Why did the Tathāgata not first dispatch a bodhisattva?
Answer: If the Bodhisattvas were each to state their inability, the Śrāvakas would have turned back at the precipice and thus lost five hundred Dharma-gates.
If the Śrāvakas were first commanded to speak, and they each recounted [the teachings], then all five hundred Dharma-gates would be authenticated as sutras.
Next, he dispatched the Bodhisattva, who was then able to fully recount the Dharma-gate previously taught.
Question:
If the inferior were to be sent first, then Ānanda should have been dispatched earlier.
Answer: They each have their respective domains; there is no fault in sending [the messenger] first.
From the words "At that time" onwards, the third section: entering the text for explanation.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, Vimalakīrti’s silent contemplation; second, the Tathāgata’s dispatching of a messenger to inquire after him.
The first part is further divided into two:
First, he reflects upon his own illness; second, he reflects upon the Buddha’s entrustment of his final instructions.
Regarding the first point: since Vimalakīrti resides at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), how could he possibly have any illness?
That he now reflects upon his own condition is precisely because he intends to rely upon this occasion to initiate the teaching for the benefit of sentient beings.
One should reflect that this is the state of the Dharma-body of the knowledge and vision of liberation, abiding in the position of the three virtues of perfect enlightenment:
the reclining represents *prajñā* (wisdom),
and the rapid movement represents *vimukti* (liberation).
The "bed" represents the Dharmakāya.
This is neither vertical nor horizontal, like the worldly letter *i*.
Why is this so? The Dharmakāya is the intrinsically pure mind; when concealed, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha, and when manifest, it is called the Dharmakāya—it is the liberation of true nature.
"Sleep" symbolizes *prajñā* (wisdom); it is like a person's restful sleep, wherein all toil, vexation, and worldly activities are stilled.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "Who attains peaceful sleep?"
This refers to the Buddhas, who constantly dwell in the Samādhi of Contemplating Emptiness, their bodies and minds tranquil and unmoving.

Now, having perfected the cultivation of causes through the contemplation of emptiness by means of Prajñā, all conditioned activities have ceased; as the principle of original purity is revealed, it is in reference to this state of quiescence that Prajñā is elucidated—namely, the liberation of true wisdom.

Regarding the swift manifestation of liberation: when Prajñā (wisdom) accords with the principle of true nature, there arises great compassion without conditions that does not abandon sentient beings; because the body is permeated by loving-kindness and compassion, one is thus able to manifest illness through skillful means.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The place where sentient beings are tamed is called liberation.

Because sentient beings are afflicted, Vimalakīrti is likewise afflicted; yet, through skillful means, he harmonizes with the light of the world without being defiled by its dust—this is precisely the pure liberation of skillful means (*upāya*).
Question:
Why did Vimalakīrti think of himself as being bedridden with illness? Answer:

Since his "sleep" is in fact the Prajñā of the Dharmakāya, he manifests through Great Compassion the illness of being bound by the conditions of sentient beings; as this matter has not yet been made manifest, his inner feelings remain unexpressed, and thus he records his reflections here.
Regarding the phrase, “World-Honored One of Great Compassion, will you not deign to show pity?”: second, this is the recollection of the Buddha’s inquiry.
While I now abide in the causal stage, I still feel compassion for sentient beings; wishing to uproot the suffering arising from the three types of conditions, I have manifested this illness.

The Tathāgata, in the stage of fruition, possesses great compassion without object that constantly desires to bestow the bliss of Great Nirvāṇa upon all beings; this is even greater than my own [desire]. How could he not show me his pity?
If you were to send someone to inquire after him, I would then be able to personally express my feelings of illness.
If this meaning were made manifest, then the afflictions of cause and effect for sentient beings arising from the convergence of the three types of conditions would all be healed.
That both these sentient beings are healed and Vimalakīrti is also healed—is this not the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata universally covering all?
"From 'The Buddha knows' onwards, there are two parts: second, the Tathāgata’s dispatching of a question.
The text is divided into two:
first, the Buddha’s knowledge of their thoughts; second, the actual dispatching of the question."

Regarding the initial statement, "The Buddha knew his intention": the Buddha, through the wisdom of tranquil illumination, intuitively discerned the underlying motive for feigning illness; his unconditioned great compassion was moved by the suffering of sentient beings.
"The wise man knows wisdom, just as a snake knows a snake.
Regarding the passage "He addressed Śāriputra" and below, there are two parts: first, the Buddha dispatches [him] to inquire, which is divided into two sections;
first, he commands ten disciples, and second, he commands five hundred.
The first section, "Commanding Śāriputra," consists of two parts:
first, the Buddha’s command; second, the acceptance of the command.

Regarding the initial command: Śāriputra was the Buddha’s attendant on the left side; because he was renowned for his virtue and held in high esteem among the assembly of śrāvakas, he was revered by both the monastics and the laity.

Although Vimalakīrti was a layman, he was profoundly versed in the Buddha-dharma; his spiritual insight and eloquence were such that it was difficult for anyone to match him in debate, which is why he was summoned first.
However, the causes and conditions concerning Śāriputra are so numerous that they cannot be fully recounted; I shall now describe them briefly.
From the moment of his conception, he possessed an intelligence surpassing that of others. Desiring to transform all the clever heretics, he first became their disciple.

Later, upon encountering the Buddha and leaving the household life to become an Arhat, he led all those clever heretics to become disciples of the Buddha, thereby manifesting the teaching of the four kinds of withered trees.

The reason I now reprimand them and remain silent without responding is that I wish to cause those who follow the "four kinds of withered" teachings to feel inner shame and dejection, so that they may come to admire and aspire to the wisdom-teachings of the "four kinds of flourishing."

When it comes to the teaching of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the previous discourse addressed to Śāriputra was intended to cause the śrāvakas to attain full faith and understanding in the fourfold wisdom of the "full letters" (the conventional).

When it comes to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Buddha first reveals his knowledge and vision to Śāriputra; then the eight classes of beings and the fourfold assembly all have their Buddha-knowledge and vision revealed, and they joyfully praise him, speaking this verse: "The one of great wisdom, Śāriputra, Has now received the Honored One’s prediction."
"We, too, shall likewise surely attain Buddhahood.
This is the complete realization of the true liberation of the four glories.
Therefore, in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda asked the Buddha:
"Who is capable of adorning the twin śāla trees?
The Buddha replied,
"The one of great wisdom, Śāriputra, is that very person."
Some say: "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is a teaching of impermanence.

Since Śāriputra entered parinirvāṇa three months before the Buddha’s own nirvāṇa, he did not hear the teaching of the twin trees from the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*; how, then, can it be said that he was fit to adorn the twin trees?"

One should know that when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* bestows predictions upon the eight classes of beings and the fourfold assembly, the meaning of the twin trees is thereby revealed; this is merely an exploration of the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
For these reasons, the Buddha dispatched [Mañjuśrī] to inquire after his illness.
"Śāriputra," and below, section two: Śāriputra respectfully declines, stating his inability [to teach].

The text is divided into four parts: first, the respectful decline of inability; second, the explanation of the reasons for this inability; third, the specific account of what he is unable to do; and fourth, the conclusion of his inability.

Regarding the first passage: in the past, he was rebuked, yet he did not understand the meaning of those words; therefore, he was unable to accept the command to go inquire after his illness. "The reason being...
[he went] beneath a tree" constitutes the second part, which describes the cause of his inability: he was because he was sitting in meditative seclusion beneath a tree within the grove.
Regarding "sitting in repose": some say it means withdrawing and ceasing like a tortoise hiding its six limbs.
By withdrawing and ceasing the six consciousnesses and the six sense objects, one cannot be troubled by Māra; therefore, it is called "withdrawing and ceasing."

Now, "sitting in repose" (*yàn-zuò*) means "peaceful. One dwells peacefully in fundamental pure dhyāna up to the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), stilling external toil and weariness. Like the dharma of nirvāṇa, one establishes this within the mind and body, realizing the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*); therefore, it is called "sitting in repose."
"Then Vimalakīrti," and so forth, constitutes the third section: the actual exposition on the inability [to sit in dhyāna]. This is divided into three parts:
first, a general reproach; second, a specific demonstration of true sitting in dhyāna; and third, a concluding summary and confirmation.

The initial general reproach—stating that "sitting in this way is not necessarily 'sitting in meditation'" (yànzuò)—is not entirely a denial; rather, it seeks to deride the fact that his secluded dwelling is not ultimate.
What kind of "seated meditation" (yànzuò) did Śāriputra practice that was censured?

Judging this passage in light of what follows, it most likely refers to the various dhyānas and the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) found within the Tripiṭaka and the "half-letters" (the Hīnayāna teachings).

Since one cannot yet attain the meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlayanā*) of the full letters (*pūrṇākṣara*), entering the various dhyānas and the cessation-concentration (*nirodhasamāpatti*) results in six losses; therefore, it is rebuked as being "not necessarily" so.
"Not necessarily" is merely a term for not understanding. If it is inconceivable (*acintya*), then that is indeed "necessarily" so.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* clarifies that the cessation of dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) involves coming and going, and that there are thirteen types of entry into the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) for those in the stage of "one more birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
The *Abhidharma-samaya-pradīpikā-śāstra* clarifies that emptiness and mind both cease in two locations.

Now, it is clarified that there are five distinct stages through which the practitioners of the Three Piṭakas and the Three Vehicles enter the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*):

first, the fundamental, universal, pure dhyāna; second, the dhyāna of contemplation based on the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*); third, the dhyāna of refinement based on the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpattayaḥ*); fourth, the dhyāna of perfuming based on the lion’s bound (or leaping) stride (*siṃhavijṛmbhita*); and fifth, the dhyāna of cultivation based on transcendence (*vyutkrāntaka*).
First, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* was brought forth, and later the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was brought forth; these were what Nanyue produced.

First, regarding those who rely on fundamental pure dhyāna: through the attainment of universal clarity and contemplation, one contemplates form as being like foam in the first dhyāna, like clouds in the second dhyāna, like shadows in the third dhyāna, and like reflections in a mirror in the fourth dhyāna.

Next, one extinguishes the grasping at form and contemplates emptiness with single-minded focus, extending even to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; although coarse afflictions are absent, one still accomplishes ten kinds of subtle dharmas, which remain afflictions and the cycle of birth and death.

The disciples of the Buddha, knowing that these are non-noble dharmas, are able to extinguish them; they also extinguish the mind that performs the extinction. Because the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) are extinguished, it is called the "attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling" (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*).
Next, to clarify the liberations (*vimokṣa*): one contemplates the impurity of the internal and external body; when the white bones emit light, one enters the first liberation.
Regarding the two spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), by extinguishing the afflictions of the first dhyāna, one enters the second dhyāna.
In the third and fourth spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the afflictions of the second dhyāna are extinguished.

From that point onward, there is no longer the appearance of foam, clouds, or mirror-images; one merely contemplates pure form (*śubha-rūpa*) and enters the third dhyāna, which is pure because its object is pure.

One cultivates the eight kinds of radiant light, extinguishes the delusions of the third dhyāna, and achieves the fourth dhyāna, the four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

If one extinguishes the perception of form and takes emptiness as the object, continuing up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one further realizes that even within this state there still exist the four aggregates and ten kinds of subtle delusions; thus, through profound contemplation, one becomes detached and advances to cultivate the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*).

If one extinguishes all feelings and mental factors, and personally realizes the cessation of feeling and perception, this is the "cessation of feeling and perception. When one turns away from them while still on the causal stage, it is called "rejection" (*prahāṇa*).
However, when the untainted state arises and the delusions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are exhausted, that same rejection is then termed "liberation" (*vimokṣa*).
If the cause is spoken of in terms of the fruit, it is also called liberation; if the fruit is spoken of in terms of the cause, it is also called renunciation (*prahāṇa*).

Yet, why is this not called liberation? An *anāgāmin* relies on the eight bases of liberation (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*) to enter the nine successive concentrations (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpattayaḥ*), yet even so, they cannot be called liberated. If this were liberation, they would have to be an arhat; how then could they still be a body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*) *anāgāmin*?
Regarding those who enter via the liberations (*vimokṣa*), these are slightly superior to the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the clear knowledges (*vidyā*).

Third, regarding those who rely on the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*): although one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) through the preceding liberations, it is done through deliberate mental application and resolve, rather than occurring spontaneously.

Now, regarding the cultivation of the liberations (*vimokṣa*), beginning from the first dhyāna and proceeding sequentially until the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), it is easy to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) spontaneously;
however, emerging from it is like waking from sleep.

Fourth, regarding the "Lion’s Bound" (siṃhavijṛmbhita): whereas previously, based on the refinement of dhyāna, one entered the meditative absorptions only in sequential order, it is now clarified that not only does one enter sequentially up to the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), but one can also emerge from the attainment of cessation without interval, proceeding sequentially back through the stages from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception down to the first dhyāna; thus, the power of concentration becomes even more superior.

Fifth, regarding the one who practices transcendence (*vyutkrāntaka*): although the aforementioned [practitioner] has attained mastery in entering and emerging from [the dhyānas] without interval, they have not yet been able to transcend into and emerge from them.

Now, this practitioner of transcendent dhyāna is able to skip from the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) into the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and even skip from the First Dhyāna into the meditative absorption of cessation, as detailed in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
This is like the leap of a golden lion; it is called "skillfully entering, emerging, abiding, and arising from hundreds of thousands of samādhis," and the power of this concentration is supreme.

Now, regarding these five branches of knowledge (pañcavidyā) as the five flavors: pure dhyāna is like milk; the liberations (vimokṣa) are like curd; the nine concentrations (navasamādhi) are like fresh butter; the masteries (abhibhvāyatana) are like refined butter; and the transcendences (vyutkrāntakasamāpatti) are like the finest cream (hṛdaya).

The "Surpassing Dhyāna" (Atikrānta-dhyāna) is able to possess such meritorious qualities as the vows, wisdom, the samādhi of non-contention, the four analytical knowledges, the three clarities, the six supernormal powers, and the eighteen transformations; it is the most supreme pinnacle among all dhyānas, and even because it transcends all other dhyānas, both its entry and exit are termed "Summits" (Mūrdhan).
Question:
Why are there four further distinctions above the fundamental purity? Answer:

Just as in the world one treats leather: thorough clarity is like soaking it in water; renunciation is like tangled hair; the nine concentrations are like entering a state of distress; mastery is like being fumigated by fire; and transcendence is like being softened and matured.
This differs from the explanations of the Sāṃkhya school regarding perfuming and cultivation, as detailed in the various analyses.
If an Arhat attains transcendence, he is called a Mahānāga; his mind is harmonized and supple, and for the three vehicles, the culmination of their practice is defined by this.

Śāriputra roams within this forest of dhyāna, using these various meditations to rest from all weariness; however, because he has given rise to these meditations without relying on the Buddha’s wisdom, [the Buddha] rebukes him, saying they are unnecessary.

The reason for this is that what Śāriputra has attained is not the cave of profound meditative concentration consisting of the nine kinds of "full-letter" (vaipulya) dhyānas; therefore, it is said they are unnecessary.
From "Now, as for sitting in quietude" (*yàn-zuò*) below, there are two parts; the second specifically demonstrates true sitting in quietude.
Within these six kinds of inconceivable sitting in quietude, there are three pairs:
first, regarding essence and function; second, regarding phenomena and mind; and third, regarding cause and effect.
The first part consists of two sections.
The first concerns the essence [of dhyāna], stating: "Not manifesting body or mind within the three realms is what constitutes sitting in meditation.

Śāriputra did not enter the aforementioned meditative absorptions by means of the Buddha’s wisdom; rather, he had to remain in a quiet place, straighten his body, and collect his thoughts before he could attain concentration, which implies that he still manifested the characteristics of body and mind within the desire realm.

If the body is like wood or stone, that is the manifestation of the body; if the mind is like extinguished ashes yet maintains the resolve to enter and emerge [from meditation], that is the manifestation of the mind. Furthermore, if one causes others to feel reverence, awe, and wonder, how could there be anything to be extinguished?

One who truly practices seated meditation does so by inclining toward the Buddha-wisdom; they enter the nine great dhyānas and the concentrations of the two vehicles at will. This is called not manifesting body or mind within the three realms.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Practicing dhyāna while remaining amidst desire causes the mind of Māra to become confused and disordered.
Not straightening the body and not directing the mental application is called not manifesting the body and mind.

When body and mind accord with the world without contradicting the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one may enter this absorption without hindering dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*). Thus, there is no fault of mental movement regarding entering or emerging from concentration, nor is there the error of manifesting signs within the three realms (*tridhātu*). This is true *pratisaṃlayana*; it is the inconceivable, true *pratisaṃlayana*.
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body enters various meditative absorptions within the Dharma-nature body, they do not manifest body or mind within the triple world; this is true dhyāna.
According to the ultimate principle, all sentient beings are in the state of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), yet Śāriputra did not realize this.

If we consider the actual facts, it is clear that within the *dharmatā-kāya* there are definitively no bodies or sense-bases belonging to the three realms; yet Śāriputra still possesses a body and mind belonging to the three realms—how, then, could he be said to be in true *pratisaṃlayana*?
Therefore, he remained silent.
This was because [the interlocutor] did not know the true essence of the practice of *yansuo* (seated meditation), so [the Buddha] demonstrated it to him.
If one cultivates the threefold contemplation within a single mind, this constitutes the six kinds of *yansuo* that lead toward the wisdom of the Buddha.
"From non-arising to sitting in meditation" next demonstrates the inconceivable function.
This is to refute the claim that the extinction samādhi is useless, on the grounds that śrāvakas, when entering meditative absorption, cannot manifest the four dignified postures.

Just as Kāśyapa entered meditative absorption without manifesting any supernatural transformations, and only did so when Maitreya emerged, we know that for those of the Two Vehicles, entering absorption is of no benefit or use to themselves or others, because they lack an essential nature.

The inconceivable samādhi possesses both essence and function; therefore, it is able to manifest the majestic deportment of the ten realms without arising from the samādhi of cessation, just as a tūṇa lute produces melodies according to the person playing it.

Bodhisattvas manifest their forms throughout the ten directions according to the capacities of beings, appearing and disappearing with sovereign ease; why do you not perfume your concentration with vows so that, in response to the stimuli of sentient beings, various dignified demeanors may be manifested? This is truly because you have not perceived true nature and lack the perfection of wishlessness (apraṇihita-pāramitā).
Useless concentration is not esteemed by beings; therefore, it is criticized as being unnecessary.

Furthermore, the body of the Dharma-nature enters various extinction concentrations (nirodha-samāpatti) to advance toward Buddha-wisdom, yet is able to manifest the ten realms and the four modes of conduct within the triple world. There is no phenomenon that it does not manifest; this is the ultimate true sitting in meditation.
Below the section on "not abandoning," there are two pairs concerning the mind of the Dharma.
To censure the clumsiness of this mind of the Dharma, it is said that one need not [abandon them].

First, regarding the censure based on the Dharma: when Śāriputra emerged from the truth, he was just like ordinary people; if he had not abandoned his various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), how could he have expected to emerge from concentration?

This would mean that one abandons the dharmas of the Path to become identical with ordinary worldly dharmas; one should know, however, that these two types of dharma cannot be mutually abandoned. Why?

Because for a bodhisattva who proceeds toward the wisdom of a Buddha, the two dharmas are without distinction; how could one abandon the dharmas of the Path and then enter back into the dharmas of the Path?
To practice what is not the path while penetrating the Buddha-way—if one cannot penetrate it, how can it be called the Way?

Each of the four teachings has its own two methods for practicing the Way. That which manifests the affairs of ordinary people refers to the good and unwholesome matters of the three karmas, such as the twenty-nine matters beginning with "though being a layperson," as well as immeasurable skillful means.

The Dharma-body is eternally in samādhi and is able to universally accord with all ordinary things; thus, within the ordinary body, it enters the King Samādhi, wherein all other samādhis are entirely contained. By means of this, it leads sentient beings into the inconceivable liberation of the Buddha’s pure land—this is precisely the ultimate true sitting in meditation.
Thus, he ridiculed the clumsiness of their path and dharma, and therefore rebuked them by saying, "It is unnecessary.
Regarding the phrase "the mind does not reach tranquil sitting," he next offers a rebuke based on the mind.

He says "it does not abide" because Śāriputra abides within when entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and scatters without when emerging; likewise, in the case of *dharmatā-dhyāna*, it abides within while in concentration and is without when emerging; in the case of *śubha-dhyāna*, it abides within and is without when emerging; and in the case of the *nirodha-samāpatti*, it abides within when entering and is without when emerging. Thus, the mind depends upon the internal and external, moving and scattering as it enters and emerges; how can this be called "tranquil stillness"?
Therefore, it is rebuked as being unnecessary.

Since a bodhisattva, by means of the wisdom directed toward Buddhahood, contemplates the dharma-nature of the Middle Way and does not even perceive nirvana or birth-and-death, nor any internal or external state that can be dwelt in or reached, how could there be a meditative extinction from which one emerges, or any internal or external state that can be dwelt in or reached?
There are two extremes of distraction that do not constitute true *pratisaṃlayanā* (seated meditation); therefore, it is said that [physical posture] is not necessarily required.
Now, when a Bodhisattva darkens the mind within the *dharmatā*, remaining neither distracted nor attached to flavors, this is the inconceivable, true *pratisaṃlayanā*.
From the phrase "Regarding all views" onwards, section three consists of a single pair that addresses cause and effect.
It demonstrates what constitutes true meditative sitting (*pratisaṃlayana*) and refutes what is not true.
First, the statement "unmoved by all views" criticizes their deviant causes, asserting that this is not true meditative sitting.
To remain unmoved by various views is itself true *pratisaṃlayanā* (seated meditation) within the causal stage.
Now, one should analyze this through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):

there are those whose views are disturbed but who do not cultivate the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); those who are unmoved but do not cultivate them; those who are disturbed yet cultivate them; and those who are unmoved and cultivate them.

Those who do not cultivate while in motion are like the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who abandon existence to grasp at non-existence, or even at that which is neither existent nor non-existent.

Like those who avoid empty space, they abandon all views in their desire to attain *nirvāṇa*, yet they do not know how to cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*). Therefore, in the *Subhadra-sūtra*, the Buddha uttered a lion’s roar, declaring that because they lack the Eightfold Noble Path, they are definitively devoid of the four fruits of the śramaṇa.

Regarding "immovable and non-cultivating": outsiders give rise to views, asserting that "this alone is the truth and all else is false," clinging to them with unyielding persistence as if grasping at empty space; they likewise do not cultivate the factors of the path.

Regarding "moving and practicing": those of the Three Piṭakas and the Two Vehicles recognize that the self and its surroundings are defiled, inverted, caused by conditions, impermanent, and in flux; because they move against this flux, it is called "moving.
