For example, regarding the perfection of the virtue of severance within the Dharma-body, when delusive obstructions are ultimately severed, these three virtues are like the worldly character "I" (the trident). Thus, the *vajra* is used as a metaphor for the Dharma-body.

Regarding the phrase "all evils have been severed and all virtues universally assembled": that all evils have been severed means that the five stages of dwelling [in ignorance] have all been eliminated.
That all virtues are universally assembled means that Mahāprajñāpāramitā guides all myriad virtues to merge with the Middle Way, reaching ultimate and perfect consummation.
Thus, the meaning of the three virtues of the Dharma-body is perfectly clear.
As for the phrase "What illness could there be? What affliction could there be?"—since all evils have been exhausted, there is no fruit of suffering; what illness could there be?
When all virtues are universally assembled in ultimate eternal bliss, how could there be any affliction?
Here, the "sickness" refers to the wisdom and severance of the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) within the Tripiṭaka teachings; thus it is called sickness.
In the Mahāyāna teachings, the wisdom and severance of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) are free from suffering; thus it is called being without sickness.
To say that there is illness is itself a twofold slander.

However, according to the old conventions of the four or five periods [of the Buddha’s teaching], it is said that the preaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* still pertains to the Buddha of the eighty-year period.

This Vaipulya teaching is identical to the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, which clarifies that his lifespan is seven hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas; yet, in order to manifest the contrast between decay and flourishing, he did not accept the ten disciples of Śāriputra. How, then, can one use the doctrine of impermanence to negate the textual meaning of this sūtra?
Below "departing in silence," section three concludes the two types of false accusation (*pāpa-dṛṣṭi*).
The text is divided into two parts:
first, concluding the false accusation of denigration (*apavāda*); second, concluding the false accusation of exaggeration (*samāropa*).
Regarding the first passage, the meaning is clear as it uses the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) as a proof.
As for "going silently," one says "silent" because it stops slander that diminishes [the teaching], and one says "goes" because it stops slander that exaggerates [the teaching].
"Going" means departing.
Since the True Body is free from ailment, why trouble yourself by begging for milk?
Therefore, I have sent you away.
To say that there is illness is itself an exaggeration.
Regarding the phrase "Do not let others hear these coarse words," those who harbor heterodox views are what is meant by "others."

Hearing that the Buddha was ill, he remarked, "The Buddha’s practice of goodness must still be coarse, for the fruits of his merit are incomplete; that he still suffers from illness and affliction—how does this differ from worldly people?
Thus, he increased his own slanderous views and urged [the others] to go there in silence.

Regarding the phrase "let there be no [such thing]," it means that the retribution for even minor good deeds results entirely in freedom from illness; thus, if they were to hear Ānanda say that the Buddha is ill, they would find it deeply strange and fail to understand the nature of a Wheel-Turning King.

If even a king, by practicing the ten wholesome paths of action throughout three lifetimes and teaching others through his own example, can attain freedom from illness through such meager merit, how much more so for the Tathāgata, who possesses an immeasurable assembly of merit and is universally supreme?

The Buddha cultivated the Mahāprajñāpāramitā for immeasurable kalpas to guide all practices, thereby attaining the ultimate truth and realizing the fruit of eternal bliss; how could he possibly be subject to illness?
If one were to say he has an illness, he would then be no different from a Wheel-Turning King, and this would surely be a great detriment to the majesty and virtue of the Pure Land and its devas.
"Go, for the person of realization has heard [this]"—second, this concludes the formation of increased slander.
The intent of this reproach is that if one says the Buddha is ill, it constitutes increased slander.
The Dharma-body is without illness; yet, if one speaks of its having illness, then there must be the fruit of illness. Where there is a fruit, there must be a cause, and that cause is unwholesome.
If there is the evil of illness, then one is an evil person; how could one possibly take such a person as a teacher?
Since Ānanda is himself a practitioner, he ought to feel shame before his fellow practitioners.
If he were to speak these words, he would bring shame upon the Bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly of disciples; therefore, it is said, "Do not cause us to suffer this shame."
Regarding the phrase "non-Buddhists" (*tīrthika*) and so forth: this would fully expose both the teacher and his disciples to shared disgrace.
Furthermore, it would increase the grave sin of slander committed by those with false views; since such a thing must not occur, he ordered them to depart quickly so that no one would hear.
If people do not hear [this], then their shame will not be made manifest; failing to reach [the truth], they will bring disgrace upon their disciples and increase the sins of slander against others.
"One should know how quickly [it reaches]"—this fourth point reiterates that the Dharma-body is free from illness.
Pó Ānàn (Breaking Ānanda’s View) addresses the notion that the living body is subject to illness; to hold such a view and speak accordingly constitutes two types of slander.
This passage contains four points of meaning.
"One should know... up to 'the body of desire'" explains the perfection of cessation (*prahāṇa-sampad*) of the Dharma-body.
Volition is itself action, and desire is itself craving; when combined with action, they moisten karma and lead to rebirth.
Within and beyond the realm of the Dharma-body, karma and afflictions are severed; therefore, it is said that this is not a body of volition or desire.

This refutes the Tripiṭaka masters' claim that the *sāvaśeṣa-nirmāṇakāya* (the retribution body with remaining [defilements]) is still the fruit of karma and afflictions within the realm of existence, and thus possesses minor ailments.
To adhere to this interpretation would constitute the fault of exaggeration (*adhyāropa*).

"The Buddha, as the World-Honored One, transcends the three realms"—this explains that the wisdom-virtue of the Dharma-body emerges beyond the two kinds of triple realms; how, then, could there be the afflictions of the triple realms within the world?
This refutation of the Tripiṭaka [teaching] holds that his remaining physical body still possessed retribution from within the realm, and therefore he was ill.
To adhere to this interpretation would constitute a slanderous denigration.

"The Buddha’s body is without outflows (*anāsrava*), for all outflows have been exhausted. This reiterates that the merit of severance within the Dharma-body is free from the two kinds of threefold outflows—those of the internal and external realms—and thus does not fall into the two kinds of birth-and-death. How could there be illness, which is the fruit of tainted outflows belonging to the internal realm?
This refutation [of the Three Baskets] holds that the remaining physical body is a tainted fruit (*sāsrava-phala*), and thus there is minor illness.
To maintain this and speak thus is to increase slander.

"The Buddha’s body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall within the categories of enumeration"—this reiterates that the wisdom-virtue of the Dharma-body is unconditioned, not conditioned by the realms or their internal states; it is devoid of the two kinds of enumerated phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). How could there be the aggregates, elements, and bases of the internal realm upon which illness might depend?

This refutes the notion that the Buddha in his physical body (*saṃbhogakāya*) still possesses the various numerical categories of phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), which would entail the existence of karmic retribution;
to hold such a view constitutes slanderous denial.

"What illness could such a body possibly have? This summarizes that since the Dharma-body possesses neither of these four faults regarding wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), how could it possibly have illness?
This refutes Ānanda’s statement and establishes two types of slander.
The previous commentary on the chapter concerning Subhūti clarified the meaning of slandering the Buddha; here, that intent is made manifest.
In the passage beginning with "At that time, I," thirdly, Ānanda harbors shame and remorse within his heart.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the expression of shame and remorse; second, the consolation provided by an ethereal voice.

Regarding the first part: formerly, he considered himself to be one of great learning who maintained the teachings without error; now, having been rebuked, he realizes that he has committed two types of slander, thereby bringing disgrace upon both his teacher and his disciples, and thus harbors shame and remorse.
Furthermore, he feared that although he was close to the Buddha, he might not have realized the Buddha’s words and had instead heard them erroneously; thus, he was rebuked.
"Immediately upon hearing this, do not feel ashamed"—this second part refers to the Buddha hearing an ethereal voice and consoling Ānanda.
Having already felt deep shame and remorse, and fearing the commission of the two kinds of slanderous offenses, I have therefore used an empty voice to provide explanation and consolation.
This "empty voice" is the voice of the Dharma-body of Vairocana, as elucidated in the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra*.

"As for the words 'just as the householder said': just as Vimalakīrti taught that the Dharma-body is fully endowed with wisdom and the abandonment of afflictions, and that this body is without illness and thus has no need to beg for milk—this is precisely true wisdom, and his words are not false."
It is only because the Buddha has appeared in this world of the five turbidities that he manifests and practices these dharmas to deliver sentient beings.

The five turbidities are: first, the turbidity of the kalpa; second, the turbidity of afflictions; third, the turbidity of sentient beings; fourth, the turbidity of views; and fifth, the turbidity of lifespan.

If a Buddha appears in this world of five turbidities, he manifests illness as a skillful means to conform to the ways of human beings, thereby delivering disciples of dull faculties who are śrāvakas; this is precisely his provisional wisdom (upāya-jñāna).
Now, for the sake of transforming the Brahmin, it is necessary to take his milk to serve as a field of merit for him; there is no need for shame or embarrassment.
These are the True Body and the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya), whose meanings are not the same.
Although the Dharma-body of the original ground is free from illness, its manifestations within the traces of the world must accord with skillful means to benefit sentient beings.
If one understands this intent, how could one incur the two types of slander?
There is no need for shame or remorse.
"Regarding 'the World-Honored One came to inquire after his illness,'" fourth, this concludes the point that [Ānanda] was incapable [of the task].
Ānanda reflected to himself: "If even Vimalakīrti’s eloquence was such as to rebuke me in this way, how could I possibly be fit to transmit the message and go inquire after his illness?"
From "In this way" onwards, the second major section commands the five hundred [monks].
Since the original sūtra text is abbreviated, these [details] are not all translated here.

If all five hundred were rebuked, it would mean that these five hundred bhikṣus had entered the Way by relying on the Tripiṭaka and each spoke of the causes of their own bodies; Vimalakīrti then used five hundred Mahāyāna dharma-gates to rebuke and humble them, manifesting the contrast between withering and flourishing through the analysis of distinct characteristics.
Since this has not been transmitted, how could one possibly apply the mind to explain it?

(Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-lüeshu, Scroll 17, Chapter 4: Bodhisattva Section [5–6], Beginning of the Bodhisattva Section) 17. (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-guǎngshu, Scroll 17) This chapter follows the "Disciples' Chapter" for three reasons: first, to refute the notion of an intrinsic self; second, to reveal the inconceivable liberation of the Dharma-body; and third, to establish the teaching of the Tathāgata’s Pure Land.
The meaning of this chapter is manifold and cannot be fathomed by ordinary minds; for now, I shall briefly explain it by means of three points:
first, to clarify the purpose of this chapter’s introduction; second, to provide a brief explanation of the term "bodhisattva"; and third, to enter the text for detailed exposition.

Regarding the sequence from the initial exposition up to the "Chapter on the Disciples": the Great Sage, the Dharma King, wishing to enable sentient beings to attain the inconceivable [reality] of the environment and its inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*), first commanded his great disciples to each describe their own inadequacy. This was because the various *śrāvakas*, having realized the partial truth (*ekadeśatattva*), were all obstructed by the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); thus, each declined the task upon being rebuked, for how could they be capable of transmitting the ultimate intent?
The Bodhisattva is not like this; therefore, he follows after life.

However, although the Bodhisattva does not stagnate in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), he still suffers from the affliction of having a self-essence (*svabhāva*); for this reason, in the past, he was always rebuked for it.

This clarifies that all three teachings are merely skillful means; since the primary retribution of the inconceivable Dharma-body has not yet been manifested, and the pure land of the true and pure dependent retribution has not yet been established, the various Bodhisattvas each declined, saying they were unable to accept the task.
Now, the intent of this clarification also briefly comprises five points:

first, to manifest the supreme wisdom of Vimalakīrti; second, to transform the provisional gates of teaching; third, to support the teachings on the Buddha-land; fourth, to refine the bodhisattvas of the provisional stage so that they may enter the subsequent flavor and receive its legacy; and fifth, to seal and confirm the completion of the sūtra.
These five names and numbers appear similar to those in the "Chapter on Disciples," yet their meanings differ and cannot be treated as identical. Regarding the first intention:

although the aforementioned disciples each recounted being rebuked without offering a reply, the wisdom and eradication of the Hearers (śrāvaka), though transcending the three realms, belong to the Hīnayāna and are thus limited and shallow in merit and wisdom; how could they suffice to fully manifest the divine wisdom of Vimalakīrti?
It would not be considered extraordinary to compete in strength with those who are inferior;

therefore, he next commanded the four great Bodhisattvas and the various Mahāsattvas. When they all declared their inability, everyone heard that the wisdom and virtue of Vimalakīrti surpassed all others, such that there was no one who did not feel reverence in their hearts or fail to submit in devotion.
If Mañjuśrī were commanded to enter the chamber to discuss the Way, everyone would immediately receive great benefit.

This intention seems to serve as a prologue for what occurs within the chamber; however, since the remaining four meanings constitute the main exposition (*samyag-deśanā*), they do not belong to the prologue when judged by the majority. This has already been analyzed in detail in various places.
Next, "intention" (*manas*) is also a transformation of contemplation.

The reason for this is that those of dull faculties who transform their teaching are called "persons who practice through faith," while those of sharp faculties who transform their contemplation are called "persons who practice through dharma. Thus, there are two:
first, the transformation of teaching; second, the transformation of contemplation.

Regarding those who first turned the teaching: because bodhisattvas of dull faculties were unable to hear the Perfect [Teaching], he opened up expedient means to guide, receive, and bring them to maturity.

Once their practice of expedient means had become thoroughly matured and they were capable of hearing the Perfect and entering the Way, the bodhisattvas of provisional capacity were first shown to be rebuked and broken in the past.
Now, wishing to turn the provisional toward the ultimate reality, it is necessary to recount this once more so that all may hear and know it.

Next, he commanded the various Bodhisattvas; there are three distinct types [of turning]: first, the turning of the provisional teachings of the Tripiṭaka; second, the turning of the provisional teachings within the *Prajñāpāramitā* of the night of attaining the Way; and third, the turning of the provisional teachings within the *Avataṃsaka*.
The initial [teaching] has two meanings:
first, gradual; second, sudden.

Regarding the gradual transformation: for bodhisattvas of dull faculties, the initial transformation of the teaching is identical to the five flavors of the śrāvakas, differing only in that it concerns a different class of person.
Why is this? Those of the three vehicles alike practice the two vehicles' severing of fetters to become "curd"; thus, both the teaching and the person are curd.
The Bodhisattva subdues the fetters; while the teaching is curd, the person remains milk.

Regarding the two types of sudden transformation: Śrāvakas cannot undergo sudden transformation within the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna] teachings; however, bodhisattvas of sharp faculties attain awakening within the Vaipulya teachings, which constitutes sudden transformation.
This is the meaning of the "indeterminate teaching" (*aniyata-śāsana*): namely, that when poison is ingested with fresh butter (*navanīta*), it causes death. Regarding the second meaning:

this refers to the Buddha’s constant preaching of Prajñā from the night he attained enlightenment. If this teaching is within the Tripiṭaka and is taught for the benefit of [certain] people, it is a "secret teaching" (*guhya-śāsana*); if it is heard separately by the bodhisattvas, it is an "indeterminate teaching."
Since this [text] comes from the Deer Park and expounds the *Prajñāpāramitā* to fully clarify the three types of wisdom, there are accordingly three kinds of bodhisattvas.

The first two types of persons are those who receive the skillful means (*upāya*) teachings within the *Prajñā*; therefore, they were subjected to the refutations and corrections of Vimalakīrti’s perfect teaching.

If one uses the *tongjiao* (Shared Teaching) to abide in all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) yet perceives the Middle Way, it is like consuming ghee that has been processed with poison, which will cause the poison to manifest and kill the person;

if one uses the *biejiao* (Distinct Teaching) to abide in the knowledge of the paths and categories (*mārgajñatā*) to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, this is like consuming matured ghee that has been processed with poison, which will cause the poison to manifest and kill the person.

Among those who practice the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), there are those who critique and those who do not. Those who do not critique have deeply grasped the intent of the teaching; because they do not cling to views of arising and lack attachment to the path, they have no need for critique.
If one gives rise to views regarding words or attachment that conforms to the path, one will be struck down and broken.
If the mind awakens and enters the Dharma-gate of non-duality, it is like the onset of poison in *amṛta* (the finest ghee) that kills the person.
The Three Illuminations (Sanming) received the *Avataṃsaka* according to its distinct teaching (*biejiao*), yet they grasped it one-sidedly and became mired in attachment;
therefore, they were subjected to this critique. Even those who have attained awakening are like matured cream in which poison has been stirred, killing whoever consumes it.
If one receives the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), there may be instances where one is rebuked or not; this can be understood by analogy with the gains and losses found within the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, among the four flavors (*sìwèi*), both those who have attained the intended meaning and those who have not are subject to rebuke during the stage of Expedient Means (*fāngbiàn*).

Why is this? Those who harbor attachments to teachings and give rise to views through their practice must be rebuked; for although their teachings and practices may be consistent with the doctrine, those teachings and practices are not yet true. Therefore, they are rebuked so that they may enter into reality.
If one receives the teaching of ultimate reality, it can be understood by analogy with the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Question: Why must it be so?

Answer: This is because the provisional teachings (upāya-deśanā) cause both [the teacher and the taught] to be abandoned, whereas the Perfect Teaching (pūrṇa-yāna) allows one to grasp the meaning without abandoning it.
In explaining this chapter, the universal and particular bodhisattvas consistently refute and break down [the provisional], while for the Perfect Teaching, this is not fixed.
Reflect upon this according to what has been stated above.
When entering into the text, apply this principle exclusively and constantly maintain it in mind; when you reach the following sections, do not harbor any doubts.
Furthermore, while the previous three teachings both criticize the illness and the teaching, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) criticizes the illness but does not criticize the teaching.
Question:

If there were those who attained the general teaching of Prajñāpāramitā from the night they attained the Way, there ought to have been those of the two vehicles who attained the Way [at that time]. Answer:
As you have asked. Question:
Must a bodhisattva practicing skillful means (upāya) necessarily and invariably be criticized?

Answer: Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has not yet been fully harmonized, it is feared that it cannot yet be entirely set aside; therefore, as previously determined, this is done to manifest the Buddha’s true intent.
Furthermore, according to the provisional teachings, even the provisional bodhisattvas merely censure the illness [of attachment] and do not censure the dharma itself; this must be distinguished.

If one considers the practitioner, both the illness and the dharma are to be criticized; however, since the dharma is intended to be transmitted to future generations, it need not necessarily be abandoned.
Question:
In the Perfect and Sudden teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*, how can a student be criticized and ordered to turn the teaching over to another?

Answer: Those of sharp faculties who have attained awakening—how could they require further rebuke? However, those whose spiritual faculties are inferior must be guided through special means. If they remain attached to the teachings and do not shift their perspective, they will lose the true intent of the *Avataṃsaka*; therefore, they must be rebuked so that they may return to the ocean of the perfect and sudden Dharma-realm of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Or, although one may have received the Perfect and Sudden teaching, it must be criticized as previously described.
This would then be a case of criticizing and obstructing the core intent of the *Avataṃsaka*, rather than criticizing the Dharma-wheel of the Sudden Teaching.
Question:
It is also said that the Nirvāṇa is constantly taught during the two watches of the night; thus, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha answered Kāśyapa:
"Not long after I first attained the Way, Bodhisattvas from the ten directions came to inquire about this meaning."
"In this regard, there may also be bodhisattvas who have not yet understood; why then do you not set forth this meaning?
Answer: Although such an intention exists, no explicit textual authority has been seen.
If one wishes to explain this, it may be understood by reference to the *Prajñāpāramitā*; the difference here lies merely in the specific textual division (*vibhāga*).
If this is indeed another name for the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā*, then what was previously clarified regarding the objects of censure is precisely its meaning.
Question:
Is the *Prajñāpāramitā* of the night of attaining the Way merely another name for the *Avataṃsaka*, or does it have a distinct teaching? Answer:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains that there are two kinds of prajñā: first, that taught in common with followers of the Two Vehicles;
second, that taught exclusively [to Bodhisattvas]. The exclusive teaching is as found in the *Acintya-sūtra*.
If one examines this text, they are merely different names.

Furthermore, a verse in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* praising Prajñā states: "If one contemplates the Buddha according to the Dharma, Prajñā and Nirvāṇa—these three are of one single characteristic; in reality, there is no difference between them."
If that is so, then *nirvāṇa* is also a synonym; why then is it [the name] only for *prajñā*? Answer:
*Avataṃsaka* is named after the Great Vaipulya Buddha; *Prajñā* receives its designation from wisdom; *Nirvāṇa* is named according to liberation.
If one consults the treatises, there is no logical error in the principle that different schools may have different names.
However, as no explicit textual evidence has yet been seen, it cannot be definitively determined.
Question:
Question: Prior to the critique by the one named Zijing, there must also have been those who were hindered by expedient means and converted through such criticism; why are these cases not set forth?
Answer: It cannot be definitively determined, and therefore they are not separately presented.

2. Explaining the transformation of contemplation (*parāvṛtti-darśana*): This refers to those of sharp faculties who practice according to the Dharma and abide in the gates of skillful means (*upāya*). Upon hearing the censure of bodhisattvas, they immediately transform their contemplation.

Since they possess sharp faculties, whether they hear the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, or hear the Prajñāpāramitā teachings spoken during the night of attaining the Way, or hear the teachings on the three types of skillful means in the *Avataṃsaka*, they achieve faith, understanding, and awakening, yet have not yet seen the True Path. However, upon hearing the reprimand of the various bodhisattvas, they suddenly attain a clear realization and enter the gate of non-duality (*advaya-dharmamukha*).

Furthermore, if there is a bodhisattva who, having heard even a small amount concerning the three aforementioned stages, is able to give rise to the resolve for enlightenment, such a person is still an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) and is like milk.
If they enter into the principle of the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*), they are then like curd.
If one enters through provisional views and perceives the conventional, this is fresh butter (*sarpis*).
If one gives rise to a semblance-understanding of the Middle Way, this is matured butter (*ghṛta*).
If one gives rise to true understanding, this is clarified butter (*navanīta*).
If one hears the rebuke of a bodhisattva and, through that flavor, attains awakening and enters the Dharma-gate of non-duality, this is called "the poison arising from that flavor which kills.
This is how the Great Being of old struck down other bodhisattvas, using the hammer and anvil to forge them into the vessels of bodhisattvahood.
At that time, each individual attained benefit; now this great assembly all possesses the capacity to hear [the teaching], which is why they are summoned next.

If each were to recount their own past experiences of being rebuked, then everyone present would receive the benefit of the "turning of the teaching" and the "turning of contemplation," just as those previously rebuked obtained benefit.
Next, he commands the various bodhisattvas; this is the underlying intention.

Furthermore, in the past, whatever teachings were heard in various places provided little benefit; now, gathered in great assembly within the Jeta Grove surrounding the World-Honored One, they hear and recount them together, whereby the benefit is immeasurable.
Since you have personally received the Buddha’s seal of approval, the meaning of the transmission of the teaching has finally attained certainty.
Question:
If the admonition of all bodhisattvas employs only a single teaching, how can it bring universal benefit?
Answer: The Master [Confucius] himself said, "Of the three hundred poems, one word summarizes them all.

When the Great Being (the Bodhisattva) uses this single Perfect Teaching to critique and admonish, those who have been hindered by adhering to provisional or real teachings all gain the benefit of the One Path; why, then, should one harbor any doubt?
Question:
When rebuking various bodhisattvas, does it invariably result in a single, complete benefit for all? Answer:

At first glance, the passages criticizing the four bodhisattvas appear to be entirely beneficial; however, as for the passages where the other bodhisattvas each present their own accounts, since those texts are not definitive, how can they be judged with certainty?

Furthermore, the Vaipulya sutras still retain elements of expedient means and are not yet entirely identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; how, then, could they be denied the benefit of those expedients?
This is the third point.

When those Bodhisattvas who have received the teachings on skillful means are exhorted, they sever their afflictions according to conditions; at that point, their offenses are eliminated, their hindrances are transformed, and their merit and wisdom increase in clarity, enabling them to behold the Pure Land. Thus, when entering a room, they see the room as empty, and furthermore, they see the lands of the Lamp-King Buddha and the Fragrant Accumulation Buddha. Accordingly, wherever they sever their afflictions, they attain birth in the three lands.

Furthermore, as merit and wisdom increase and become more luminous, and in accordance with the sentient beings he has tamed, when he later attains Buddhahood, all such beings will come to be born in his land; this is the teaching supporting and completing what was previously stated regarding the purification of the Buddha-land by the Tathāgata.

Regarding the fourth intention, as stated in the *Dharmadhātuprakṛti-śāstra*: "If those of sharp faculties enter the dharmadhātu through the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, those of middling faculties enter the dharmadhātu through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and those of inferior faculties enter the dharmadhātu through the *Nirvāṇa*."

Because *āma-sarpis* (raw ghee) is negated as being *pakva-sarpis* (cooked ghee), it becomes *sarpir-manda* (clarified butter) at the stage of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, whereby one enters the *dharmadhātu*.

Because *dadhi* (curd) is negated as being *āma-sarpis*, it serves as *pakva-sarpis* for the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and becomes *sarpir-manda* at the stage of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, whereby one enters the *dharmadhātu*.

By churning milk, it becomes curd; reaching the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, it becomes fresh butter; reaching the Lotus Sūtra, it becomes matured butter; reaching the Nirvāṇa Sūtra, it becomes the finest cream (amṛta), and thus enters the Dharma-realm.

If it were not so, one would be unable to cause those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties to all enter the Dharma-realm; thus, this would merely constitute an entry into the introductory sequence of the three sutras.
Question:
Since this sutra clearly elucidates entry into inconceivable liberation, why does it not clarify entry into the Dharma-realm?
Answer:

The superior turning of the teaching and contemplation for entering the gate of non-duality is no different from the *dharmadhātu* of the *Avataṃsaka*; however, for those who have not yet realized this entry, it pertains to the final three flavors (*rasa*).
Question:
If that is so, why does the *Dharmadhātuprakṛtinirdeśa* not explain this?
Answer:

The Fangdeng (Vaipulya) and the Dapin (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra) are largely the same with minor differences; because they are largely the same, there is no distinction between the two locations, yet because of their minor differences, there is a distinction between the two *sūtras*.
Question:

Previously, it was clarified that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is for those of sharp faculties; how can the current *Dharmadhātuprakṛti-śāstra* now state that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* is for those of superior faculties?

Answer: The former was based on the classification of those belonging to the three vehicles (*triyāna*), whereas the *Dharmadhātuprakṛti-śāstra* is based on those belonging to the single Buddha vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).
Question:

Question: The *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) consistently judges the teachings by stating that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Lotus Sūtra* share the same flavor (*tongwei*). Why, then, can it be said here that upon reaching the *Lotus Sūtra*, there is "matured ghee" (*shusuo*)? Answer:

When the *Xuanyi* judges the flavors according to the teaching (*jiao*), the two sutras are of equal flavor; however, this current discussion is based on the person (*ren*), and thus upon reaching the *Lotus Sūtra*, there is the stage of matured ghee.
Question:
If the flavors are judged according to the person, would there not also be those like "fresh ghee" (navanīta) among the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*? Answer:
It is as you have asked. Regarding the fifth point:

it clarifies that the previous criticisms and rebukes arose in response to specific capacities; although they provided immediate benefit at the time, they were not authorized by the Buddha and thus cannot be called a sutra.
Had he not been commanded to inquire after his illness, there would have been no occasion to recount the excellence of his former reproaches; therefore, he was commanded to inquire after his illness.
Because each was commanded to speak, what was previously taught was heard by the entire assembly, all of which was authenticated by the Tathāgata as scripture for the benefit of future generations.
For these five reasons, it is necessary to next summon the four great Bodhisattvas and the various Mahāsattvas.
Second, the formal explanation:
regarding the translation of the names and meanings of this chapter, they are fully detailed in the *Xuanyan wen*; here, we shall clarify only the differences in the teachings.

First, the Tripiṭaka Bodhisattva takes the four truths of arising and ceasing as their object, gives rise to compassion and great vows, and awakens the bodhicitta; through the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas and the six pāramitās, they subdue afflictions until they are fully matured and enter the stage of avaivartika.

The second type consists of bodhisattvas who, taking the four truths of non-arising as their object, give rise to great compassion and solemn vows, resolve upon bodhicitta, cultivate the six perfections of non-arising, sever the afflictions within the realms, and enter the stage of avaivartika.

Third is the Mahāyāna of the Separate Teaching (biejiao): taking the immeasurable Four Truths as its object, it gives rise to compassion and great vows, and one awakens the bodhicitta; by practicing the immeasurable Six Perfections up to the Ten Perfections, one severs the ignorance as vast as the sands of the Ganges and enters the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika).

Fourth, the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) take the unconditioned Four Noble Truths as their object, giving rise to compassion and great vows to awaken the bodhicitta; they cultivate the unconditioned Six Perfections up to the Ten Perfections, perfectly severing the ignorance within the dharma-realm and entering the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika).
The horizontal and vertical differences in the stages of practice following the arousal of the bodhicitta are fully detailed in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).

However, the Great Sage employs the four *siddhāntas* within the four inexpressibles to respond to the four types of faculties and conditions among sentient beings who seek the Buddha-wisdom; thus, he expounds the four teachings to clarify the meaning of the Bodhisattva as three provisional and one real, and as being neither provisional nor real, yet both provisional and real.

Regarding what is now called the "Bodhisattva Chapter": the four great bodhisattvas and all other bodhisattvas are entirely the retinue of Śākyamuni’s Dharma-body. The Tathāgata, responding to conditions to benefit sentient beings, manifests the bodies of four Buddhas and expounds the four Great Vehicles.

The Dharma-body Bodhisattvas likewise each manifest as four kinds of bodhisattvas according to the capacities of those they encounter, acting as attendants to the Dharma King to guide and receive the four types of conditions, each causing them to faithfully accept the three kinds of skillful means.

When his practice of the Way had somewhat matured, he wished to redirect that practice so that they might study the ultimate Way of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao); however, this redirection could not be achieved unless he first refuted their teacher and disciples.
It would be impossible for a Buddha, having personally taught sentient beings, to suddenly alter his own tracks or change his course; such a thing is not permissible.

Since Vimalakīrti has already extensively demonstrated that he dwells on the superior stages of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), he is thus able to rebuke those who occupy the superior stages of the various provisional teachings.

Since each of the Bodhisattvas of the higher stages had manifested their own submission through skillful means (*upāya*), those among their retinues who were abiding in skillful means felt their minds inwardly broken; they came to despise their own practices as not yet reaching the ultimate truth and all looked up with admiration for the Perfect and True Great Way. Some immediately gave rise to the perfect mind, while others attained sudden enlightenment and realized true non-arising; all of this was due to the skillful guidance provided by the four great Bodhisattvas and the various Mahāsattvas.

Now, having been summoned to inquire after his illness, if each were to recount their own refutation, it would further benefit the assembly at this time by accomplishing five kinds of benefits; therefore, it is called the "Bodhisattva Chapter.
Question:
All thirty-two thousand were neighbors to the fruit [of Arhatship], and their status was no different from that of Vimalakīrti; why were they all suddenly refuted and broken down?
Answer: Although its meaning has already been briefly clarified in many ways, it shall now be explained further. Some say:
These bodhisattvas represent the actual *upapatti-phala* (neighboring fruit), whereas Vimalakīrti represents the provisional *upapatti-phala*, which is superior.

Some say: "They are equally actual *upapatti-phalas*. As the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states, 'The ten stages have three births': these bodhisattvas represent the birth of commencement and the birth of abiding, while Vimalakīrti represents the birth of completion; thus, he is superior to the bodhisattvas."

Now, I shall provide a definitive judgment: both the various bodhisattvas and Vimalakīrti possess both fundamental and manifested aspects, and are identical in their provisional and ultimate truths; they have merely come together to assist the Buddha in bringing sentient beings to maturity.

The Four Great Beings and others conceal their ultimate reality and employ skillful means to assist in the establishment of the provisional teachings; Vimalakīrti and Aṅgulimāla conceal their provisional means and employ ultimate reality to assist in the establishment of the ultimate teachings.
Skillful means are like the anvil and ultimate reality is like the hammer; together they fashion the vessels of sentient beings.
If we discuss benefiting beings, both the provisional and the real benefit them.

If we discuss the striking, both the hammer and the sounding board are inconceivable; together they benefit sentient beings, yet this remains beyond the knowledge of the two vehicles and lesser bodhisattvas—how much less could ordinary people of the mundane world know the relative heights of their fundamental and manifest traces?
Question:

Regarding the aforementioned ten disciples who, together with their ten mental factors (*caitasika*), assisted the Dharma King to manifest and establish the Half and Full Teachings; and the various groups of five hundred followers who each propounded the cause of the body, for which Vimalakīrti’s refutations and rebukes were all grounded in specific reasons.
What do these four great bodhisattvas further represent? Answer:
These four are likely like the rain of four kinds of flowers in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which symbolizes [the Buddha’s] opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
Furthermore, from below, four great leaders emerge; what they represent is likewise so.
Among the thirty-two thousand, there are four who sustain life, which likely corresponds to these four gates.
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* adds four great Bodhisattvas to speak of forty stages; if one examines this chapter, it also seems to accord with that intention.

How is this known? For instance, the single phrase "Praising Maitreya" reveals bodhi by means of the quiescent principle of True Suchness (tathatā), appearing as though it intends to open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (buddhajñānadarśana).
Therefore, it is said that "all sentient beings are themselves the marks of bodhi"; this likely refers to the marks of the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*).

Next, [the Buddha] refutes Prabhāvyūha and points out one by one that all practices (*sarvacaryā*) are none other than the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); this likely intends to demonstrate the marks of the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*).

Next, he rebukes the Holder of the World (Lokadhara), causing him to realize that the realm of Māra and the realm of the Buddha are of one suchness and without duality; that the members of Māra’s family practicing the lamp of inexhaustibility is itself the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle; and that the deeds of Māra and the deeds of the Buddha are a harmonious fusion of good and evil—this is intended to lead him toward the realization of the characteristics of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Next, he rebukes Shan-de, saying: "In practicing *dāna*, you treat the high and the low as non-dual; within your wealth, you embody the Dharma. You honor those superior to you who are difficult to surpass and relieve those inferior to you who beg; that there is no distinction between compassion and reverence is called the 'Assembly for the Gift of Dharma. This appears to be the sign of one about to enter the tenth stage (*bhūmi*)."

The *Ahitā* contains many layers of meaning; with a single utterance, there are diverse interpretations. Why must it necessarily correspond in every instance to the stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanwei*)?
However, if one were to search through the text superficially, I fear it might indeed be so.
Question:
If that is so, Maitreya is precisely one in the position of the successor; he ought to manifest the profound—how can he [teach] what is shallow? Answer:
Because the Great Man is supreme, he must be addressed first.
The Dharma should proceed from the shallow to the profound; therefore, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision were revealed to Maitreya.
Furthermore, although the stages were manifested in relation to persons, the intention did not lie in their relative depth or shallowness.

Why is this? In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), from the very first stage, all the merits of every stage are fully possessed; thus, the initial opening [of the teaching] immediately reveals awakening and entry.
The manifestation of the stages for the four types of people is likewise so; it is simply the four positions of the Perfect Teaching.
Question:
If one person, such as Maitreya, were to refute [this view], would there not be the same benefit of transformative teaching and contemplation as described above? Answer:
Maitreya, as the Regent Bodhisattva, transforms sentient beings through both provisional and ultimate teachings, and those he transforms are not fixed.

Some may see Maitreya being rebuked; those who rely on the provisional teachings each abandon their practice of teaching and contemplation. Those who rely on the Perfect Teaching but have not grasped its meaning fixate on the words while forgetting the intent, causing their attachment to the Dharma to extinguish itself.
If one attains the realization of the meaning, one knows that these [teachings] are merely the anvils and hammers used together to benefit sentient beings.
Question:

Above, it was clarified that the various Bodhisattvas have passed away while employing skillful means; why can it now be said that Maitreya and his fellow practitioners received the teachings of ultimate reality?
Answer: The former was merely a general statement.
Since those in the position of succession adapt to the capacities of beings, how could they possibly adhere to a single standard or remain fixed like one who waits by a stump?
However, matters have both secondary and primary aspects, which is also a matter of majority.
Question: If this is so, how does this differ from the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*? Answer:
This sutra specifically addresses those bodhisattvas of sharp faculties who can attain this meaning.

For the followers of the two vehicles and those bodhisattvas of dull faculties, it merely functions as the transformation into *ghṛta*. If it were like the *Avataṃsaka*, it would be accessible only to those bodhisattvas who have received the perfect teaching, while the followers of the two vehicles and lesser bodhisattvas would not hear it at all;
however, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, everyone is able to enter.
From "At this time" onwards, the third section provides a word-by-word commentary.
This chapter is divided into two parts:
first, the summoning of the four great bodhisattvas; second, the summoning of the various bodhisattvas.
The initial section consists of four parts;
the first is the command to Maitreya.
This section is divided into two parts:
First, he was commanded to inquire after the illness; second, he declined on the grounds of incapacity.

As for the reason for this prior command: among the four teachings, there is no Maitreya who is not a candidate for succession (*parivartin*). Now that the Perfect Teaching has vanished and only the three [lesser] teachings remain, those who receive the Buddha’s provisional teachings all revere Maitreya.
Maitreya is the Great Teacher of the future who shall succeed to the seat of the Buddha.
Regarding the name "Maitreya," some say it was established from his clan name;
however, I maintain that it is not a clan name, but rather a personal name.

Why is this? Maitreya is translated here as "The Benevolent One" (Cishi). In the past, he was a king named Dharmaruci; because he nurtured the people of his country with compassion, the people called him "The Benevolent One."
From that time until now, he has always been named Maitreya.
His clan name is Ajita, which translates here as "Unconquerable. Some say:

"Ajita" is merely a name; since one has not personally examined the original text, it is not yet appropriate to hold to it definitively. Regarding the term "Maitreya," the sūtras and śāstras clarify that there are three different types of compassion (maitrī): [1] the compassion of loving-kindness (*maitrī-maitrī*); [2] the compassion of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-maitrī*); and [3] the compassion of equanimity (*upekṣā-maitrī*). Thus, they are not the same. Furthermore, the *Mahāyāna-saṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "The Bodhisattva Maitreya, dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven, manifests various forms to teach and transform sentient beings. This indicates that he is able to manifest in various bodies according to the capacities of those to be converted. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* also says: "The Tathāgata Maitreya, having attained the stage of Buddhahood, will appear in the world. This means that when the time for his manifestation arrives, he will attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, we know that the Bodhisattva Maitreya is not yet a Buddha.
