First, the object-condition of sentient beings; second, the object-condition of dharmas;

third, the objectless condition. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The loving-kindness that takes sentient beings as its object apprehends the marks of sentient beings; it is a contaminated dharma."
"Compassion with a dharma-object (dharmālambana-maitrī) is either contaminated (sāsrava) or uncontaminated (anāsrava).
Unconditioned great compassion (anālambana-mahāmaitrī) is exclusively uncontaminated.
Furthermore, according to the four teachings, there are likewise four kinds of Maitreya.
The first three teachings accord with conditions and their respective paths of cessation are extinguished when they reach their limit.
Bestowing happiness and giving rise to compassion constitutes the teaching appropriate to that stage.

While Maitreya bestows the happiness of the appropriate teaching, it is only the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*) that can bestow the happiness of the paths of cessation belonging to the preceding three types.
Just as a magnet attracts iron, so too is Maitreya of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Because there are four Buddhas, there are likewise four positions for his assistants.
Of these four Maitreyas, three are provisional and one is real.
Maitreya is a long-time resident of this Sahā world; as an assistant to the Buddha, he has primarily practiced the teachings of the three provisional means (*triyāna*).

Vimalakīrti is a Great Being from another land who has come to travel in this realm; as an assistant to the Buddha, he has primarily manifested the teachings of the single ultimate reality (*ekayāna*). He rebuked Maitreya in order to bring sentient beings to maturity and lead them into that reality.

Furthermore, the provisional and the real appear and disappear according to what is appropriate, being indeterminate; the Dharma-body is eternally quiescent, like empty space. Since even the real does not exist there, how can one speak of the existence of the provisional?
It is simply that, in responding to conditions to benefit sentient beings, they strike against one another; how could the provisional and the real be fixed?
Now, as the Buddha’s final command rests upon this matter, "Maitreya" and those who follow represent the second section: declining on account of being unable to bear the task.
This text is divided into four parts:
First, the refusal; second, the explanation for the refusal; third, the formal account of being rebuked; fourth, the conclusion of the inability. Regarding the first section:

because in the past he preached the practice of non-retrogression to the King of Tuṣita Heaven, it was of no benefit to him and thus became the subject of rebuke; how then could he bear to carry out the mission of going to inquire after his illness?
Regarding "the practice of thus arriving," secondly, this describes the reason for being summoned.
It was because he expounded the practice of non-retrogression to the King of Tuṣita Heaven.

As for why the King of Tuṣita came to Maitreya’s abode, it was because the various devas of Tuṣita had previously heard Śākyamuni bestow a prophecy upon Maitreya that he would be born in Tuṣita to serve as their teacher; therefore, they sought refuge in him in advance and came at this time to request the Way.

Maitreya expounded the practice of non-retrogression for their sake because those devaputras had previously heard the provisional teachings of the Mahāyāna and resolved their minds upon it; fearing that they might regress due to the heavy influence of celestial pleasures, he therefore taught them the practice of non-retrogression.
Regarding the term "non-retrogression," it is only upon seeing the principle that one enters the stage of non-retrogression.
Abiding immovably in the principle, one is able to give rise to all manner of wholesome qualities; this is metaphorically likened to the earth.
Because one attains the principle within the causal stage, there is the sense of being oriented toward the fruit; therefore, it is called "practice."
However, each of the four teachings has its own three stages: position (*bhūmi*), practice (*caryā*), and mindfulness (*smṛti*).

If one speaks of the three types of non-retrogression for a *śrāvaka* bodhisattva, their practice of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*—entering the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Peak (*mūrdhan*), and Patience (*kṣānti*)—is itself the stage of non-retrogression.
If categorized by number, the three grades of the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) are divided into three types of non-retrogression.

If following the *Abhidharmasaṃyuktavastu*, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) constitute the stage of non-retrogression, the stages of "warmth" (*ūṣmagata*) and "summit" (*mūrdhan*) constitute the non-retrogression of practice, and the stage of patience constitutes the non-retrogression of mindfulness.

Regarding those of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao): from the stage of Nature (Xingdi) up to the Arhat, those who have attained equal merit through the six stages are "non-retrogressive in position" (wei bu-tui). Those at the stage of the Pratyekabuddha and those who have attained equal merit through the seventh stage are "non-retrogressive in practice" (xing bu-tui), as the Bodhisattva cultivates skillful means. At the eighth stage, the Bodhisattva’s path-observation flows as a dual stream, which is termed "non-retrogressive in mindfulness" (nian bu-tui).
If the eighth stage is equal to that of the Pratyekabuddhas, it is only from the ninth stage onward that one attains non-retrogression in thought (*citta-avivartana*).

For those of the Separate Teaching (*prthaktīya*), the Ten Abidings constitute non-retrogression in position; the [Ten] Practices and [Ten] Dedications constitute non-retrogression in practice; and upon entering the stages, when the three contemplations manifest before one, this is non-retrogression in thought.

In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the initial stage of the ten levels of faith constitutes non-retrogression in position; from the middle stage of the ten faiths onward, it constitutes non-retrogression in practice; and upon entering the first dwelling of the ten abodes (the Stage of Initial Resolve), one attains non-retrogression in thought.

Furthermore, the three types of non-retrogression at the stage of "semblance" (*sādharmya*) correspond to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), while the three types of non-retrogression at the stage of "partial truth" (*bhūta-amśa*) correspond to the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*). The former three are provisional (*upāya*), and the latter one is real (*tattva*).

Maitreya clearly understands the Buddha’s teachings regarding the provisional and the real; he employs the provisional by setting aside the real when preaching to the devas, and for this reason, he is subject to reproach.
Question: Maitreya knows the capacities of others; for what reason does he suppress his actual realization and employ expedient means, only to be rebuked and refuted?

Answer: These devaputras ought to have previously heard the teaching of expedient means. Therefore, Maitreya employs expedient means as the anvil, intending to manifest the hammer of Vimalakīrti’s teaching of ultimate reality. By doing so, they together perfect these devaputras as vessels for the Path; thus, he manifests himself as receiving the rebuke and refutation.
Among them, some who heard Maitreya’s discourse failed to grasp its correct meaning; yet, upon hearing [Vimalakīrti] rebuke Maitreya, they immediately attained entry [into the Dharma].
"At that time, Vimalakīrti... and so forth constitutes the third section: the formal narration of the event of being rebuked.

The text consists of five parts: first, a general determination; second, a formal reprimand, refutation, and deconstruction of the objection; third, a summary of the faults and an exhortation to abandon them; fourth, a detailed exposition of the characteristics of true Bodhi; and fifth, the benefits obtained by the various devaputras.

At the outset, it is generally established that "The World-Honored One has granted the prediction to you, Venerable One, that in one more life you shall attain Bodhi. The reason for this establishment is that he intends to refute and dismantle [the opponent's position]; therefore, it is necessary to establish [the premise] first.
Regarding "one birth," this refers exclusively to his current birth in Jambudvīpa.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Three births ago he was born in Tuṣita; now he is to be born in Jambudvīpa."
The meaning of *sambodhi* has already been clarified in the Profound Text (*Xuánwén*).
However, the four teachings differ in how they clarify the attainment of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

Regarding the Tripitaka Teaching: Maitreya will be born in a future life beneath the Bodhi tree, where both his active afflictions and residual habits will be exhausted; this is called the "prediction of bodhi," as set forth in the *Shorter Maitreya Sūtra*.

Regarding the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*): although the fundamental afflictions within the realm of desire have been eliminated, residual habits (*vāsanā*) remain unexhausted. When one takes a final birth beneath the Bodhi tree, one severs all residual habits through the wisdom of "correspondence in a single thought-moment" (*ekacittakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*). This is termed the "Prediction of Enlightenment" (*bodhi-vyākaraṇa*), as recorded in the *Mahāmaitreya-buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*.

As for those of the Separate Teaching (Pṛthagdharma), Maitreya’s Dharma-body has extinguished nine grades of the delusions of ignorance and dwells on the Ground of No Defilement (Vimalā-bhūmi); with one grade remaining along with its residual habits, he will later be born in Jambudvīpa at the site of the terrace of enlightenment to manifest the exhaustion of that final grade of ignorance and its habits; thus his Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) is perfected, eternally abiding and immutably still.
This is precisely the matter described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where Sudhana enters the tower and beholds the signs of Maitreya’s future attainment of Buddhahood.

As for the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): Maitreya’s Dharma-body has exhausted the forty-one grades of ignorance and dwells in the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyagbodhi*). With one grade of ignorance and its residual habits (*vāsanā*) still remaining, he will subsequently be born in Jambudvīpa at the site of the Path of Quiescence (*nirvāṇa-maṇḍala*), where he will attain great enlightenment with sudden clarity. Once that final grade of ignorance and its habits are both exhausted, this is the ultimate, wondrous enlightenment that uses the traces to manifest the fundamental reality. The three bodies of Bodhi are neither vertical nor horizontal, like the character "I" (𑖀) in the world, and it is also like Sudhana entering the tower and beholding the signs of Maitreya’s future attainment of Buddhahood in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Regarding the three provisional teachings and one ultimate reality: although Maitreya’s Dharma-body is eternally quiescent and his original ground is wondrously transcendent—such that how could one fathom their relative heights?—he nonetheless accords with the capacities of beings to benefit them, assisting Śākyamuni and continuing his transformative ministry; therefore, he must receive a formal prediction (vyākaraṇa).
According to the perceptions of sentient beings, there are four faculties as conditions; thus, four kinds of predictions are bestowed, each heard according to their respective capacity.
Now, Vimalakīrti fulfills what they hear, expounding with a single voice so that each understands according to their kind.

If it were definitively established that Maitreya has received the prediction of one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), this would mean that all four types of "one-birth" [candidates] are definitively established.
Regarding the section beginning with "As for its application," part two provides a critical refutation through objection.
The text consists of two parts:
first, from the perspective of the gate of arising; second, from the perspective of the gate of non-arising.
Now, I shall provide both a general and a specific interpretation.
First, regarding the specific interpretation: the initial section, based on the gate of arising, directly rebukes the bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka.

Why? Because the Tripiṭaka pertains to the half-syllables (*ardhakṣara*) of arising and ceasing; thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "For the sake of disciples with dull faculties who are śrāvakas, [the Buddha] taught the characteristics of dependent origination as arising and ceasing."
Second, regarding the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*), this refers to the critique of the Mahāyāna teachings for bodhisattvas.

The Mahāyāna takes non-arising and non-ceasing as its gateway to the "complete letter" (*paripūrṇākṣara*) teaching; thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The Buddha taught the characteristics of dependent origination as neither arising nor ceasing for bodhisattvas of sharp faculties."

The reason for criticizing based on "non-arising" (anutpāda) is to criticize the general and specific bodhisattvas within the Mahāyāna, as well as to criticize the faults of the verbal views of "arising" in the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), such as attachment to the path (shundao'ai).
Regarding the second point, the general interpretation: it universally refutes the notion that Bodhisattvas of the four teachings all possess both birth and non-birth.
For the Three Treasuries (Tripitaka), "birth" refers precisely to birth.
For the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), "birth" refers to entering into the partial truth; this is the non-arising of all phenomena, and even the arising of Prajñā is non-arising arising.
In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the wisdom of the Middle Way cultivated through conditions is likewise "non-arising arising.
In the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), arising through true cultivation is also "non-arising arising"; even if one loses this meaning, it must be rectified.

Regarding the statement that "all four teachings are non-arising": although those of the Tripitaka [teaching] have not yet severed their afflictions, how could they not know the principle of the True Truth?
When viewed from the perspective of practicing the cause in anticipation of the fruit, the cause is arising while the fruit is non-arising.
In the Shared Teaching, the cause is the non-arising of principle within the realm of desire, and the fruit is the non-arising of both phenomena and principle within the realm of desire.

In the Distinct Teaching, the cause is the non-arising of principle both within and without the realms of desire, and the fruit is the non-arising of both phenomena and principle beyond the realms of desire.

In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the "non-arising" (*wusheng*) is at first glance the same as in the distinct [teachings], yet there is a difference in the establishment of true reality, conditions, wisdom, and cessation.

If Bodhisattvas of the four teachings each look toward their respective fruits and practices while seeking causal causes and desiring prophetic predictions (*jibie*), they are all rebuked—whether they rely on arising or non-arising within their own respective divisions.
Although two interpretations have been provided, with respect to the intent of this chapter, the distinct interpretation is correct.

Now, within that distinct interpretation, first, regarding the gateway of arising according to the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*), there is a specific refutation through censure; this consists of three parts:
first, the fixedness of the three times; second, the refutation; and third, the citation of evidence.

Regarding the first passage: according to the Abhidharmikas, the three periods of time exist substantially. Although past wholesome dharmas have passed away, they are not extinguished because they are bound by the cord of acquisition (*prāpti*).
Although future [wholesome dharmas] do not yet exist, they arise when the time arrives.
Wholesome dharmas of the present are accomplished within the mind; therefore, all [dharmas] exist substantially.

According to the Dharmaguptakas, [dharmas] are non-existent across two time periods: past dharmas are non-existent because they have truly ceased despite being real dharmas; however, although they exist only as provisional names, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of their retribution is not lost.
Future dharmas are non-existent because they do not yet exist.
Present wholesome dharmas are existent because they are accomplished within the mind.
Although these two schools clarify the existence or non-existence of the two or three time periods, both maintain that there are three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The Sarvāstivādins clarify the three characteristics as existing simultaneously, whereas the *Shelun* masters (Sautrāntikas) clarify them as existing at different times.
"Simultaneous" means that arising, abiding, and ceasing occur at once.
"Successive" means that the time of arising is not the time of abiding, and the time of abiding is not the time of ceasing.
For this reason, the three periods of time were previously established.
"If one passes beyond to non-abiding," secondly, this is the formal refutation of the attainment of prediction across the three periods of time.

"If it were a past birth, that past birth has already ceased": since both the body and the wholesome [deeds] have both perished, and a dharma that has already ceased possesses neither body nor wholesome [deeds], how could one receive a prediction?
If one were to take the past by means of the present and receive a prediction regarding the future, why would one not grant the prediction in the past rather than in the present?

As for the statement, "If it is to arise in the future, the arising of the future has not yet arrived," since the goodness of the future does not yet exist, if that future goodness already existed, it should be called "already come" and not "future."
If [the future] does not yet exist, then there would be neither body nor merit; how, then, could one bestow a prediction based on the future?
If it were based on the future, and one could bestow a prediction regarding the present when the future does not yet exist, then sentient beings as well should likewise receive predictions.

Regarding the statement, "If there is present birth, present birth has no abiding": since the wholesome mental states of the present arise in accordance with the mind, and when the mental conceptions cease, the wholesome states also cease accordingly; and since the ceasing consciousness does not reach the future, how can one use present wholesomeness to receive a prediction for the future?
This refutes the existence [of dharmas] throughout the three periods of time.
If the past and future do not exist, how can one receive a prediction (vyākaraṇa) based on the wholesome [karma] of the past?
If it is argued that the present exists and that one may receive a prediction in reference to the present, [we reply that] the present has no duration; it perishes as soon as it arises.
If one cannot even abide in the present, how can one properly reach the future and receive a prediction of enlightenment based on the present?
Furthermore, since all three periods of time are empty and the three periods themselves do not exist, how can one receive a prediction based upon them?
Emptiness is without a prediction [of enlightenment], yet to conceive of it as existing is itself a perversion.
If one were to receive a prediction based on such a perversion, then all sentient beings—who are likewise entirely subject to perversion—should also be granted a prediction.
This refutes the non-existence [of dharmas] across the three periods of time.
Regarding the phrase "As the Buddha’s arrival also perishes," thirdly, it cites the Buddha’s own words as proof.
This specifically proves that the present has no abiding and that one cannot receive the prediction of a future birth.

Why is this? Maitreya was not yet satisfied. If both the past and the future were entirely non-existent, then it would be impossible to bestow a prediction of Bodhi based on a body in the past or future; yet now the Buddha bestows a prediction for the future based on the present body. How, then, can you say that because the present lacks duration (*sthiti*), one cannot receive a prediction for the future? As for citing the Buddha’s teaching that "there is birth, there is aging, and there is cessation" as proof, this is intended to refute Maitreya’s calculation that clings to a single lifetime and maintains that the present remains stationary; thus, by means of this very body, he refutes the notion of receiving a prediction for the future.
Regarding the phrase "also arises" and so forth: if one relies on the Sarvāstivāda doctrine that the three characteristics exist simultaneously, then arising itself possesses cessation.
Although there is a single lifetime, when sought through reasoning, there is no momentary abiding; how, then, could one receive a prediction for the future based on the present?
Question:
The three characteristics and the four characteristics do not mention aging; how can it now be said that the Buddha taught that there is also aging? Answer:
The four characteristics differ from one another, and "aging" is itself "alteration.

The reason why aging is cited rather than "abiding" is that Maitreya clings to the Buddha’s teaching that among the three or four characteristics there is a characteristic of abiding; it is with reference to this characteristic of abiding that he receives his prediction in the present.

Vimalakīrti again cites the Buddha’s words, stating that among the three characteristics there is only aging and no abiding, thereby proving that the present lacks abiding; thus, one cannot receive a prediction for the future based on the present, for if you, O worthy one, do not accept this, you contradict the Buddha’s words.
Although there is a distinction between the present and other times, the three characteristics are extremely rapid.
Although it is said that there is "abiding," the Buddha taught that this too is "aging.
If abiding were itself aging, it would be the characteristic of transformation.
Since there is no characteristic of fixed abiding, how can one receive a prediction of future enlightenment based upon this?
Some masters claim that Vimalakīrti used emptiness to refute the prediction;
however, this interpretation deviates from the fundamental tenets.
Examining the text of this sutra, it still employs the teachings of the Tripitaka regarding arising and ceasing to perform the refutation; when, then, would emptiness be used?
The section beginning with "If by non-arising" constitutes the second: the Gate of Non-Arising.

The reason for summarizing this section is to censure those who, while adhering to the general and specific aspects of the Mahāyāna as well as its perfect teaching, lose their true intent; who, longing for the fruit and practicing the cause, seek a prediction of non-arising, thereby causing the mind to move in delusion and obstructing entry into the Right Path.
Why is this? For those in the three teachings all see the prediction of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
As stated in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, there are four kinds of predictions:

First, the prediction for those who have not yet resolved their minds; second, the secret prediction; third, the prediction in the presence [of the Buddha]; and fourth, the prediction upon seeing the non-arising of dharmas.
Those of the Tripiṭaka who suppress their fetters do not receive the prediction of non-arising, but only obtain the first three.

Regarding those who have not yet awakened the resolve: although they may still be bound by all fetters, or may be practitioners of the Two Vehicles using skillful means, or possess the root-nature of the Tripiṭaka or Mahāyāna, they are nonetheless granted a prediction [of enlightenment] even though they have not yet awakened the resolve. This is like when the Buddha, at the edge of the Jeta Grove, granted a prediction for the pigeon and the sparrow.

Regarding "prophesying in secret," this refers to those who are nominally designated as bodhisattvas and bodhisattvas on the stage of dry wisdom (śuṣka-vijñāna-bhūmi) within the stage of subduing patience (kṣānti); these are mostly prophesied in secret. However, bodhisattvas on the stage of nature (gotra-bhūmi) who possess compliant patience (anuloma-kṣānti) are all prophesied openly before them.
Question:
For what reason was it recorded secretly? Answer:

There are bodhisattvas whose mental conduct is not yet mature; if they hear of their prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), their minds become lax and heedless, and thus they do not receive the prediction in the present.

Within the Mahāyāna, the three teachings all involve severing the fetters and entering the stages, and there are predictions of non-arising (*anutpāda*). The first three are not the true [prediction]; seeing non-arising is the true reception of the prediction.
Why is this? Because in these three cases, one has not yet seen the principle, has not attained mastery, and has not yet established the fulfillment of self-benefit and the benefit of others.

If one sees non-arising, then even while dwelling within birth and death, one acts with sovereign ease, accomplishing both self-benefit and the benefit of others without any decline in merit; therefore, these three are the true predictions of enlightenment.
The bodhisattvas of the three teachings pray for this prediction with their hearts; therefore, [the text] rebukes Maitreya to refute these three [views].
The text is divided into two parts:
first, refutation based on the principle of non-arising; second, refutation based on the practice of non-arising.

Regarding the first point: the three teachings differ in their understanding of non-arising (*anutpāda*). In the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), it merely explains the non-arising of partial truth; in the Distinct and Perfect Teachings (*biejiao* and *yuanjiao*), it explains the non-arising of the Middle Way.
The principle of these two types of non-arising is fully elucidated in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).
While the recorded stages (*vyākṛta-pada*) in the three teachings are generally the same on the surface, their underlying meanings differ; they must not be conflated.

Regarding the four types of recorded stages in the three teachings: those who have not yet resolved their minds for enlightenment in the three teachings are recorded as having the Mahāyāna root-nature appropriate to their respective teachings, even though they remain bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*).
Alternatively, it may be a provisional teaching for those of the Two Vehicles, whereby they are granted a prediction of enlightenment even before they have yet resolved their minds toward awakening.

Furthermore, in the three teachings, those who are nominally designated as bodhisattvas—specifically those ordinary persons at the stage of subduing patience—are frequently granted predictions either secretly or openly.
The ordinary bodhisattvas within the three vehicles all receive the prediction of manifest enlightenment (*sammukhībhūta-vyākaraṇa*).
These three types of prediction are not definitive.
In the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*), if one enters the stage of the eighth person or the stage of seeing, one receives the prediction of non-arising (*anutpāda-vyākaraṇa*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to a srotāpanna is, for a bodhisattva, the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
This refers to the stage of receiving the prediction [of enlightenment] upon seeing the partial truth of non-arising.

Why is this? Because the eighty-eight [afflictions] to be abandoned through the vision of the truths are all exhausted and enter the stream of the untainted path; this is the stage of vision, called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

If one further advances to contemplate non-arising, abandons the afflictions of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), practices profound meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and sports with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), then one accomplishes the benefit of oneself and others, matures sentient beings, and purifies the Buddha-lands.

If the faculties of sentient beings in the three vehicles have matured, they immediately realize the path through the eight phases of enlightenment; therefore, the Buddha bestows the prediction of bodhi upon them within the Mahāyāna of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
Second, in the distinct teaching (Biejiao), the first stage, the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi), constitutes the vision of true non-arising and the receiving of the prediction.

The reason for this is that upon ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*), one awakens to the truth and first perceives the True Path; that is, one immediately perceives the principle of perfect, true non-arising (*anutpāda*). At that moment, one severs the first grade of ignorance beyond the realms (*dhātu*) and exhausts the delusions of individual views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); this wisdom and severance constitute the stage of the prediction of non-arising.

If one is granted the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of the eightfold marks of a Buddha, it may at first glance appear similar to the Shared Teaching (p’ung-chiao); however, it differs in that it uses the provisional traces to manifest the fundamental reality, and the prediction is for the attainment of the fruit of the eternally abiding Buddha.

Now, classifying this according to the Shared Teaching (tongjiao), the realization of the partial true principle and the severance of views within the realm of desire—whether as wisdom or as abandonment—is termed the "non-arising" of the Bodhisattva.

Here, according to the Distinct Teaching (biejiao), the realization of the perfect true principle and the severance of views both within and outside the realms of desire—whether as wisdom or as abandonment—is termed the "non-arising" of the Distinct Teaching.

Thus, with each moment of mind becoming quiescent, one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). Through the self-practice of the *dharmakāya* and the transformation of others by the *nirmāṇakāya*, one will certainly attain the fruit of Buddhahood, which is eternally abiding. Therefore, upon ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*), one receives the true prediction of non-arising from the Buddha; this is the definitive prediction.

Regarding the third, the prediction of non-arising in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): receiving the prediction at the first stage, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*shizhu*), is precisely the prediction of the true non-arising of the Perfect Teaching. Why is this?

Because the Stage of Initial Resolve is equivalent to the Ground of Joy (*huānxī dì*) in the Distinct Teaching (*biéjiào*); however, the gateways of their teachings differ in clarifying the severance of delusions, like the difference between peeling an onion and slicing it.
Various masters have failed to grasp this meaning and have harbored much doubt regarding these words.
However, upon examining various sutras and treatises, this principle is frequently found; one should grasp its essential meaning and apply it, as is fully explained in the *Xuanyi*.

This refers to the stage of the initial resolve; whether in terms of wisdom or abandonment, it constitutes the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) in the Perfect Teaching, and is precisely the prediction of non-arising in the Perfect Teaching.

Having merely received the three teachings, one has not yet attained the state of non-arising; with a mind full of longing, one falsely constructs conditions, and all who seek in this way lose their way.
Although the Perfect Teaching is not erroneous, if thoughts arise from the mind, it is like agitating water and clouding a pearl.
Because of these faults, he uses Maitreya as a foil for his censure.

The reason for using him as a foil is that Maitreya occupies the position of the "Successor to the Three Teachings" (sanjiao buchù) and is about to exhaustively fathom the source of non-arising within those three teachings.
Although those who seek the three teachings may understand this stage in their initial resolve, none have yet entered it.

If one were to reprimand Maitreya for being recorded as a Bodhisattva in the final stage of the three teachings, that would be to judge the Great Being by the principles of the three teachings, which are difficult to scrutinize.

If even Maitreya has not yet received his prediction, how could those newly initiated bodhisattvas of the three teachings—who pray for non-arising and hope to attain true prediction—not awaken to this truth and each cease their expectations?
If a Bodhisattva of the Shared or Distinct [Vehicles] ceases their seeking for the mark of non-arising, they may then enter the stage of the Perfect Vehicle’s prediction of non-arising.

If a Bodhisattva of the Perfect Vehicle knows that within the stage of non-arising there is no receiving of a prediction, and likewise does not give rise to the thought of seeking a prediction of non-arising, then the water of the mind becomes clear and the image of the jewel manifests of itself.

Furthermore, when one abiding in the stage of insight (*darśana-bhūmi*) according to the Shared Teaching is rebuked during Maitreya’s final moment of mind, the internal [delusions] are shattered and broken, whereby one enters the stage of the Perfect Unarisen Prediction (*an-utpāda-vyākaraṇa*).
In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the first stage (*bhūmi*) is equivalent to the first dwelling (*vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*);
thus, it is not included among those subject to censure. If one perceives Maitreya during the thirty mental states (*citta*), this is censured from the perspective of principle (*li*).
If these mental states are relinquished, one may enter the first dwelling of the Perfect Teaching and receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

If those who have first resolved their minds in the Perfect Teaching, as well as the disciples of the five grades, give rise to thoughts of aspiring to enter the stage of true non-arising and receiving the prediction of enlightenment, the water of their minds will become stirred and turbid, and they will be unable to attain the purity of the six sense organs.

Now, having heard the Great Being’s rebuke of Maitreya—that even those who have nearly exhausted the state of non-arising are still criticized on account of principle for lacking the meaning of receiving a prediction—how much more so for those at the initial stage of the five grades who yet hope for non-arising?
The mind of conceptualization and recollection is immediately extinguished.
If the pure mind is constantly unified, one then gives rise to a semblance [of realization] and enters the stage of the Ten Faiths.

If one attains purity of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), it is as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "Although they have not yet attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), their mental faculty is pure in this manner."

This is because one hears and is able to receive and uphold the teachings on the marks adorned by a hundred merits of the countless Buddhas of the ten directions as they preach the Dharma for sentient beings.
Since there is no forgetting or error, how could the coarse obstacles of discursive thought, recollection, or longing arise?

If even those at the stage of the Ten Faiths are thus, how much more so for one who has entered the Dwelling of the Initial Resolve? Yet, the reason it is necessary to rebuke Maitreya is that there is a specific intention behind it.

When it says, "If one receives a prediction of enlightenment through non-arising, then non-arising is itself the true position," this is specifically using the principle of non-arising to refute Maitreya; within that principle, there is no such thing as a prediction.

Why is this? The bestowal of the prediction (vyākaraṇa) is fundamentally based on the fulfillment of wisdom and the abandonment of afflictions; thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Bodhi is a designation for fulfillment.
If, in principle, there were neither arising nor ceasing, there would be no wisdom or abandonment; how then could one speak of the fulfillment of wisdom and abandonment?
Thus, both the partial and the perfect, as well as non-arising, are all neither wisdom nor abandonment.
If even wisdom and abandonment do not exist, how much less so the fruit of Bodhi?
That "non-arising is the true state" means that both the partial and the perfect, as well as non-arising, are all the true state; this is the ultimate principle.
If we clarify the ultimate according to principle, this ultimate principle is not itself a stage, yet it is the foundation of all stages.
It is like the position of the Son of Heaven being the ultimate; because of this, there exist the positions of civil and military officials.

Those today who occupy the stages of a Bodhisattva across the three teachings do so entirely through the principle of non-arising; thus, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "All worthy and holy ones are distinguished by means of the dharma of non-action (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)."

The stage of non-arising is precisely the equal and true Dharma-realm; since the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings, how could there be the principle that one may receive the three teachings and attain Bodhi in a single lifetime?
Therefore, within the state of ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*), there is neither the bestowal of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) nor the attainment of the fruit of enlightenment (*bodhiphala*).

The reason for this is that both types of non-arising are neither cause nor fruit; how, then, could one receive a prediction within the causes of the three teachings regarding the fulfillment of future wisdom and the abandonment of afflictions?
Since the two kinds of non-arising (anutpāda) within the state of true reality (bhūtakoṭi) are not fruits, how could one discuss attaining the fruit of bodhi as elucidated by the three teachings?
Therefore, it is asked: "How is it that Maitreya receives the prediction of [attaining Buddhahood] in one more birth?"

If even Maitreya, when approaching the immediate vicinity of the ultimate fruit and the state of rightness, has not yet received a prediction, how much less can one who has merely first resolved to practice the three teachings hope to enter the state of rightness of non-arising and receive the prediction of Bodhi?

For this reason, [the text] rebukes Maitreya for receiving a prediction of fruition (phala-vyākaraṇa) based on his neighborly status, intending thereby to refute those who rely on the three teachings and harbor expectations for the stage of the prediction of non-arising (anutpāda-vyākaraṇa).
Thus, when both the common and specific [aspirations] are sought in error and are transformed into the Perfect Teaching (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa), all expectations are likewise extinguished.
Question:
Vimalakīrti rebuked only Maitreya; how can we know that his underlying intention was to censure all three [bodhisattvas]? Answer:

The preceding text states, "He expounded the practice of non-retrogression for the King of Tuṣita Heaven," while the subsequent passage says, "In reality, there is neither one who gives rise to the mind of *sambodhi*, nor anyone who retrogresses. The stage of non-retrogression is precisely the entry into the correct position of non-arising; it is the stage of receiving the true prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

Bodhisattva Chapter, Part Two: 18. A Brief Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll 18. From the phrase "For the sake of" onwards, section two:
refuting the notion of receiving a prediction of enlightenment based on a single lifetime by means of the practice of non-arising.
The reason for refuting [the opponent's position] by means of their own practice is that Maitreya raised a hypothetical objection.
The objection states:
"In principle, it is not possible for there to be the reception of a prediction (vyākaraṇa)."
What prevents taking non-arising as the object of practice, whereby through the completion of such practice, wisdom and severance are attained, and one receives the prediction of Bodhi?
The text consists of four parts:
first, the dual determination; second, the dual refutation; third, the dual conjunction; and fourth, the dual conclusion.
First, regarding the "paired determination": does it arise from Suchness, or does it cease from Suchness?

The reason for this inquiry is that Maitreya’s mind was still not fully satisfied; he wondered whether, if there is no principle of arising, then Suchness itself would be unconditioned and thus remain unrecorded.
However, because sentient beings have been deluded regarding the principle since beginningless time, there is birth and death.

When Buddhas and Bodhisattvas contemplate non-arising, their true wisdom becomes manifest; as this light of wisdom arises, the darkness of delusion gradually fades away. If the illumination of wisdom reaches its ultimate limit, then false delusions are completely exhausted. When wisdom and severance are perfected, it is called the fruit of Bodhi.
How could it be that one receives a prediction (vyākaraṇa) by merely criticizing according to principle?
Therefore, does one first receive a prediction through the fulfillment of the fruits of wisdom and abandonment regarding both arising-as-such and ceasing-as-such, as previously established?

Regarding this dual establishment, it is implicitly based on the predictions for the bodhisattvas of the three teachings concerning their wisdom and abandonment regarding arising-as-such and ceasing-as-such.

If one considers the Shared and Distinct Teachings, their events are the same while their principles differ; for the Shared and Complete Teachings, both events and principles differ; whereas for the Distinct Teaching, the principle is the same while the events differ.
Question:
How can the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles] have the same principle yet different practices? Answer:
They are the same because they share the Middle Way; they are different because of the distinction between the two modes of cultivation.
"If [you say] 'by means of ultimate existence there is cessation,'" this is the second double refutation.
Since you have silently accepted the meditative concentration, I now apply a double refutation based on that practice.

Furthermore, regarding the profound summary of the three teachings, it is stated that one receives the prediction of Bodhi in a single lifetime through wisdom and severance; this constitutes a dual challenge based on the two truths of the partial and the perfect.
First, concerning the Shared Teaching: the partial truth of the Shared Teaching is precisely the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*), and this principle is not something to be severed by wisdom.

If one contemplates True Suchness (tathatā), wisdom arises and delusions are extinguished; although True Suchness itself is without arising, it can give rise to wisdom. This wisdom arises from True Suchness and does not depart from it; this is precisely the merit of wisdom arising from True Suchness.

Although suchness is not itself extinguished, one perceives the extinction of delusions within suchness; this extinction is inseparable from suchness, which constitutes the virtue of abandonment as the extinction of suchness.
Now, Vimalakīrti challenges this by saying:
"If one receives the prediction based on the arising and extinction of suchness, then since arising proceeds from suchness, and suchness has no arising," [how can there be such a prediction?]
From the perspective that there is cessation according to suchness, there is no cessation according to suchness.

The intent of the objection is precisely this: the essence of suchness is neither arising nor ceasing; yet, with reference to suchness, one speaks of arising and ceasing, and thus possesses the virtues of wisdom and abandonment.
If there were arising and ceasing, it would not be called "suchness" (tathatā), but would instead be conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

If it were not arising and ceasing and yet were not conventional truth, then it would be truly without arising and ceasing; thus, suchness is neither arising nor ceasing, and one cannot say that the wisdom of arising and ceasing proceeds from suchness to effect cessation.
Therefore, the pure teaching states: "From suchness there is arising, yet suchness has no arising;
from suchness there is cessation, yet suchness has no cessation.
If wisdom and abandonment were not established through the non-arising and non-cessation of suchness, how could there be any arising, cessation, wisdom, or abandonment apart from suchness?
Thus, there would be no basis for receiving the prediction of the knowledge and abandonment of a single lifetime based on the practice of non-arising.
Furthermore, since the mind that takes non-arising as its object accomplishes knowledge and abandonment, such knowledge would be self-arisen;
yet if it were by virtue of the principle of the object, it would be other-arisen.
If the subject and object are conjoined, this constitutes co-arising;
if they are separated from subject and object, this constitutes the wisdom and abandonment that arise without cause.

Thus, Nāgārjuna’s verse states: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves. How, then, could the mind that takes True Suchness as its object give rise to wisdom and abandonment and thereby receive a prediction of enlightenment?

Up to and including the point that things do not arise without a cause—all these follow the first proposition and collectively cite verses from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* to correctly refute "arising from another" through a fourfold analysis. Why is this?

Maitreya says that because one attains the prediction [of enlightenment] by generating wisdom from causes and achieving the wisdom that severs practice, these two pairs distinguish between the Separate and Perfect Teachings; each category is pervasive, yet it is difficult to scrutinize—do not lose even a single phrase.
However, regarding the two teachings—the general and the specific—the general teaching takes the partial truth as its object, while the specific teaching takes cultivated practice as its object.
Furthermore, in the specific teaching, cultivated practice is taken as the self-nature, whereas in the perfect teaching, true cultivation is taken as the self-nature.
Be careful not to be indiscriminate.
Question: Why is it that the Separate Teaching takes "cultivation based on conditions" as its own nature, while the Perfect Teaching takes "true cultivation" as its own nature? Answer:
The universal and specific functions of wisdom achieve Buddhahood; since these are merely objects, their conditions are themselves.
The perfect function of reality (*tathatā*) achieves Buddhahood; since the cultivation of conditions consists merely of the adornments of merit and wisdom, *tathatā* is itself the condition.
Question:

Since the Truth of the Common Teaching (Tongjiao) is the reality of the negation of existence, it merely gives rise to wisdom (*jñāna*). Wisdom is that which belongs to the practitioner, and thus is said to be "self.
Principle (*li*), being merely the objective realm, may be considered "other."

Question: Since the principle elucidated in the Separate Teaching is the same as that of the Perfect Teaching, why is it not the same as the Perfect Teaching but rather the same as the Shared Teaching?
Answer: Although the principle is indeed the same as the Perfect Teaching, the capacities of the practitioners and the teachings differ.

To clarify separately the contemplation of the True [Dharmadhātu]: although the True is eternal, its principle is not itself wisdom. When one uses wisdom to contemplate the principle, true wisdom has not yet been manifested; thus, the wisdom that takes this as its object through cultivation is not called "eternal. Therefore, it is not the same as the Perfect [Teaching].
Question:
The Separate and Common teachings both take [the conventional] as their own object; for the time being, the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) can be understood by analogy with the Common teaching.
Since the Perfect teaching takes the Truth (*tattva*) as its own object, how are its four permutations to be understood?

Answer: Wisdom and cessation are not self-generated, nor are they accomplished through conventional cultivation; they are not generated by another, nor are they accomplished through conventional conditions; they are not co-arisen, nor are they accomplished through the synthesis of true conditions; yet they are not produced without cause, nor are they accomplished apart from true conditions—such is the wisdom and cessation of the Perfect Teaching.
If, when examined through the four propositions, wisdom and severance cannot be found, then one will not receive the prediction of attaining the Perfect Teaching in a single lifetime.

However, it is precisely because of the difficulty of the Vimalakīrti’s intent that the true cultivation of wisdom and severance arises spontaneously from within the Perfect [Teaching]; this thorough investigation is something that the two sets of ten [propositions] alone are incapable of achieving.
If one does not deeply perceive this meaning, the principle of true cultivation according to the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) will be difficult to maintain.
If even the true aspect of the Perfect Teaching is thus precarious, how much more so for the provisional, distinct, and conditional modes of cultivation? How could they possibly be easily sustained?
Based on the intent of the "One Difficulty" and "Three Difficulties" from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, the distinctions remain perfectly clear without confusion.
Question:
By employing only a single approach, how can you cause those who cling to the three teachings to each hear a different account and each abandon their respective attachments?
Answer:

Formerly, when I returned to my native village of Shan, I saw that at Daoyin Temple, Zhang Gong had commissioned a depiction of one set of Vairocana Buddha on the northern wall of the main hall for Emperor Xuan of the Liang dynasty, along with a painting of a tortoise.
The two eyes of that image follow the movements of people, gazing at them all; the eyes of the tortoise are likewise.
If even the wondrous phenomena of the mundane world can be thus, how much more so is the inconceivable, sublime wisdom in which Vimalakīrti abides?
The most difficult task is to cause each of the three [categories of beings] to abandon their own afflictions of clinging by breaking through them.
From the phrase "All sentient beings" onwards, the third section treats both [the subject and object] in parallel.
The text is divided into two parts: first, taking the four types of suchness as parallel points; second, the formal conclusion of these parallels. Regarding the first part:
first, suchness with respect to all sentient beings; second, suchness with respect to all phenomena; third, suchness with respect to all worthy sages; and fourth, suchness with respect to Maitreya.
If one deeply investigates the meaning of these four "simultaneous" (ping) practices, they are also esoterically summarized according to the Three Teachings.

First, regarding the general sense of the four "simultaneous" practices: three are "concordant simultaneous" (*shunping*), proceeding from the beginning to the end; one is "inverse simultaneous" (*niping*), proceeding from the end to the beginning. This first [category] concerns the *tathatā* (suchness) of sentient beings.
Regarding "conformity and parallelism": sentient beings are themselves provisional persons, and the suchness of provisional persons is identical to the suchness of Maitreya—identical and non-dual.

If the suchness of sentient beings is neither arising nor ceasing and cannot receive a prediction of enlightenment, then the suchness of Maitreya is likewise so; how then can he alone receive a prediction?

If Maitreya attains the prediction of enlightenment through suchness that is neither born nor extinguished, then these two suchnesses would be different; if they were different, they would not be suchness.
If there is no difference in suchness, then the prediction should be identical, and even the non-prediction would likewise be identical.
Whether it be the "penetrating" (tōng) or the "non-penetrating" (fēi), these do not constitute three distinct categories.

Second, regarding all phenomena as being in accord with suchness: all phenomena, whether sentient or non-sentient, are suchness. "Sentient" refers to the five aggregates as substantial dharmas; "non-sentient" refers to external lands and so forth. All of these are entirely suchness, identical to the suchness of Maitreya, one and without duality.
This merely substitutes insentient things for sentient beings; every sentence is identical, and thus they must be explained by analogy.

Why is this? Because the Buddha does not bestow predictions upon insentient dharmas; hence the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "If a nyagrodha tree were able to cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom, I would likewise bestow upon it the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Because they are without mind, they are not granted a prediction [of enlightenment].
Therefore, they are considered parallel, yet distinct from sentient beings.
Third, regarding the various sages and worthies, they are parallel in accordance with the principle.

Thus, the worthies and sages of the three vehicles of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings are all suchness; they are identical to the suchness of Maitreya, being one and without duality—this is also analogous to what preceded.
From the phrase "if sentient beings" onwards, every sentence is the same; explain them by following this analogy.
Prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, those of the two vehicles who were worthies and sages all lacked the prediction of enlightenment;
therefore, they are considered "parallel. Fourth, regarding Maitreya, he returns to and parallels the preceding three cases; hence, it is called "returning."
This consists of three layers, namely those combined with the preceding three sets;
in each instance, it is stated that "it is exactly as before, without duality," regarding whether there is a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) or no prediction, and so forth.
The intended meaning remains entirely the same.

The second [section] is based on the Separate Teaching (pratyekavyavasthāna), and the third is based on the Perfect Teaching (pūrṇavyavasthāna); both employ the fourfold parallelism, which can be understood by analogy.
"From 'If Maitreya' up to 'non-dual and non-different'" constitutes the second [part], the conclusion of the parallelism.
There are also four intentions: first, concerning sentient beings; second, concerning all dharmas; third, concerning the various worthies and sages; and fourth, concerning Maitreya.

These four sections also esoterically relate to the three teachings: the first relates to the Shared Teaching (tongjiao), which includes both the three [teachings] that follow and the one that reverses.

First, regarding sentient beings, it is stated in accordance with their collective bonds: "If Maitreya is to receive the prediction of enlightenment, then all sentient beings should also receive the prediction.
Since the two [Maitreya and all beings] are identical, they should both obtain the prediction together.

Vimalakīrti himself then explained: "That which is suchness (tathatā) is neither dual nor differentiated. If there were duality or differentiation, one might allow for one person to receive a prediction and another not;
since there is neither duality nor differentiation, all should equally receive the prediction.
Question:
What is the difference between "two" and "different"? Answer:
Second, regarding their distinct natures alone, differences entail that their characteristics are not the same.

Second, concerning the simultaneous conjunction of all dharmas; third, concerning the simultaneous conjunction of the various noble sages—these are omitted from the text for brevity, but may be understood by analogy with the conjunction of sentient beings.
Regarding the fourth point, concerning Maitreya’s “reversal and alignment,” the text is abbreviated and does not set it forth; one must rely on the previous explanation of reversal and alignment.
If the various worthy sages do not receive a prediction of enlightenment, then Maitreya likewise would not receive a prediction.
Why is this so? For suchness is neither dual nor differentiated.
If all sentient beings do not receive the prediction of enlightenment, then all dharmas are likewise the same.
Secondly, regarding the distinction between the Separate and Perfect [Teachings], one may understand by analogy that Zhiyan’s fourfold summary applies universally as well.
If Maitreya were unable to provide a comprehensive explanation, then the meaning of receiving predictions across the Three Teachings would be undermined; thus, he was shown the refutation.
The section beginning with "If Maitreya" below provides a fourfold summary and explanation.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, an explanation based on the wisdom of destruction; second, an explanation based on the merit of destruction.
Regarding the initial passage, it is also explained esoterically by means of the wisdom and virtue of the three teachings.

First, regarding the explanation according to the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-chiao*): awakening (*bodhi*) is contrasted with the afflictions of sentient beings; the suchness (*tathatā*) of the afflictions of sentient beings and the suchness of awakening are non-dual and not different.
If Maitreya were to attain *sambodhi*, then all sentient beings should likewise attain it.
In this regard, Vimalakīrti himself explains that "all sentient beings are themselves the mark of *bodhi*."
Since sentient beings are themselves the mark of bodhi, and as such do not arise from themselves, there can be no further fulfillment of the wisdom of fruition-bodhi to be predicted.
Second, regarding the specific explanation: while they are generally the same as the universal [explanation], they differ in their application within the context of "seeing."

Third, regarding the explanation according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*): the afflictions of sentient beings possess the characteristic of wisdom, just as a person’s face possesses the characteristic of merit. This characteristic of bodhi is itself the characteristic of suchness (*tathatā*) and the characteristic of wisdom.
All sentient beings and Maitreya possess these marks; the Buddha observes that both types are worthy of receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Although this encompasses the two preceding teachings, the intent of the sutra lies in the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna*).
Question:
Question: Why are the three teachings used only for refutation, while the Śāstra uses only the Perfect Teaching?
Answer: Refutation is for the purpose of destroying attachments; explanation is for the purpose of establishing the true meaning.
In the previous teachings, there were neither persons nor practices; since the teachings themselves were refuted, they were all non-existent.
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the refutation of attachments is itself the teaching, and persons and practices are manifest therein; therefore, it correctly refers to the Perfect Teaching.
This concludes the explanation that "True Cultivation is like non-arising" means the absence of the virtue of wisdom (jñāna-guṇa); thus, one does not receive the prediction (vyākaraṇa).
"If Maitreya arrives, he will no longer undergo further extinction. Second, this is an explanation that concludes by refuting [the notion of] severed merit (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
It also implicitly refers to the three teachings.
First, regarding the refutation of the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sāmānya*): since the nature of nirvāṇa and sentient beings is not different, both are equally extinguished and liberated.
Therefore, Vimalakīrti himself explains: "The Buddhas know that all sentient beings are already in the state of nirvāṇa and cannot be extinguished again.

Since sentient beings inherently possess the characteristic of nirvāṇa, and as there is no further extinction, there can be no recordable extinction of the quality of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) within the fruit [of Buddhahood].

Second, regarding the refutation of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha): if the Suchness of sentient beings is identical to the mark of Nirvana and thus cannot be extinguished, then there would be no extinction through the Nirvana of ultimate virtue—the final severance of ignorance at the stage of the final mind of the Ten Grounds.
Furthermore, regarding the refutation of attachments, it can be understood that the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) applies these categories universally.
In the preceding teachings, the refutation of the practices of those who follow the teachings can be seen as analogous to the above.

This explanation—that True Suchness (Tathatā) is imperishable—constitutes the virtue of non-interruption; therefore, [the stage in question] cannot yet receive the prediction of Great Nirvana (Mahāparinirvāṇa).
"From 'Therefore, Maitreya' onwards, [the text] constitutes the third section: the formal conclusion of the fault and the reprimand.
This is further divided into three parts:
first, the formal conclusion of the fault; second, the exhortation to abandon the view; and third, the explanation."

1. Regarding the refutation of the fault: If there were no skillful means to teach the fruit of bodhi, yet one were to speak of this bodhi to induce others' minds to give rise to the view of bodhi, there would be the fault of deceiving others.
Therefore, Vimalakīrti himself said: "In reality, there is no arousal of the mind for supreme enlightenment (bodhicitta), nor is there the stage of non-retrogression.

If even the perfect bodhicitta cannot be apprehended, and thus there is no one who retrogresses, how could there be any provisional teachings regarding the arousal of the mind or the stage of non-retrogression?
Since the cause cannot be obtained, there is likewise no fruit that can be obtained.
To request a prediction of the fruit when no fruit exists is to delusively entice the mind.
Question:
If this is indeed the Buddha’s teaching, then Maitreya’s prediction must be the Buddha’s own deception; what concern does it have with Maitreya? Answer:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states, "When the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment, he did not perceive even a single dharma as real."
"An empty fist deceives young children; thus one leads and delivers all beings.

Although the Buddha initially used such means to entice and encourage them, when they reach the ultimate reality, these must be abandoned; therefore, he uses this to conclude the fault and rebuke Maitreya.
Regarding "Maitreya’s arrival and his vision": second, the exhortation to abandon views.
The teaching that in the expedient means of bodhi there is no person—if one clings to this and does not relinquish it, it will obstruct entry into the single reality.
Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "All [views] prior to this are termed wrong views"; for this reason, they must be abandoned.
Question:
Why does it cause Maitreya to exhort the devaputra to abandon his view?

Answer: Maitreya instructed him to resolve his mind on awakening and cultivate the stage of non-retrogression, yet because he did not believe the words of others, Maitreya was sent back to urge him to relinquish [his former position].
"Therefore, he attained it with utmost sincerity" is the third point, explaining the intent behind urging him to relinquish it.
Regarding those who break through both body and mind, there are four different teachings.

First, as for breaking through the Tripitaka: in the Sūtras of the Śrāvakas, it is likened to a poor man seeking the daughter of a wealthy family; the family of the girl also says, "If you wish to have my daughter, you must purify your house."

Regarding the statement on the three types of *bodhi* for the Bodhisattva at the final moment of mind: one who wishes to attain *bodhi* should cultivate the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Only when the planting of these marks is fulfilled does one attain *bodhi*.
This refers to the attainment of the body.

The subduing of the fetters and their ripening at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), the descent upon Māra, and the attainment of the extinction of ambrosia (amṛta) beneath the Bodhi tree—these are what is meant by "attainment through the mind.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refutes this in detail, asserting that it cannot be attained through either body or mind.

Second, regarding the refutation of the common [view]: if one cultivates the various marks and signs with an empty mind, purifying the Buddha-lands and adorning the environment and the primary body, this is called attaining the body.
When sitting at the site of enlightenment, severing both the active afflictions and their residual habits through the wisdom of single-minded correspondence, this is called attaining the mind.

To refute this, as the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person follows a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata."
This, moreover, cannot be attained through body or mind.
Third, regarding the refutation of distinctions: if one says that by the cessation of this form one attains eternal form, this is attainment through the body;
the same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, which would then be attainment through the mind.
Now, examining these words: does one obtain permanent form through the extinction of impermanent form, or does one obtain permanent form without the extinction of impermanent form?
When examined through these four propositions, it cannot be found; that is to say, it cannot be attained by means of body or mind.

Fourth, regarding the refutation of the "perfect" [nature]: the wondrous color of the true cultivation is manifested by the mind itself; it does not need to be manifested through the cultivation of conditioned merit and wisdom, and thus it cannot be attained through body or mind.

Furthermore, if one were to attain bodhi through the manifestation and fulfillment of the essence of form and mind through true cultivation, this would likewise be a matter of attaining it by means of body and mind.
Therefore, as previously refuted—wherein "suchness" is like that which has no arising—the suchness of dharmatā is form;

the dharmatā of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness does not arise. This non-arising is the fulfillment of the outflow-free (anāsrava), and thus it cannot be attained by means of body and mind.
Below "Quiescence" (Section IV), there is an extensive exposition of true Bodhi.

The reason for this extensive exposition is that, since the previous [section] has both refuted [wrong views] with difficulty and exhorted the abandonment of [false] views, those who believe in partial teachings would have no way to turn their hearts toward the truth, and those who follow the Perfect Teaching but have not yet entered it would likewise remain ignorant of the correct principle. Therefore, it is necessary to extensively demonstrate the correct principle of Bodhi through twenty-five sections.
The text consists of three parts:

first, one section that briefly explains the title of the true-mark bodhi; second, twenty-two sections that clarify bodhi by means of true wisdom and abandonment; third, two sections that conclude with true wisdom and abandonment as bodhi by returning to the wondrous principle of the true mark.

The reason for this is that previously, when the ignorance to be destroyed was severed, one could not receive the prediction of enlightenment; now, once the attachments and illnesses of those who have received the four teachings have been removed, he again explains that the meaning of true wisdom and severance is entirely Bodhi. Thus, the Bodhi of the three virtues is like the worldly letter *I*, which is precisely the Perfect True Bodhi.
The explanation of these twenty-five phrases relies exclusively on the Perfect [Teaching].
Regarding "Quiescence is Bodhi": all dharmas converge upon the mind, and the mind is itself the Middle Way.
The principle of *tathatā* is fundamentally unborn from the beginning and is now without cessation.
That which is unborn is not wisdom; that which does not cease is not annihilation. This is the meaning of true quiescence, and it is also the non-arising of the Great *Nirvāṇa*.
That which is non-arising and ineffable is called bodhi; this refers to the bodhi of the true reality (*dharmatā*) according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

As for the statement "extinguishing all marks," if one does not know the bodhi of true reality, it cannot be said that grasping at the marks of the four teachings gives rise to afflictions and birth-and-death.
These four kinds of characteristics give rise to sixteen characteristics that manifest all characteristics; thus, there is the turbulent movement of all afflictions and birth-and-death.
If true-mark bodhi is non-arising, and non-arising is ineffable, then the four gates are all extinguished.
How much more so, then, would the delusions regarding the three types of fourfold gates—such as arising and non-arising—and all other marks not be extinguished?
The intention of the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) is that the markless true reality can extinguish all marks; therefore, he says they are "extinguished."
Below "non-contemplation," second, there is the correct application of true wisdom to severing [delusions], which is itself bodhi.
This is further divided into two parts:
first, a brief explanation; second, a detailed explanation.
The first section is briefly divided into two parts:
the first two sections correctly elucidate the virtue of true wisdom, which is true bodhi, that is, *mahāprajñā*;
the subsequent four sections elucidate the virtue of true abandonment.
"Non-contemplation is bodhi" means that the cessation of skillful contemplation is itself non-contemplation.
"Free from all conditions" means being free from the cultivation of conditions and from all conditions whatsoever.
Regarding the statement "non-practice is bodhi": if one realizes true emptiness, there is nothing to be practiced; thus, all myriad practices are themselves bodhi.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "If the mind and its mental factors do not practice, this is practicing prajñā."

"Non-recollection" means not recollecting the four kinds of predictions of enlightenment nor any phenomena; this true practice of contemplation is itself the enlightenment of the virtue of true wisdom.

"Severance is bodhi because it reaches the state of non-attachment" (T2): this second point, explained in four sections, clarifies that the virtue of true severance is itself bodhi, which is the virtue of liberation.

Regarding the statement “severance is bodhi”: when True Suchness (tathatā) manifests and the afflictions of view and thought are severed, this is the bodhi of the virtue of severance (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
To relinquish the grasping that gives rise to views of bodhi and all other views is what is meant by “relinquishing all views.”
"Enlightenment is detachment" means that it is detached from the contemplative practices and all phenomena elucidated by the four teachings; it is the enlightenment of the merit of true severance.
"Detached from all deluded thoughts" means being detached from the causal cultivation of the four gates and all deluded thoughts.

Regarding the statement "hindrances are bodhi": if one knows that within the equal and true dharma-realm, Buddhas do not deliver sentient beings, this is something that even all Buddhas cannot practice; it obstructs the vows and various skillful means of the teaching gates. This is precisely the merit of true severance.

Regarding the statement, "Not entering is bodhi": if one knows that *tathatā* (suchness) is ultimately without marks (*animitta*), one does not enter into the provisional teachings on *nirvāṇa* nor into any phenomena (*dharma*). Because one does not enter, there is no attachment; this is precisely the bodhi of the quality of true severance (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
"Conformity is bodhi. Below this, secondly, it extensively explains that the abandonment [of defilements] by true wisdom is itself bodhi.
In this section, for the most part, the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) is explained at length, while the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) is briefly mentioned.
Why is this? Enlightenment is wisdom, while severance belongs to nirvana; therefore, they are distinct.
This constitutes two parts:
the first nine sections primarily concern the virtue of wisdom, and the subsequent seven sections concern that which cannot be attained through body or mind.

"Conforming to this is bodhi": if one observes and does not perceive the bodhi of the four teachings, one is then conforming to the true suchness of the Middle Way of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
"Abiding in this is bodhi": if wisdom does not abide in the four teachings nor in any phenomena, it is precisely abiding in the dharma-nature of the Perfect Teaching.

"Reaching this bodhi": if one contemplates that all dharmas and the bodhi of the four teachings are ultimately unattainable, one is then able to reach the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) within true suchness (tathatā).

"Non-duality is bodhi. If there were expedient means that taught bodhi and all dharmas in a biased manner, this would constitute the sensory object of dharmas confronting the internal faculty of mind; thus, it would be duality.
Contemplating that these two dharmas are both unobtainable, one enters the gate of non-duality and perceives the Middle Way, thereby becoming detached from the two deaths.
This stage belongs to the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
"Equality is bodhi": if one contemplates nirvana and saṃsāra as equal, this is equality with the Buddha-nature of empty space; it is the bodhi of the virtue of true wisdom.

“Unconditioned is bodhi. If one contemplates that the nature of dharmas is profound, eternally quiescent, it is truly unconditioned, not subject to the transitions of birth, old age, sickness, and death.

"Wisdom is bodhi. Through various skillful means and teachings, one enters the truth by relying on cultivation; yet one does not perceive the mental activities of sentient beings. In the true wisdom of the Perfect Teaching, which is quiescent yet ever-illuminating, the mental activities of sentient beings manifest spontaneously within that wisdom, clearly and distinctly understood.

"Bodhi is not [something that arises]" means that while various skillful means and teachings clarify that wisdom cultivated through conditions enters into and accords with principle, which is then termed "true wisdom," the essence of perfect, true cultivated wisdom is itself the principle of quiescence; it is not a case of wisdom coming to accord with principle.

"Non-conjunction is bodhi. From the perspective of ultimate principle, although expedient means and true wisdom are conjoined with ignorance and have not yet been able to abandon habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), when the essence of true cultivation-wisdom does not conjoin [with them], one is then able to abandon the fundamental categories of habitual tendencies.
This first section pertains to the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
It is extremely difficult to discern what to reject and what to accept;
one must reflect upon it thoroughly. From "Awakening has no location" onwards, the subsequent seven sections cannot be understood through body or mind.
This one [aspect] cannot be attained by means of the body.
In the partial teachings, the wisdom of bodhi relies upon the form-body (rūpakāya), taking the form-body as its locus; this is that which can be attained by means of the body.
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the bodhi of form and mind are non-dual; since there is neither subject nor object, it is "without location," and thus cannot be attained by means of the body.
Because "the provisional name reaches equality," these six points clarify the meaning that true wisdom-bodhi cannot be attained by means of the mind.

"Designation is bodhi. The mind is a designation; the four kinds of bodhi exist only as names. If one contemplates them as empty, one perceives the Buddha-nature; thus, true wisdom-bodhi cannot be attained by means of the mind.
“Awakening is like a magical creation. All phenomena are like magical creations, and thus all four kinds of awakening are like magical creations.

If one knows that, being like a magical creation, they are all unattainable, then one neither grasps at the characteristics of awakening nor abandons afflictions; this is the awakening of true wisdom.

“Non-distraction is bodhi. Distractions caused by afflictions, conceptualizations arising from conditions, and the movement of thoughts during cultivation are all forms of distraction. To know that these distractions are all unattainable is to still the mind and reach the fundamental source; when the inner mind is constantly tranquil, there is no longer the distraction between object and wisdom.
"Good tranquility is bodhi. If one practices through the conditions of skillful means without yet being in accord with the principle, it cannot be called true goodness.
To have objects of perception and discursive thought is itself distracted ideation; it is not called tranquility.
In the Initial Mind of the Perfect Teaching, wisdom is identical to True Suchness; this is termed "good.
Its illumination occurs without the movement of thought; this is termed "quiescence.
Wisdom is identical to the Dharma-nature; that the Dharma-nature is unstained is what constitutes "intrinsic purity."

“Non-apprehension is bodhi. If one knows that the four teachings on bodhi and all phenomena are non-existent, and the mind does not grasp or cling to them, this is the perfection of bodhi—being free from the mind that seeks bodhi through objective conditions and from all phenomena.

"Non-differentiation is bodhi. While various provisional teachings clarify that bodhi is distinct from afflictions (*kleśa*), if one knows that bodhi is not different from afflictions, this is precisely the bodhi of the merit of equalizing wisdom (*samatājñāna*) according to the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*).
"Because it is incomparable and most difficult to know": third, this explains the inconceivable three virtues of bodhi as a conclusion.
"Incomparable is bodhi": inconceivable true suchness (*tathatā*)—as wisdom and cessation—is all phenomena; since one phenomenon cannot be compared to another phenomenon, it is beyond metaphor.
"Subtle and wondrous is bodhi. The provisional teachings are not subtle; in the Perfect Teaching, all dharmas are suchness (*tathatā*), and suchness is itself wisdom and cessation.
