If one contemplates this characteristic correctly—as fully explained in the "Entrance into the Non-dual Dharma Gate"—one abandons the two extremes and correctly manifests the Middle Way; herein, its meaning is further elucidated.
The reason the Tathāgata asks this question is that, as previously established, there is no distinction in unimpeded wisdom, for the merit of the bodies and knowledge of all Buddhas is equal.
The Buddha wishes to demonstrate that the Dharma-body of the Mahāsattva is no different from that of the Buddhas; therefore, he asks how one contemplates the Dharma-body.
If one distinguishes the Dharma-body, the Dharma-body must have a specific referent; that which is referred to is precisely the Buddha-land, and thus this question arises.
Another interpretation states:
The Buddha as the Response-body possesses names such as boundaries, cities, and lands; but since the Dharma-body is profound and quiescent, how could it have any land?
Now, this interpretation is not so. Even though the Dharma-body of the Buddhas is neither defiled nor pure, it can, according to conditions, traverse both the defiled and the pure simultaneously.
Now, if the Buddha’s Dharma-body is neither object nor wisdom, yet can simultaneously illumine both object and wisdom, for what reason could it not discern the true realm of the land?
Therefore, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "The realm of inconceivable wisdom; the illumination of inconceivable wisdom.
Is this inconceivable realm not precisely where the numinous wisdom of the Dharmakāya dwells?

The *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* states: "Vairocana is the most wondrous Dharma-body," and further says that he possesses a land called the Constantly Quiescent Light (*nitya-praśānta-raśmi*) which pervades all places; is this not indeed the true realm?
Second, the specific response.

Within the contemplation of the three periods of time, regarding the phrase "not coming from the prior limit": if one were to see future dharmas entering the present, then it would be possible for them to arise or to come, and it would be possible for them to have limits or to be limitless.
Fundamentally, one does not perceive any coming of the future; how much less could there be a further entry into the present?
Therefore, there is no coming from the prior limit (*pūrvānta*).

Regarding "no going to the posterior limit (*aparānta*)," if there were a phenomenon that ceased and entered the past, one could speak of its cessation and its departure, and one could say whether it has gone or has not gone.
Since no dharma is seen to enter the past, for this reason, it does not go toward the future limit.
As for the phrase "it does not abide now," if there were a dharma existing in the present, one could say it exists and abides, and one could speak of it as either permanent or impermanent.
Since no dharma can now be found existing in the present, how can one say it "abides"?
Therefore, it cannot be found when sought throughout the three periods of time.
Another interpretation states:
Prior to the vajra [wisdom], there is no permanence, bliss, self, or purity; subsequent to the vajra [wisdom], there is permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
This current interpretation is not so; prior to the vajra [wisdom], there is permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Why is this? The dharma of buddha-nature is inherently present from the beginning; it is not something that has only recently come into being.
Following the attainment of the diamond-like samādhi, there is no longer impermanence, suffering, non-self, or impurity.
Why is this? A sutra states:
"A Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages further practices the affairs of ordinary beings for immeasurable kalpas.

If the Dharmakāya were to arise as a response within the six realms and undergo birth and death like an ordinary being, it would likewise possess impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity; therefore, while it appears identical to others, it is not truly the same.
The other [master] explains:
"The Nirmāṇakāya (Transformation Body) is simply the Nairmāṇika (Emanation), and the Nairmāṇika is simply the Nirmāṇakāya.
My current interpretation is not so; the Nirmāṇakāya can act as the Nairmāṇika, but the Nairmāṇika cannot act as the Nirmāṇakāya.

Ordinary beings, non-Buddhist practitioners, seers possessing the five supernatural powers, and various devas and spirits are all capable of transformation, yet these cannot serve as a true response [to the needs of beings].
That which is transformed is likewise merely a temporary, provisional existence, unable to sustain it from beginning to end.
Now, we shall distinguish what is "appropriate" (*ōng*) and what is "identical" (*dō*). That which is identical throughout its beginning and end—the dharma of a single period—is termed "appropriate.

When the Tathāgata, with a mind free from discrimination and through spontaneously functioning wisdom, responds to the capacities of sentient beings according to their conditions, he employs this response without any obstruction. He does not exert effort in mental application; it is like a bright mirror where an image appears as soon as it is presented, such that the reflected image corresponds exactly to the object without any further discrepancy.
Just as when celestial immortals manifest transformations, they must first form a thought and apply effort before a transformation can occur;
so too, when one exerts the mind and moves the hand to draw a human figure, it is not necessarily the case that no thought is involved at all.
The distinction between the sublime and the non-sublime can be understood through these two analogies.
Regarding "not observing form": the mind is like a magician who creates various forms.
If one knows that the magician is a deceiver, then one no longer perceives the forms conjured by him.
Now, form is produced by the magician that is the mind; since this very mind cannot even be apprehended, where could such form be seen?
Therefore, one does not contemplate form.
Regarding "not contemplating the suchness of form": if one perceives form as different from suchness, then one would be dissolving form into suchness.
Because one does not currently perceive the distinction between form (*rūpa*) and suchness (*tathatā*), one does not contemplate the suchness of form.
Regarding "the nature of form" (*rūpa-svabhāva*), some say that suchness is simply nature, and nature is simply suchness.
There may be this interpretation:

now, the Sage does not permit the same dharma to be stated twice nor the same signification to be proclaimed twice. Now, taking this nature as the Buddha-nature, one does not contemplate form as empty in the conventional sense, nor does one contemplate form as such emptiness in the ultimate sense; one does not contemplate the Buddha-nature as the Middle Way within emptiness. Because one calculates that the Middle Way possesses the Buddha-nature, one gives rise to a craving for the path (*anulomikī chanda*), which constitutes the "fall from the summit" (*mūrdha-pāta*).
Therefore, the preceding text states: "Both 'self' and 'nirvāṇa' are empty; there is only the illness of emptiness, and even this illness of emptiness is empty.
Now, not contemplating nature is the absence of attachment to the path; therefore, one does not contemplate nature.

Regarding "not arising from the four great elements": although one contemplates this body, one does not give rise to delusion regarding the four great elements as ordinary beings do, nor does one give rise to [limited] understanding regarding the four great elements as those of the two vehicles do.
Being without delusion and without liberation, it is said not to arise; being identical to empty space, this is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
As for the "six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*), they are able to accumulate the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) and construct birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
It is not like the accumulation of the six sense bases of ordinary beings; thus, the eyes and ears have already transcended, surpassing the spheres of the six faculties of ordinary beings.
As for "not being within the three realms," it is because it has emerged from both the ultimate and the conventional truths.
"Having abandoned the three impurities" means being free from the three kinds of defilements of the realms.
"Conforming to the three liberations" means that by taking the single true reality as an object, one conforms to the three liberations.

Regarding the phrase "the three knowledges are equal to ignorance," the source of ignorance is precisely the reality of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). This dharma-nature has no equal; there is no wisdom that can equal it. This is called "equal to the unequaled" (*asamasama*).

As for the three types of clear knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*): with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), one can clearly illuminate the future; with the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), one penetrates the present; and through the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), one exhaustively observes the past, reaching back to the beginning of ignorance.
Although even those in the ten stages do not perceive its beginning, only a Buddha can know both its beginning and its end.

Since it is said that "observing the true mark of the body, one observes the Buddha in the same way," and since the Buddha has exhausted the beginning of ignorance, we now know that its beginning is equal to that of ignorance itself.
Regarding "the exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣaya*): one is able to know the outflows of the five stages; because ignorance and delusion are exhausted, it is called "equality.
"One characteristic" (*ekalakṣaṇa*) is the characteristic of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
"Diverse characteristics" (*nānālakṣaṇa*) are the distinctions of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
Now, the true mark (lakṣaṇa) is neither real nor conventional; therefore, it is neither one nor different.
"Not self" means that wandering to another country is called the "mark of the other," while arriving at one's father's house by chance is called the "mark of the self."

This should be extensively refuted through the application of true cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and conditional cultivation (*pratyaya-bhāvanā*), as well as the principles of self-arising and other-arising.
By severing and detaching from these notions of self and other, one enters into the true reality (*tattva*).
"Not non-characteristic" means it is not [mere] nirvāṇa.
"Non-apprehension of marks" means it is not saṃsāra;
being not saṃsāra, it is not an ordinary person (pṛthagjana). It is not nirvāṇa, nor is it the two vehicles (dviyāna).

It is not this shore, thus it is not the conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya); it is not the other shore, thus it is not the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya); it is not the middle stream, thus it is not the various afflictions (kleśa).
"Leaving behind this shore, which is neither this nor that, and departing from the other shore, which is neither not-this nor not-that.
As for "transforming sentient beings," this generally clarifies the functional application of the Dharmakāya.
Neither this nor that is precisely neither birth-and-death nor nirvana.
Neither by means of this nor by means of that is precisely the wisdom that contemplates the two truths, wherein both the object and the wisdom are simultaneously illuminated.
"Cannot be known by wisdom" means that because all phenomena are dispersed, it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
"Cannot be cognized by consciousness" means that because all phenomena are aggregated, it is termed consciousness (*vijñāna*).
This is precisely the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of birth and death.
"Neither darkness nor light" refers to the resolution of delusion; the resolution of delusion is itself birth-and-death and nirvana.
The name is the mundane, while the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is the supramundane; therefore, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding "neither strong nor weak": birth and death are harsh and coarse phenomena, which are termed "strong"; wisdom is that which supports principle and is easily awakened to, which is termed "weak.
Because it is neither strong nor weak, it is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
"Being not in a location" means that the Dharma-nature does not reside within the boundaries of birth and death; how could it exist within a specific realm? Therefore, it is said to be "not in.
"Not departing" means that the land of eternal quiescent light is also omnipresent throughout all locations; therefore, it is said to be "not departing."
"Neither conditioned nor unconditioned" is like the Gate of Inexhaustibility.
"Neither demonstrating nor explaining" is like Vimalakīrti’s silence.
"Non-giving" is not the other shore of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
"Non-avarice" is not like the shore of stinginess and secrecy characteristic of ordinary beings;
the same applies to the other six perfections.
Nirvana, being ultimate and true, is sincerity; saṃsāra, being empty and false, is deception.
"Non-coming" means arriving by means of the path of reality to achieve perfect enlightenment.
"Non-going" means departing from the triple world by means of that same path to reach omniscience (*sarvajñā*).
Transcending this coming and going, one neither emerges as a follower of the Two Vehicles nor enters as an ordinary person.
"The path of language is cut off," as when Vimalakīrti remained silent.
"Not a field of merit" is as when Subhūti was rebuked;
"not not a field of merit" is as when Subhūti was consoled;
"not one worthy of offerings" is as when Subhūti was rebuked.
"It is not that they should not be honored": the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, is called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).
"Identical with the limit of reality and equal to the nature of phenomena" means to be in profound accord with ultimate truth.
"Inconceivable" refers to the dharma of the inconceivable liberation. This applies even to movement;
it is the same for all sentient beings. It is likewise for every single being.

Those who are without discrimination enter into the single true reality (*ekalakṣaṇa*) and do not perceive high or low; they are without loss and without falling into the three types of outflows (*āsrava*) within the three lands (*tridhātu*).
Phrases such as "neither joy nor weariness" are all explained in reference to the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three lands.
Regarding "that which has not yet existed" and "that which will exist," one should explain this meaning by applying the verse on the three periods of time to the *nirvāṇa*.
Third, the conclusion.
Fourth, the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox, as in the text.

Second, regarding Śāriputra’s question: Śāriputra is the one who initiates the teaching. Since he already knows that the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) and its true nature of the Great Being are identical to those of all Buddhas, he next asks in order to reveal the capacity for the unimpeded great function of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), which transforms sentient beings according to conditions. Thus, he questions.
This question still compares the underlying intent of the Tripiṭaka:
if the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka has passed away, he is no longer born; if a Bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka still possesses afflictions and obscurations, he is subject to birth.
If that is so, one must ask from where he passed away to come and be born here.
Regarding this, there are two parts:
first, the snapping of the body; second, the Buddha’s revelation of the country where he resided.
The first section is divided into two parts:
first, the question of the son; second, the answer.
Within the answer, there are five sections:
First, a counter-interrogation; second, an illustration by analogy; third, a question; fourth, an answer; fifth, a citation of the Buddha’s words as an explanation.
Regarding the counter-interrogation: "If within your liberation there is still no death or birth, how could there be death or birth within my *dharmakāya*?"
Since you are not like that, how can you pose this question?
Second, "For example, as a magician causes illusions to vanish and illusions to arise"—how could these be real?
If there were no authentic records, one could not say that there is passing away and rebirth.

Fifth, in the citation of the Buddha’s words for explanation, it says: "Although a bodhisattva passes away, they do not exhaust their roots of goodness," which differs from the two vehicles, who are said to exhaust their roots of goodness by extinguishing the body and exhausting wisdom.
The Bodhisattva is not extinguished, and the merit produced by their wisdom likewise cannot be extinguished; by means of these roots of goodness, they are able to benefit sentient beings.
They do not increase evil, unlike ordinary people who accumulate [karma] without exhausting their roots of goodness.

This is not like the extinction and disappearance of the Two Vehicles; because their roots of goodness do not perish, they are able to respond to lands of defilement and purity, yet they do not perpetuate the good or evil of either the defiled or pure lands.
The Buddha’s answer regarding the Pure Land is divided into three parts:
first, the Buddha explains the Pure Land where he dwells according to conditions; second, Śāriputra offers praise; third, the Mahāsattvas provide an exposition.
The explanation consists of five parts:
first, the question of whether the sun conjoins with darkness; second, the answer; third, the question of how the sun rises; fourth, the answer; and fifth, the detailed exposition.
This clarifies that the person [in question] shares with all Buddhas the Dharma that corresponds to the two bodies (dvikāya), and so forth.

Second, from the passage "The great assembly thirsts with longing to behold the Land of Wonderful Joy" onwards, it describes the manifestation of the Pure Land, which is the dwelling place where Great Beings (mahāsattva) roam and reside.
There are three intentions here:

first, to verify the Pure Land of the Great Being; second, to inspire the assembly of the present time to cultivate the practices for a Pure Land; and third, to cause them to resolve to be reborn there.
For this reason, there follows this section of text, which is divided into seven parts:

first, the great assembly’s thirst and desire to see; second, the command to manifest [the Buddha]; third, the fulfillment of the command by moving [the Buddha] there; fourth, the Buddha’s exhortation for the assembly to practice; fifth, the generation of the resolve for enlightenment by the great assembly; sixth, the return to one's original place after benefiting others; and seventh, the praise by Śāriputra.

Regarding the current statement, "The great assembly thirsts with longing to see," it is because they have heard that the Land of Utmost Joy is the dwelling place of this Great Being; therefore, they look up to him with single-minded longing.
Second, the Buddha’s command to manifest, which is twofold:
first, clarifying that the Buddha’s quiescent illumination perceives and knows her thoughts; second, the actual command to manifest.
Third, the act of manifesting in response to the command, which is sixfold:

1. With a single mind, he intended to move the world-system of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and the Forest of Lapis Lazuli; 2. He manifested his supernatural power; 3. Those who possessed supernormal powers perceived it as a marvel; 4. The Buddha declared that this was the deed of Vimalakīrti; 5. Those who lacked supernormal powers were unaware of it; 6. Upon entering this land, there was no diminution [of its splendor].
Fourth, the Buddha exhorts the assembly to cultivate the practice of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, the exhortation to contemplate the adornments and purity of that land; second, the assembly’s response that they have already seen them; and third, the formal exhortation to practice.

Regarding the practice of immovability: as clarified in the response to the elder’s son within the "Buddha-land" chapter, and likewise as entering a room to offer consolation and subdue others; practicing on what is not the Path while penetrating the Buddha-path—this very gate of the exhausted and the inexhaustible is the practice for the Pure Land.
Fifth, regarding the assembly’s arousal of the mind for practice, there are two aspects:
first, the arousal of the mind; second, the making of vows.

There were fourteen *nayutas* who attained awakening immediately. All of them—having been addressed by the various teachings and various miraculous transformations as the formal discourse was nearing its conclusion—were shown this Pure Land and were collectively exhorted by the Tathāgata. Therefore, at that single moment, fourteen *nayutas* attained awakening.

Second, regarding the making of vows: since pure conduct is profound and subtle, it is not easily discernible; therefore, one should take an oath to be born there and practice therein, for the Buddha’s prophecy states that one shall indeed be born there.
There are two kinds of receiving a prediction (vyākaraṇa):
first, the distant; second, the near.
If, after making a vow, one will certainly be born there, this is a near prediction.
If one cultivates the causes for pure conduct, one will necessarily attain the fruit of rebirth in a pure land; thus, that Buddha-land is a "distant prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*).
Sixth, as in the text.
Seventh, Śāriputra’s praise, which consists of six parts:

1. A Buddha asks whether [the disciple] has seen [the truth]; 2. He respectfully replies, "Indeed"; 3. He makes a vow for the sake of all sentient beings; 4. He himself receives an entrustment; 5. He praises the merit of hearing the sutra; 6. He further emphasizes the profundity of the resulting blessings.
Regarding the "Exemplification and Elevation" section, it is explained through six successive rounds as in the text.
If one follows the intended meaning of these words, this constitutes the section on Dissemination (*pravartana*).

However, since it clarifies that Śāriputra is a person of the Hīnayāna who is not capable of upholding the Great Canon, he does not belong to the section on Dissemination; rather, his presence serves merely to provide an introductory impetus for the dissemination.

13. Chapter on the Dharma-Offering (10). Commentary on the Chapter on the Dharma-Offering: This chapter specifically clarifies how Śakra propagates the sūtra and upholds the Great Dharma; it constitutes the third section, that of the Propagation.
There are generally two categories:
"Circulation" (liutong) is named after its metaphorical meaning, like the source of the Qi River.
"Shi" (exegesis) refers to the process of spreading from above to below, termed "flow" (liu), while being free from any obstruction or blockage is termed "penetration" (tong).

Now, by employing this Sūtra of the True Mark, the unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma, for the sake of sentient beings in future generations, I ensure there shall be no obstruction; I cause all who have a karmic affinity during the final age to be moistened and nourished. This is because my compassion is pure and profound.
This text consists of two parts:

first, from this chapter onward, it clarifies how the Heavenly Kings protect the Dharma; it extracts the ritual offerings of Candracchattra and elucidates the benefits of such protection, thereby profoundly revealing the gravity of the virtue of propagating the sutra.
Second, from the "Entrustment Chapter" onwards, it clarifies how the Great Sage earnestly and solemnly entrusts [the teaching], ensuring that it must be propagated even during the final age.
This section consists of two parts:
first, the Heavenly King praises the propagation of the sutra; second, the Tathāgata confirms and completes his intention.
The first part consists of three sections:
first, praising the Dharma; second, praising the person; and third, making a vow.

Now, it is said that the Lord of Devas desires to protect and uphold the Great Canon and cultivate the sublime gateways. To possess this sutra and maintain the resolve for its universal nurturing is precisely to make an offering of the Dharma to the Dharmakāya.

As the *Vyākhyā* states: "Kapilavastu is the birthplace of his physical body, while Magadha is the birthplace of his Dharma-body; out of gratitude for these two, he dwells predominantly in these two countries to preach the Dharma."
"Between these two countries, in order to repay the Dharmakāya, [the Tathāgata] mostly preached the Dharma in the country of Magadha.
To protect and uphold [the Dharma] is itself the offering of the Dharma.

Furthermore, when Śakra, Lord of Devas, together with Brahmā, jointly requested him to preach the Dharma, the Tathāgata accepted their invitation and observed their capacities; knowing they were not yet capable of receiving the Mahāyāna, he instead opened the gates of the Hīnayāna teachings.
Now that the Hinayana teachings have been established, it is next appropriate to expound the Mahayana.
This present teaching on the inconceivable liberation is likewise a response to a former request.
As the *Śāstra* states: "The exposition of the *Prajñāpāramitā* was also a response to the requests of Brahmā and Śakra."
Having received this invitation, Śakra, Lord of Devas, joyfully undertook its protection.
If one were to say that because the Lord of Devas had attained the stage of Anāgāmin, he would not propagate the Great Teaching, this refers to what is called an Anāgāmin within the Tripiṭaka.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the Lord of Devas dwells in ten inconceivable Dharma-gates; how could he not be capable of propagating and disseminating this teaching?
Furthermore, as the Lord of Devas, he leads and transforms his subordinates, setting the highest example for all to follow.
Within this praise of the Dharma, one first praises the inconceivable function of liberation and subsequently praises the Dharma of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
Since there is no Dharma without which a person cannot be formed, and no person without which the Dharma cannot be manifested, it is necessary to praise both together.
The "Hundred Thousand Sutras" refers to the sutras of the initial teaching, such as the *Āgamas*.
Since the *Āgamas* also bestow predictions upon Maitreya, what prevents him from preaching the Dharma in the presence of Mañjuśrī?

Furthermore, within the Common Teaching (tongjiao) and the Distinct Teaching (biejiao), this Dharma-gate of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao)—the path of complete fulfillment whose essence and function are inconceivable—has never been heard; it was previously unheard of.
This praise of those among humans is twofold:
first, the explanation of the merit of hearing the sutra; second, the illustration by way of contrast of those who practice according to the Dharma.
"Closing off the various evil realms" refers to the goodness of cessation (*śamatha*), while "opening the gates of goodness" refers to the goodness of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
“Practice” (xing) is contemplation (guan), and “stopping” (zhi) is concentration (ding).
Herein, the two are distinguished according to cause and effect.

Regarding the phrase “being protected by the Buddha’s mindfulness,” this clarifies that one has cultivated the two causes of stopping and practice and is in deep accord with the principle; therefore, the Buddha bestows his protection upon that which is worthy of it, hence the expression “protective mindfulness.”
However, because the Buddha universally protects sentient beings, as long as they have no sores, poison cannot enter them.
If one cultivates the causes of this practice of *śamatha*, this constitutes the meaning of a "sore of faith," and one will likewise receive his protective mindfulness.
Regarding the contemplation of the mind: simply bringing the mind to rest through *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) is called awakening.

When all manner of deluded thoughts arise in agitation, one employs the two methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to observe them, ensuring that no further discursive thoughts can take root; in this way, the mind is constantly protected by awakening.

"Subduing the non-Buddhists" refers to subduing the two delusions of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi- and kleśa-saṃyojana*), as well as the paths of the sixty-two heterodox views and various false calculations.
Having attained the Bodhisattva path, one is able to subdue the Māra of afflictions, as previously explained, up to the four Māras, eight Māras, and ten Māras.

Therefore, the preceding text states: "Initially at the Bodhi tree, he subdued Māra by his power; having attained the extinction of ambrosia and perfected the path of enlightenment, he is now unimpeded regarding all dharmas, and his resolve is able to crush and subdue all non-Buddhists."

This refers to one who has resolved their mind to practice and study the perfect contemplation; upon entering the stage of initial resolve, they are immediately able to achieve the Way through the eight phases of enlightenment and are thus called a Buddha, subduing Māra and his host of resentful enemies, and delivering all beings.

"Cultivating the Buddha-way" refers to external transformation, whereby one manifests as a Buddha through the eight phases [of enlightenment]; meanwhile, within the inner mind, one cultivates the stages of the path within the Dharmakāya to fulfill the remaining Buddha-dharmas.
"Abiding securely in the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) is as explained in the section on the characteristics of the bodhimaṇḍa within the *Prabhāvyūha*.

"Treading in the footsteps of the Buddha" means practicing what the Buddhas have practiced and dwelling where the Buddhas have dwelt; that all Buddhas have come in this manner and I likewise have come in this manner—all such expressions are praises from those who have attained the neighboring fruit (*sāmantaka-phala*).
"Those who uphold and recite it"—from this point onward is the third aspiration for its widespread propagation.
Second, from "The Buddha said, 'Excellent! onward is the section that confirms and completes the three preceding segments of Śakra’s discourse.
First, an account of his praise of the Dharma; second, an account of his praise of the person; third, an account of his making of vows. Regarding the first:
“I rejoice in you” clarifies that this sutra is the inconceivable bodhi of the Buddhas of the three periods of time; this is the account of his praise of the Dharma.
The phrase "the inconceivable bodhi of the Buddhas of the three periods" refers precisely to the dharma of the true mark; it is by means of this true mark that the Buddhas attain bodhi.
The second section, from "If men and women receive and uphold this sutra, they shall be making offerings to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present," describes those who praise [the teaching].
This is divided into four parts:
first, the estimation of merit; second, the question; third, the answer; and fourth, the formal estimation.
Within the preceding analysis, there are two parts:
first, making offerings to the Buddha while he is present; second, erecting stupas after his parinirvāṇa.
Second, the question is as stated in the text.
Third, the response is twofold:
first, answering that [the offerings] are many; second, explaining why they cannot be exhausted.
In Mahāyāna sūtras, there are many comparisons showing that making offerings to the *saṃbhogakāya* does not equal those made to the *dharmakāya*.

Why is this? Such correct speech results in the merit of the birth-body (*janmakāya*), which neither moves nor issues forth; whereas the merit of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) can both move and issue forth.
Because it brings about transcendence from birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is said that such merit does not tend toward *bodhi*.
Second, that which can lead toward Bodhi:

with respect to reality, it is called the "revealing cause" (*vyañjana-hetu*); with respect to other things, it is called the "producing cause" (*janana-hetu*). The producing cause is the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*); merit is immovable, does not issue forth, and does not reach Bodhi, for its qualities are subject to exhaustion.
Regarding reality, it is the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*); "reality" refers to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and the revealing cause is that which illuminates it.
Being in accord with the true mark, one is able to progress toward Bodhi; its inexhaustible merit is equal to space and the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
How could it be measured by the limited dharmas that are previously mentioned—meritorious, immovable, and non-emergent?
Making offerings to the *saṃbhoga-kāya* is called a cause for birth; it does not lead to Bodhi.
Making offerings to the Dharma-body is truly called the "cause of realization," for it enables one to proceed toward Bodhi.
Therefore, its merit cannot be measured or limited.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Giving while abiding in signs is like a person entering darkness, who sees nothing."
"Practicing giving without dwelling on signs is like a person with eyes who, when the sun shines brightly, can see all manner of forms.
The empty space of the eastern direction is inconceivable; the southern, western, and northern directions are likewise difficult to fathom."
The Dharma-offering is supreme.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the mother of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
If the mother falls ill, her children are filled with sorrow."
If the Dharma of true reality were not extensively applied to sentient beings, then, in consideration of sentient beings, one would speak of the "sickness" of true reality.
If one were to offer worship to only a single Buddha, there would be no merit regarding other Buddhas.
If one slanders a single Buddha, there is no offense regarding the other Buddhas.
If one makes offerings to the Buddha-mother, the mark of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one simultaneously attains merit before all Buddhas of the three periods of time and the ten directions.
If one slanders the Mother of the Buddhas, one becomes an enemy to all Buddhas.
Therefore, it is said of the Lord of Devas: "The Bodhi of all Buddhas is born from this; the characteristics of Bodhi are immeasurable."
In the fourth correct measure (*pramāṇa*), he also describes the aforementioned praise of the two practices of faith and dharma:
"Hearing this inconceivable sūtra and having faith and understanding" describes the accomplishment of the person who practices through faith.
"Practicing merit in abundance" refers back to the aforementioned practice of the Dharma.
Third, it describes his vow to propagate, uphold, and disseminate this sutra.
From the passage "In the past, under the Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja... onwards, the text consists of four parts:

First, clarifying the causes and conditions for the past dharma-offering; second, clarifying the identity of Prince Candracchattra; third, correlating the past with the present; and fourth, concluding the commentary to establish the perfection of the exposition.
Regarding the causal conditions, the text is divided into three parts:

first, it clarifies that there is a Buddha; second, it clarifies that there is a royal decree instructing the sons to perform offerings; third, it clarifies that the sons respectfully received the decree and proclaimed its practice.
Second, from the passage "The king had one son named Candracchattra" onwards, the text consists of nine sections:

first, the prince sits alone in contemplation seeking a supreme offering; second, he is startled awake by a voice from the sky; third, he continues to inquire about the supreme Dharma; fourth, a deity exhorts him to question the Tathāgata; fifth, he goes to invite the Buddha; sixth, the Buddha provides the explanation; seventh, hearing the Dharma, he attains the *anulomikī-kṣānti*; eighth, the Buddha grants him a prophecy for protecting the Dharma; ninth, he leaves the household life to practice the Way as an offering to the Dharma.
Regarding the teaching for the sixth Buddha, the text is divided into two parts:
first, the elucidation of the supreme and wondrous Dharma;
second, from the passage "If one hears such sutras and believes and understands them," the elucidation of the mind of making offerings.
Within the supreme Dharma, there are four parts:
first, from the words "The Buddha said" onwards, it clarifies the most wondrous Dharma;
second, regarding "the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas," it discusses the causes in terms of the Dharma.
3. From "capable of causing sentient beings to sit at the site of enlightenment" onwards, this discusses the fruit in terms of the Dharma.
4. From "all Buddhas and worthy sages" onwards, this refers to that which is praised by the Buddhas, thereby authenticating its cause and fruit.
Now, the first point is explained.

Regarding the phrase "the profound sūtras that have been taught": although the principle of the true mark (dharmatā) is neither deep nor shallow, for the sake of those with two types of capacities—those who perceive depth and those who perceive shallowness—it is spoken of as being both deep and shallow within that which is neither deep nor shallow.
The shallow refers to the sūtras of the Tripitaka, both general and specific; the profound refers to the teaching of the ultimate Perfection, and is thus called the "profound sūtra.
The characteristics of the profound sūtra are precisely as described above by the Great Being regarding the meaning of contemplating the true mark of the body; this is the profound sūtra of purity.
"Difficult to believe" means that it is as if there were a great thousand-fold sutra scroll within a single mote of dust, yet no one would believe it.
The principle of true reality (bhūtatathatā) resides solely within the mind; there is no need for the trouble of seeking it afar.
Because it is not recognized despite being near at hand, it is said to be "difficult to believe.
As for "difficult to receive": if there is something received, there is something practiced; if there is nothing received, there is nothing practiced.
If one accepts and believes in the true nature (*dharmatā*), one is able to practice; if one does not accept and believe in it, one cannot cultivate it.

"Subtle and wondrous" (*sūkṣma-adbhuta*) is another name for the inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*); it is also the subtle and wondrous self and dharmas of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), which are wondrous and difficult to conceive.
"Pure and unstained" means it is not defiled by the three kinds of views and afflictions; it is like space, devoid of both purity and impurity.

"That which cannot be attained through thought or discrimination" means it cannot be reached by the movement of thoughts or the operation of conceptualization; rather, through non-thought and non-discrimination, one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), a state that cannot be fathomed even by those who rely on the provisional or specific expedient means of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*).
2. Clarifying the Cause.

Regarding the phrase "encompassed by the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas," this clarifies that the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas consists of the prior practice of hearing and retaining [the teachings].

It is called a "treasury" (kośa) because it is a secret treasury of the three virtues that is neither vertical nor horizontal and has no accumulation; it contains all phenomena, which all enter therein.

Regarding the "Dhāraṇī Seal": *dhāraṇī* means that which can obstruct and sustain; it sustains the good so it is not lost and obstructs evil so it does not arise. This non-arising and non-loss is what is called a "seal" (*mudrā*).

"Attaining the stage of non-retrogression" means that one maintains all wholesome dharmas without any falling back; it is also the station of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) from which there is no regression.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Accomplishing the six perfections":
to skillfully discern that which accords with bodhi means to be well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena while remaining unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
"Supreme among all sutras" means that it stands above all sutras within the Tripitaka and across both the common and distinct teachings.
"Entering great compassion" refers to giving rise to unconditioned compassion (*nirālambana-maitrī*), such as the thirty-two kinds of compassion mentioned above.
"Free from all Māras" means being free from the eight Māras, the ten Māras, and so forth.

It also means being free from the three kinds of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). The celestial Māra belongs to birth and death and causes one to transmigrate through craving; because the Bodhisattva is free from this, he is said to be "free from Māras."

"Furthermore, regarding 'wrong views,' this refers to all views among the three types of skillful means; everything prior to this is termed wrong view, and within the true nature (dharmatā), one is entirely free from these various views."

Regarding "conforming to causes and conditions": the nature of causes and conditions is itself the true mark (*dharmatā*). To conform to this true mark, one deeply contemplates all phenomena; possessing the two types of emptiness—of birth and of phenomena—the cause and condition is precisely the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Taking the true mark as the object, one cultivates the samādhi of the two types of emptiness.
Third, clarification by way of the fruit:
"Sitting at the site of enlightenment" means that if one can thus perform the perfect contemplation of the true reality (*dharmatā*), entering into the *prajñā* of *nirvāṇa* is termed "abiding."

When abiding in the stage of "Initiating the Mind," one is immediately able to achieve enlightenment through the eight phases and manifest as a Buddha according to conditions; therefore, it is said that "at the very moment of first initiating the mind, one sits upon the site of enlightenment.
As for "turning the wheel of Dharma," this refers to the three teachings—Perfect, Sudden, and Gradual—and thus it is called "turning the wheel of Dharma."
"Devas and nāgas together offer praise" means that having sat at the site of enlightenment and become a Buddha, one benefits all beings, and is revered by humans and devas.
"Entering the treasury of the Buddha-dharma" means dwelling securely within the secret treasury for all sons [of the Buddha].
The Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) subsumes forty-two levels of worthy sages, while the Partial Teaching (Pianjiao) subsumes twenty-seven; both are the treasury of the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding "all-encompassing wisdom," it means to cause all those who receive either the partial or the perfect teaching to enter the Buddha-wisdom.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Such persons as these, I now likewise cause to enter the Buddha-wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "expounding the path practiced by all bodhisattvas," bodhisattvas take the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as their path; although they may receive other teachings, they ultimately lead [all beings] back to the true mark.

Regarding the phrase "in accordance with the meaning of the true nature" (dharmatā): whether cause or fruit, nothing can be separated from the true nature; it is based upon this true nature that the teachings of the partial and the perfect are distinguished.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "If there are those of profound wisdom, for them this Dharma is taught," which refers to the teaching on the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

It further states: "If they do not understand this Dharma, then within the other profound teachings of the Tathāgata, they are instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened," which refers to the teaching of the partial and gradual [vehicles], proclaiming non-self, abiding in emptiness, and cessation, and so forth.

Regarding "able to save those who violate the precepts": within the teachings of the provisional means (*upāya*), all that deviates from the perfect ultimate is termed "violating the precepts"; however, once one enters the Perfect [Teaching], there are no longer any faults of the provisional means.
Furthermore, within the Hīnayāna, those who have violated grave precepts have no means for repentance;

however, in the Mahāyāna, one can wash away such transgressions through the correct contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda-samyag-darśana*). Therefore, it is said that [the Mahāyāna] saves all who have broken the prohibitions.
Regarding "frightening all Māras and non-Buddhists": because one has severed both the mind of craving and the mind of views, there are no five fears.
Fourth, being praised by all Buddhas.
One immediately accords with the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), such that the initial resolve can itself bring about Buddhahood; therefore, this is what all the sages praise and extol.
"Turning one's back on birth-and-death" means turning one's back on the three kinds of birth-and-death.
"To manifest nirvāṇa" means to demonstrate the hundred phrases of liberation.
"That which is spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions" means that all Buddhas, following the same path, collectively proclaim this true reality (dharmatā).
Second, regarding the phrase "if one hears such sūtras as these," this clarifies the mind of making offerings.
This is divided into two parts:
first, clarifying practice through faith; second, clarifying practice through the Dharma.

If, upon hearing the teaching of the Dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one immediately gives rise to understanding within that hearing and attains unimpeded penetration, this is called the mind of offering through practice by faith (*śraddhācaryā*).

If, whether hearing it or not, one practices according to the Dharma, contemplates the emptiness of causes and conditions, severs all false views, perceives the principle of the true mark, and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*), this is called the mind of offering through practice of the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*).
Furthermore, this is explained by means of the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).
That phenomena are ultimately unapprehendable is called "reliance on the meaning" (*arthapratisaraṇa*).

Since the teachings of the Buddhas are fundamentally intended to suit the capacities of sentient beings and must not be dogmatically clung to, one does not rely on the letter (*na vyañjanapratisaraṇa*).
Consciousness is a phenomenon possessed of afflictions; therefore, one must not rely upon consciousness.
Sūtras of expedient meaning are teachings of threefold skillful means; because they are not ultimate reality, they cannot be relied upon.
Sūtras of definitive meaning are what may be relied upon.
Human beings possess a physical body; therefore, they cannot be relied upon.
One who reaches the very source of ignorance knows that all things are originally unarisen, and thus ultimately there is no cessation.
To contemplate that causes and conditions are inexhaustible is to realize that delusion is like space—incapable of being exhausted.
Seventh, regarding attaining the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*) upon hearing the Dharma, this consists of two parts:
first, the benefit of attaining the patience of compliance; second, the offering of gratitude by untying the precious robe as a reward.

If one explains "gentle forbearance" according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), "gentle" means gentle subduing; this refers to the stage of the Iron Wheel during the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), wherein the six sense faculties are purified. If one gives rise to true illumination and enters into principle, one immediately attains the forbearance of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Making offerings by disrobing consists of two parts:
first, the act of making offerings; second, generating the aspiration to practice the Dharma-offering.
One requests that majestic spiritual power be bestowed so that enemies may be subdued and the Great Dharma may be proclaimed and spread.

Eighth, regarding the prophecy of Buddhahood: it merely records that his descendants will be those who propagate the Dharma and protect it, having a karmic affinity with sentient beings and being able to establish the Great Dharma; I have not yet seen any text recording him as one who will become a Buddha.
Discussing this from a broader perspective, one should also clarify that [the concept of] "leaving me" (*niḥsaraṇa*) has not yet appeared in the *Qiwen* (Analects).
Ninth, clarifying the practice of the dharma-offering through leaving home and practicing the Way.
This consists of two parts:
first, clarifying the protection of the Dharma by those who have left the household life; second, clarifying the extent of those transformed.
That one million people resolve their minds on Bodhi is based on what is taught in the Perfect Teaching (Ekanaya).
Fourteen nayutas of beings resolved their minds upon the two vehicles; this was done by employing skillful means to entice and guide them.
By using these two methods—the perfect and the partial—to lead and benefit sentient beings, it constitutes the offering of the Dharma.
Third, the conclusion correlating the ancient and the present is as in the text.

Fourth, the exposition confirms the aforementioned aspiration to propagate the sutra, maintain it, and proclaim it, while also ensuring that all those who practice the sutra are entirely harmonious and at peace.
14. Chapter on the Entrustment (10). Explanation of the Chapter on the Entrustment. This chapter is the second within the section on the circulation [of the sutra].
The preceding section clarified the vows made by Śakra Devendra to propagate the sutra; this section distinguishes the entrustment issued from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata.
"Entrustment" (*shuku*) has the meaning of "to hand over.
It refers to entrusting the reality-dharma of signlessness to those who shall propagate and protect it.
"Burden" (*ru*) has the meaning of "to carry" through toil and hardship.
Now, taking this Great Dharma as his sole responsibility, he causes external difficulties to be dispelled and internal practice to be proclaimed and realized; therefore, it is called "entrustment.
According to the text, there are three parts:
first, the Buddha’s entrustment to Maitreya; second, the entrustment to Ānanda; third, the great assembly’s joy upon hearing the sutra.
The entrustment to Maitreya consists of two parts:
first, the Buddha’s entrustment; second, Maitreya’s reception of the mandate.
Within the Buddha’s entrustment, there are three sections:
First, the formal entrustment of this sutra; second, its explanation; third, the discernment of its gains and losses.
Within the formal entrustment, there are two parts:
first, the entrustment of the honored sutra; second, the command to protect it through supernatural powers.

Regarding the phrase "that which was accumulated over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas is entrusted to you": according to the explanation in the Tripiṭaka by Kātyāyana, it clarifies that one practices and studies the Buddha-dharma for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and during the hundred eons [of the final stage], one plants the marks [of a Buddha] so that the path of Buddhahood manifests before one.
These are the shallow and proximate teachings of the Tripitaka and the Hīnayāna; the number of kalpas required for their cultivation, study, and practice is small.
If one examines this meaning according to the *Śāstra*, the Buddha-dharma is immeasurable—how could it be fully mastered through what is learned over three asaṃkhyeya-kalpas?

Only after passing through immeasurable billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and practicing the profound Dharma-gates of the Buddha-dharma, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, can one fulfill the profound and wondrous Mahāyāna; for this reason, the kalpas of training are also many.
Now, it is said that [this] was practiced over immeasurable kalpas; thus we know that this sublime scripture of the Mahāyāna is entrusted to Maitreya.
Second, the phrase "you should use your supernatural powers to proclaim it widely so that it shall never be interrupted" is an injunction to protect and preserve it.

The reason this Great Dharma is entrusted specifically to Maitreya is precisely to clarify that he shall succeed to the position of the Honored One; his wisdom and severance of afflictions are perfect and complete, he possesses the karmic affinity with sentient beings, and he is fully endowed with supernatural powers capable of propagating and protecting the teaching so that it shall not be interrupted.
If sentient beings of the final age have long been removed from the sages, not only will their spiritual faculties be darkened and turbid, but obstacles will also arise in abundance.
Just as places where many treasures reside are inevitably rife with enemies and bandits, so too when the Way is lofty, demonic forces flourish, and hindrances and difficulties come into being.

If one does not obtain the secret assistance of the power of the Sages, external obstacles will invade and oppress; yet if one is graced by the addition of their divine light, it shall cause the mind to open and penetrate.

When internal causes and external conditions are thus harmonized, the Jewel of the Dharma will never be interrupted; for this reason, I command that the power of my spiritual faculties be bestowed upon those sentient beings who are capable of hearing it.

In this regard, one should cite the case of Upagupta, who was harassed by Māra, causing countless people to fail to attain awakening; consequently, those who were to be converted were deluded by Māra, so Upagupta used his supernormal powers to bind Māra. The benefits gained by all who heard the sutras thereafter were beyond measure. This, too, likely reflects the intention of using supernormal powers to propagate the sutras.
Regarding the second interpretation, from the passage "Why is this? In future ages... onwards, there are two parts:
first, clarifying that even in the final age there are those with the capacity to attain the Way; second, clarifying that failing to hear this sutra results in the loss of wholesome benefits.

It was explained previously that in the final age, there are those with the potential to attain the Way; however, because the conditions for awakening differ among ordinary beings, some gain benefit by seeing the Dharma King in person, while others awaken through longing after his passing. Thus, the Sūtra says: "For those who should be saved by means of extinction, he manifests extinction. This is like the case of a mad son: though the father is actually alive, he says he has died and leaves behind various fragrant medicines. When the son feels remorse and regret, he takes the medicine and is immediately healed.

If one does not see the Buddha, one should reproach oneself for a lack of diligence and feel shame at not having encountered the Buddha’s era; through this, one enters the Path and attains liberation from afflictions and delusions.

Thus, one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, out of one hundred thousand who left the household life, ninety thousand attained the Way. One should know that the spiritual capacities of those following the Buddha are likewise immeasurable.
In this regard, one should cite the case of Kuṭadanta, who, while the Buddha was still alive, sought to go forth from the household life and searched for a teacher of wisdom equal to Śāriputra.
When the Buddha told him that such a person could not be found, he immediately withdrew and returned to the teachings of the non-Buddhists.
The Buddha prophesied for him that the conditions for this person to attain the Way would lie after his own parinirvāṇa.

Later, he became a disciple of Ānanda; he delivered immeasurable people and led those who attained the Way to number as many as the sands of the Ganges. The people of the time revered and praised him as a "Buddha Without Form."

This explains that in future ages, among devas, humans, nāgas, and ghosts, there will be those who possess the conditions for generating the aspiration for enlightenment; since they delight in the Great Dharma and will certainly attain liberation, one must not fail to propagate such a sublime teaching so that they may hear it.

Second, regarding the statement, "If one does not hear this sutra, it will be a great loss": if one hears only the provisional teachings of the Tripiṭaka, one loses the benefit of the Great Vehicle’s "poisonous drum."

The *Samantabhadra-dhyāna Sūtra* states: "When five hundred years remain before the Dharma is extinguished, if one single-mindedly cultivates this Lotus Samādhi, one will immediately attain the purification of the six sense faculties."

Thus we know that even in the final age there can be those with the capacity to enter the Mahāyāna; if they do not hear this sutra, they will forever lose the benefit of the Dharma, and therefore it must be proclaimed and disseminated.
Third, from the passage "Bodhisattvas have two characteristics" onwards, is the discrimination between gain and loss.
This consists of two parts:
first, distinguishing between gain and loss; second, extensively citing errors for explanation.
Within the section on gain and loss, there are three subsections:
First, the presentation of the characteristics; second, the brief explanation; third, the explanation by way of persons.
If this pertains to the Tripitaka Teaching, it mostly elucidates all phenomena through the distinct phenomena of causes and conditions.
Those who rely on this for study are persons who have newly resolved their minds [on enlightenment].
The distinct and perfect teachings of the various Mahāyāna sūtras are without reliance or dependence, transcending all mind and consciousness.
What is called a "profound sutra" is this: that desire itself is the Way, and so too are hatred and delusion.
Within these three dharmas, all Buddha-dharmas are fully contained; if one seeks Bodhi apart from these three dharmas, it would be like [seeking] heaven while separated from the earth.
This refers to the ability to penetrate the true nature of these three poisons as being ungraspable, like empty space, yet capable of giving rise to all Buddha-dharmas.
That sutra states: "One who deeply penetrates this Dharma does not violate the precepts;
one who deeply penetrates this Dharma also does not cling to non-obstruction.

Many practitioners claim that the three poisons are the Way, yet by clinging to this non-obstruction, they destroy right precepts and right view. How can such a person be said to have penetrated the nature of the three poisons?
One who attains this is neither defiled nor attached; such a person truly accords with the intent of the sutras.

The Dharma of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is neither cause nor fruit, yet it is spoken of as cause and fruit. Therefore, it is said that some things are causes but not fruits, such as the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu); others are fruits but not causes, such as Great Nirvana (mahāparinirvāṇa).

Now, the nature of the three poisons is neither cause nor effect, yet it is spoken of as cause and effect. To speak of them as cause is to say that the three poisons are the Dharma which fully possesses all Buddha-dharmas; to speak of them as effect is to say that all sentient beings are eternally in the state of quiescence and cannot be further extinguished.

If one can hear this teaching on the two paths of cause and effect within desire—without disparagement or attachment—and gives rise to no fear, you should know that this person is a bodhisattva who has long practiced.

In this way, such a bodhisattva delights only in the profound Dharma of true reality, no longer taking pleasure in flowery rhetoric, literary elegance, or ornate embellishments to explain the fundamental principles of the Dharma.
Inferring from this, one knows that he is a bodhisattva who has long practiced.

If one delights in verbal eloquence, such that the words spoken are ornate with literary flourishes and refined phrasing, they may indeed please the listener for the moment; yet in the end, it is like adding water to milk—this is not the practice of those who have long cultivated the true nature (dharmatā).
Judging by this, one knows that he is a bodhisattva who has newly resolved his mind.
He is like a person of the present day who, through frequent calculation and analytical questioning and answering, claims to have eyebrows and eyes.
Furthermore, having heard the Mahāyāna teaching on non-attachment, they consider it to be mere vacuity and fail to give rise to faith or joy.

In this regard, one should cite the case where Sudatta requested the Buddha to preach the Dharma for an elderly woman; the woman turned her back toward the Buddha in all ten directions, and the Buddha manifested his form in all ten directions, yet she still refused to believe and accept it.

Later, Ānanda manifested as a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) to skillfully guide and receive them; their hearts were filled with joy and they developed faith and submission, returning to the Buddha to hear the Dharma and cultivate the Path.

Why is this so? It is because in the past, when this śrāmaṇera’s upādhyāya spoke many words regarding the profound reality (*dharmatā*), he could not understand them upon hearing them and did not give rise to faith or admiration.
Upāli taught by means of causes, conditions, and the characteristics of dharmas to instruct others; his listeners' minds accorded with these matters, and they developed a fond attachment to them.
For this reason, although they now hear my words, they do not penetrate their hearts. Their spiritual capacity lies with Ānanda, who will turn his mind toward the Path.
Although Ānanda may cause others to give rise to faith, they will ultimately attain the Way only by relying upon me.
Thus we know that the method of literary embellishment is merely a condition for pleasing the ear, not the ultimate principle.
Skillful means are introduced as a gradual progression toward awakening, and thus they are not discussed here.
It is the profound Dharma of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) that serves as the essential for attaining the Way; this is what is meant by the analogy of the "poisoned drum."

Based on this, it clarifies two types of persons: those who have newly resolved their minds and those who have long practiced; one can discern their success or failure simply by observing whether their words are ornate or direct.
Second, from the passage "Furthermore, there are two dharmas regarding sutras never heard before," onwards, it extensively enumerates what is erroneous.
This consists of two parts:

the first clarifies two dharmas to explain why those who are newly trained should not slander or stay far away [from this teaching]; the second clarifies two dharmas to explain why those who have long practiced should not treat it with contempt or grasp at its signs.

Regarding the previous mention of those who disparage and do not associate [with the teaching]: herein, the Bodhisattva Priyarūpa speaks only of the Dharma of the true mark (*dharmatā*), clarifying that within all phenomena there exists the nature of peace and bliss (*sukha*).

Jayaśas, having received the Dharma from the Tripitaka Master, was perfect in his deportment and observed the dhūta practices with unimpeachable discipline. Suddenly hearing what Nandika had said, which contradicted the teachings he had studied, he was greatly astonished and alarmed. He reviled and slandered him, refusing to believe or accept it, and immediately performed the ritual of formal expulsion against this Nandika.
Even the act of expulsion constitutes a transgression that leads immediately to hell.

This refers to those who have newly resolved their minds [to attain enlightenment] but, having received the provisional teachings, slander the Prajñāpāramitā and do not believe in the profound sūtras.
Such individuals must be understood according to the depth or shallowness of their capacity.
Second, at times they do not slander this Dharma, yet they lack a heart of respect and intimacy toward those who uphold the Dharma, or at other times they speak of their faults and evils.
This, too, is a loss of the [proper] characteristics; none of these are those who have long practiced the taming of the mind.
Second, the manifestation of arrogance and grasping at signs:

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that if a bodhisattva gives rise to a contemptuous attitude toward a fellow practitioner who has newly resolved their mind on awakening, thinking, "This person knows nothing," [this is a fault].
By giving rise to this single thought of pride, one instead destroys the merit of countless kalpas and must once again undergo retribution.
Only when that karmic retribution is exhausted can one finally resolve to cultivate the mind, thereby restoring one's virtuous conduct of today.

Speaking from this perspective, a mind of contempt is a grave transgression; it not only obstructs the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), but one will further incur the calamity of retribution. Therefore, it is specifically identified as wrong.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, although they understand the profound Dharma, engage in conceptualization by grasping at signs regarding the stages and gradual progression; by grasping at signs and conceptualizing, they give rise to fixed notions, which is again a state of mental agitation and not the ultimate path.
Why is this? Because the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is pure and serene, such that it does not possess even a single characteristic, let alone two.
It is beyond words and cannot be demonstrated; those who speak of it lose its principle, and those who demonstrate it deviate from its essence.
With a mind of such conceptual discrimination and deliberation, how can one accord with the Dharma of quiescence?

Whether it be the doctrines of three times, four times, or five times; the "half" and "full"; or the four schools and six schools—these are all names and categories established by Dharma masters who have explored and gathered the intent of the sutras. While their judgments and explanations of the various gates of meaning may be deemed reasonable, they are none of them the singular, ultimate art of the wordless.

The true intention of our school is not like this: the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm is in dark resonance with the ultimate reality, and we do not wish for the mind to be at variance or in conflict with sentient beings. Although these four teachings are established, they are intended solely to provide a comprehensive explanation of the texts of the various sutras and to exhaustively reach their source; ultimately, one does not dogmatically adhere to the meaning of the four teachings.

At times there may be three teachings, two teachings, one teaching, no teaching, or eight teachings; their appearance and disappearance are not constant, and their number is indeterminate. They transform with sovereign ease according to the needs of individuals for explanation and interpretation, ensuring that this mind does not harbor even the slightest attachment, nor allow one to cling to one's own views while deeming the understandings of others to be incorrect.
If one acts in this manner, it is merely a matter of contentious debate and not a method for entering the Way.
Master Nanyue spoke a verse: "When a dog sees its reflection, it fights; it refuses to stop fighting and eventually dies of thirst," and so forth.
This present selection is based on this distinction, not on the intention of practicing the Path.
However, because the mental paths of practitioners differ, although there are various types, they do not exceed two modes of cultivation:
first, the noble teaching of the Dharma; second, the noble silence.

One must recognize the appropriate means and skillful methods regarding one's own mind; if it is stagnant or obstructed, and one cannot open the mind through the path of silence, one should listen to the Dharma or associate with virtuous friends who can open the human mind.
Alternatively, one may seek the principles of the teachings within the sūtras and thereby awaken this mind.

At times, however, listening to the Dharma may cause agitation such that one cannot achieve stillness and concentration; if seeking the meaning of the sūtras becomes a source of entanglement and one realizes that mental cultivation is yielding no profound benefit, one should immediately close the eyes, compose the body, and settle the mind within the path of silence.

Whether speaking or remaining silent, one should discipline the mind; examining the coarse and making it harmonious, one should skillfully master giving and taking, and discern the true from the false. At such times, one may cultivate tranquility as appropriate; at such times, one may cultivate wisdom as appropriate.
For example, heaven and earth regulate yin and yang through alternating sun and rain, whereby all things are able to grow.

If there were constant rain without sunshine, seeds would rot; if there were constant sunshine without rain, sprouts and shoots would wither; in neither case could all things be produced. It must be properly balanced before it can be beneficial.

If the practitioner is thus, remaining in one-sided silence, they will sink into dullness and be obstructed by darkness; if they employ only conceptual discrimination, various views will arise in competition. In this case, the provisional and the ultimate do not harmonize, and the Teacher does not manifest.
One who skillfully applies their efforts enters the Way with sudden clarity; seeing a flash of lightning at night, they enter the sublime Dharma.
This is how those who study the Way properly discern right from wrong and distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Just as seasonal rain falls repeatedly and the five grains grow repeatedly, so too does the rain of Dharma fall repeatedly and wholesome dharmas grow repeatedly."
"If one does not repeatedly discipline oneself through what the Noble Ones have declared as noble silence, the grain of true reality will not grow.
If one is biasedly attached to knowledge and views, one will ultimately never enter into the principle."
Therefore it is said: "Though one may read a hundred thousand sutras, if false views grow long with all manner of errors, the poison of self-attachment will be exceedingly fierce.
Though one claims to carry the eternal child within, a barren woman will never give birth."

If, upon hearing the Dharma taught by the Noble Ones, one immediately awakens to it, attaining thorough penetration and sovereign clarity regarding all phenomena, this is called "practice through faith" (śraddhānusārin).

If, upon hearing it, one does not attain awakening, but through the four foundations of mindfulness contemplates deeply, penetratingly, and illuminatingly until reaching its very depths, this is called "practice through Dharma" (dharmānusārin).

Within noble silence there are also those who practice by faith and those who practice by Dharma; likewise, when practicing dhyāna-contemplation, if one contemplates a single object, it then penetrates all objects universally, the mind-ground becomes clear and bright without even a trace of doubt or obstruction, like the wind in the sky—this is called practice by Dharma.

If, when applying oneself to contemplation, one cannot attain awakening, and despite exerting effort with sincere devotion, one remains repeatedly ignorant; yet, if through hearing from a spiritual friend or seeing it in a scripture, one suddenly becomes as clear as a cloudless sky, with inner and outer completely transparent—this is a person who proceeds by means of faith.

Furthermore, transforming what has been received into speech—acting according to what one has heard—is the noble silence; hearing in accordance with what one has practiced is the noble teaching of the Dharma.
First, regarding "Maitreya addressed the Buddha": this precisely clarifies his receiving of the command and the imperial decree.
This is divided into three parts:
first, Maitreya receives the mandate; second, the various bodhisattvas receive the mandate; third, the four kings receive the mandate.
Regarding the first, there are two sections:
First, receiving the mandate; second, the exposition of its fulfillment.
Within the first, there are two parts:
first, receiving the sincere mandate; second, receiving the exhortatory mandate.
From the passage "Receiving and upholding the Tathāgata for incalculable kalpas" onwards, this constitutes the acceptance of the exhortation.
Within this section, there are two parts corresponding to the two types mentioned above:
first, the acceptance of the intent of the sutra’s general teaching; second, the acceptance of the intent of protection through supernatural power.

In this context, it is stated: "One establishes [the teaching] by means of the power of mindfulness. If one relies on the Practice of Peaceful Conduct (sukha-vihāra), whatever Dharma is taught will accord with emptiness and augment that power of mindfulness.

It is also like when a person preaches the Dharma: while they are deliberating upon only one or two points, by the time they reach the moment of speaking, they perceive three or five layers of meaning.

This may be because their mind has entered the gateway of the doctrine and is thus able to discern it clearly, or it may be that the profound void assists their mindfulness by bestowing its empowerment upon them.
Second, the Buddha’s confirmation and fulfillment.
Second, the various bodhisattvas receive the mandate and make their vows.
Third, the Four Kings receive the mandate and make their vows.

Second, regarding the command for Ānanda to proclaim the sutra: Ānanda’s conduct remained within the Lesser Vehicle, and he had attained the body of an Arhat; once he entered the state of nirvana without remainder, his karmic existence would have been forever exhausted. How, then, could he have received and proclaimed this Great Sutra?

This *manasikāra* (mental attention) ensures that [the teachings] are transmitted and upheld without error; thus, for the purpose of compiling the Dharma-piṭaka, he was commanded to proclaim the sūtra.

If we speak according to his fundamental capacity, he is able to uphold all the Buddha-dharmas of the ten directions; how could it be possible that he would allow them to be extinguished and unable to proclaim this sūtra?
This is divided into three parts:
first, the Buddha’s command; second, the inquiry regarding the name of the sutra; and third, the Buddha’s response concerning the two names.
The essential purport is none other than the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) universally subsumes all phenomena; to grasp its essential point is to grasp all phenomena.
Third, when the great assembly heard this sutra, they were all filled with great joy.

*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-brief-commentary*, Scroll Ten. On the twenty-ninth day of the third month in the third year of the Jōwa era, I, [the scribe], applied my brush like the *nǎo* grass of Jiangnan to transcribe the "Go-kyō" (Gansu-script) from the mountain peaks. Although I could not decline the fragrant command of the diligent lecture assembly, I still fear that I may only be able to follow in the footsteps of the wondrous legacy of our Gate Master.

In the second year of the Genwa era, the year of Bingchen, during the first ten days of the ninth month, I transcribed this work. It is stated that these ten volumes of the *Ryaku-sho* follow the ancient *kuten* punctuation system.
When the new edition from Edo was sent to the Yamato region, the monk-official Seiken of the Chiku-in Hall at Sannomonzeki respectfully commanded me not to decline the task despite its difficulties.
From the second month of last spring until the fourteenth day of this month, the task of applying vermilion was completed.

As the "Inquiry into Illness" chapter and those preceding it were not present in the original scripture, I have consulted the oral tradition and inferred the phrasing of the original text. Should there be any discrepancies in the textual divisions, future scholars may compare them against the original scripture when they encounter them.

I had originally intended to have the beginners among the assembly at this mountain monastery transcribe it with vermilion ink for my own preservation; however, as I suddenly passed away in Wajū and was sent to Edo, I was unable to verify and reconcile the text.
Mongqi was frequently ill and harassed by others, which caused him to make errors; thus, there are instances of mistakes.

Furthermore, regarding the disordered passages within the eighth fascicle, I have verified them against the original draft; two folios (dīng) of the text have been set aside, and you may examine them closely upon seeing them later.
Recorded by Kaitō on the twenty-first day of the sixth month in the eighteenth year of Kōei (1641), at the Secluded Pavilion in the inner quarters of Rinsen-in.
